In his remarks, Governor Nwifuru said that the number one mission for Ndigbo in 2027 elections was to re-elect President Tinubu, describing the APC as the only political party with a clear and identifiable manifesto capable of sustaining the country’s development and truly advancing the course of Ndigbo.

He dismissed suggestions of his involvement in any political coalition, stressing that his loyalty remained with the APC, urging urged supporters to vote for APC candidates at all levels in the 2027 elections.

Similarly, Soludo, represented by his Deputy, Dr Gilbert Ibezim, said the South-East had a responsibility to support Tinubu’s re-election in appreciation of his administration’s achievements, adding that the region stood to benefit more from continued collaboration with the federal government.

Also speaking, the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Hon. Benjamin Kalu, urged Igbos to embrace political inclusion by supporting Tinubu’s re-election.

Kalu said the Igbo had not produced a president of Nigeria in the past 60 years, and was therefore not party to any one-term arrangement for the Presidency of Igbo extraction by anybody.

He, however, stressed that the Igbo needed to to strengthen its political alliances across the nation to actualise a full two-term Igbo presidency in the near future.

He recalled that Tinubu, while serving as governor of Lagos State, maintained cordial relationships with Igbos and included them in his cabinet.

He commended the Tinubu administration for establishing the South East Development Commission (SEDC).

He described it as a major step towards addressing the region’s developmental challenges.

Meanwhile, addressing the rally, the First Lady conveyed President Tinubu’s goodwill message and urged Nigerians not to be discouraged by the economic challenges associated with the President’s reforms, insisting that the country was moving towards prosperity.

She likened the process to childbirth, noting that although the period of labour could be painful, it ultimately led to delivery.

“Mr. President said I should greet everyone. We have done reforms and we are now in prosperity. Don’t allow anyone to deceive you. The worst is over. We are stepping into prosperity,” she said.

The First Lady described the empowerment initiative as an indication of the APC government’s commitment to translating its promises into practical interventions, noting that the party was combining political mobilisation with economic support.

The First Lady urged the women to mobilise support for President Tinubu and APC candidates in the forthcoming 2027 general elections, asking them to hold political aspirants accountable for their records of empowerment and development interventions.

Other dignitaries at the massive rally were Wife of the Vice President, Mrs Nana Shettima; wife of the Senate President, Mrs. Uloma Akpabio; wives of the South East governors; Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Doris Uzoka-Anite; Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr. Kingsley Udeh (SAN); and Minister of Women Affairs and Social Development, Mrs Imaan Sulaiman-Ibrahim.

Also present were the APC Deputy National Chairman (South), Dr Ben Nwoye; National Women Leader of the APC and Director-General of the Women Wing of the Presidential Campaign Council, Dr Mary Alile-Idele; South-East Zonal Woman Leader of the APC, Dr Oby Ajih; members of the National and State Assemblies, local government chairmen and other party stakeholders.

The rally by the Remi Tinubu-led Women Mobilisation Directorate of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, which kicked off in the South East, will also be held across the remaining five geopolitical zones of the country.

World.title: In Zamfara, 9 a.m is 9 a.m: How Lawal is killing ‘African time’ mentality, By Yusuf Ladan
World.content:
Nigerians are widely known for what is popularly described as “African time” a culture of lateness where an event scheduled for 9:00 a.m may not begin until 10:00 a.m or even 11:00 a.m.

Over time, this habit has become normalised in our society, with people often arriving late to appointments, meetings and official functions without considering the inconvenience it causes others.

However, my working experience as part of the press team of Zamfara State Governor, Dauda Lawal, has significantly changed my perception of time management and challenged my long-held African Time stereotype.

On my first day in Gusau, I approached government functions with the usual mindset, assuming that even when an event was scheduled for a particular time, there would always be some extra minutes before it commenced.

Like many Nigerians, I would sometimes add a few minutes to the scheduled time before setting out for an event, believing that punctuality was not necessarily a strict requirement.

But that assumption was quickly challenged.

On my first day attending an official function involving the governor, I arrived only to discover that I had been locked out just a few minutes before the scheduled commencement time.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It was then that I was told something that has remained with me: “Governor Dauda Lawal’s 9:00 a.m. means 9:00 a.m., and his 2:00 p.m. means 2:00 p.m.” That experience became a turning point for me.

Gradually, I adjusted to the governor’s schedule and developed the habit of arriving at least 30 minutes before his expected arrival.

For over a month of observing his official engagements, I have yet to witness Governor Dauda Lawal arrive late for a scheduled function.

In fact, there was an occasion when the governor arrived ahead of schedule while some participants were yet to arrive.

This consistency has gradually influenced the conduct of government appointees, political office holders, civil servants and other participants attending official functions.

People now understand that keeping to time is not negotiable because the governor does not compromise on punctuality.

Beyond the personal discipline it demands, this culture sends a strong message about leadership, respect for other people’s time and the importance of institutional efficiency.

When a leader takes time seriously, those working with him are compelled to do the same. It also helps to change the mindset that lateness is an acceptable part of our social and official engagements.

My experience in Zamfara under Governor Dauda Lawal has taught me that punctuality is not just about arriving early; it is about discipline, responsibility and respect for others.

Perhaps, one of the less-discussed changes taking place in Zamfara under Governor Dauda Lawal is this growing culture of punctuality.

In Zamfara, at least from what I have personally observed, African Time is gradually losing its place. Governor Dauda Lawal has made it clear that when time is fixed, it must be respected.

And that is a leadership lesson worth taking beyond the walls of Government House.

* Yusuf Ladan is a Gusau, Zamfara State-based journalist

World.title: 2027: Christian, Muslim youth groups sign peace accord ahead of elections
World.content:
Christian and Muslim youth organisations in Lagos have signed an interreligious peace accord, committing to reject political violence, religious intolerance and the use of young people as political thugs ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The accord was signed on Saturday at the South-West Zonal Interreligious Peace Accord Summit organised by the Youth Wing of the Christian Association of Nigeria (YOWICAN), in collaboration with the National Council of Muslim Youth Organisations (NACOMYO).

The summit was held at the Senator Oluremi Tinubu CAN Secretariat, Alausa, Ikeja, Lagos, with the theme, “Building Bridges of Faith and Politics: Strengthening Peace, Unity, and National Development Through Christian-Muslim Collaboration.”

The groups said the 2027 elections would test Nigeria’s unity and urged young people not to allow politicians to recruit or manipulate them into violence.

In the communique issued at the end of the summit, the groups said the signing of the accord represents their collective determination to reject political violence, religious manipulation, hate speech and other divisive actions “capable of threatening the peace and stability of the country.”

They also called on Christian and Muslim youths to promote tolerance and peaceful coexistence in their communities, institutions and places of worship.

Peaceful coexistence

Speaking at the summit, the Chairman of CAN in Lagos State, Stephen Adegbite, said the peace accord aims to foster religious tolerance, reject political violence, and promote peaceful coexistence ahead of the elections.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Adegbite criticised politicians who make derogatory statements against their opponents.

“What we must do is what youths have done today; both Christians and Muslims have done well to bring peace and restore confidence in our great nation,” he said.

He urged young people to lead by example, saying the summit was intended to demonstrate that Christians and Muslims want peace before, during and after the elections.

“We don’t want anybody to be killed for any elective position,” he said.

Mr Adegbite also cited the Bible and the Quran as texts that promote peaceful coexistence.

Peace message to grassroots

The National Secretary of NACOMYO, Shehu Ibrahim, said the accord is particularly important as the country approaches the 2027 elections.

Mr Ibrahim said the organisation would take the message of peace to communities across the country, including through Imams, Friday prayers, Islamic schools and other religious gatherings.

He said the groups would mobilise young people at the grassroots to discourage violence during the elections.

Also speaking, the Lagos State APC Youth Leader, Damilare Orimoloye, said young people must understand that disagreements do not have to result in violence.

“Peace speaks against violence, how to tolerate each other, showing love amidst misunderstanding,” Mr Orimoloye said.

He added that disagreements were likely during the election period, making tolerance and peaceful communication important.

The South-West Chairman of YOWICAN, Nnamdi Obasi, said the summit was significant because Christian and Muslim youths needed to bridge existing gaps and avoid being used against one another.

He urged young Nigerians to remain united and resist attempts by politicians to exploit religious differences to create conflict as the 2027 elections approach.

What the accord says

The communique, signed by YOWICAN’s National Chairman, Orowolo Daniel, and National Secretary, Nehemiah Michael, alongside NACOMYO’s National Secretary II, Shehu Ibrahim, and its representative for the Southern Secretary, Mudashir Bello, outlined seven commitments.

Among them is a rejection of the recruitment and manipulation of young people as political thugs, as well as a commitment to religious tolerance and peaceful coexistence.

The groups also called on religious, traditional, community and political leaders to discourage intolerance, political manipulation and incitement to violence.

They said the peace message should extend beyond the summit to states, local government areas, communities, schools and religious institutions.

The groups further resolved that the peace accord should not end with its signing but should serve as a framework for continued dialogue, mutual accountability and peacebuilding between Christian and Muslim youths.

They urged Nigerian youths, political leaders, religious institutions and other stakeholders to work towards a peaceful and inclusive 2027 election.

World.title: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest Formula One world champion at age 20
World.content:
Mercedes’ Italian driver Kimi Antonelli celebrates winning the world championship title at the end of the Mexico City Formula One Grand Prix, at the Hermanos Rodriguez racetrack in Mexico City on November 1st, 2026. (Photo by Yuri CORTEZ / AFP)

Kimi Antonelli drove the perfect race to finish third in his Mercedes at the Mexico Grand Prix and seal his place in Formula One history as the youngest world champion.

Max Verstappen took the chequered flag but all eyes were on the young Italian who takes the crown at the age of 20 years and 68 days, more than three years younger than Sebastian Vettel in 2010.

He is the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

World.title: CAF picks Nigeria’s Samson Adamu as new General Secretary
World.content:
Nigerian Samson Adamu has been appointed the new General Secretary of the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

CAF announced the appointment on Sunday, on its website following a comprehensive recruitment process conducted by the continental football governing body.

The News Agency of Nigeria reports that Adamu had been serving as acting General Secretary since March, following the resignation of Veron Mosengo-Omba.

Mosengo-Omba subsequently became president of the football federation in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

CAF President, Patrice Motsepe, was quoted in the statement on its website as saying that the appointment followed a competitive recruitment exercise, during which the position was widely advertised and several candidates interviewed.

Adamu has worked with CAF for eight years, serving first as Director of Competitions and later as Director of Tournaments and Events.

“Adamu brings extensive experience in African football administration, having joined CAF in 2018 as Director of Competitions before subsequently serving as Director of Tournaments and Events.

“He has played a leading role in the delivery of several major continental competitions, including CAF’s flagship tournament, the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations,” Motsepe was quoted as saying.

A graduate of the FIFA Master programme in International Management, Law and Humanities of Sport, Adamu brings considerable institutional knowledge and experience to his new role.

NAN reports that Adamu is expected to oversee CAF’s day-to-day administration and support the implementation of its strategic priorities.

He is the son of Amos Adamu, a former Director of Sports in the then Ministry of Sports and a former FIFA Executive Committee member.

The appointment places Adamu among a distinguished line of CAF General Secretaries, including members of Egypt’s Fahmy family.

Mourad Fahmy served from 1961 to 1982, followed by his son, Mustapha Fahmy, from 1982 to 2010, and grandson, Amr Fahmy, who held the position from 2017 to 2019.

World.title: FIFA U17 WWC: Flamingos sail into semi finals, to meet Brazil
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos booked their place in the semi-finals of this year’s FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup finals after securing a 1-0 victory over Venezuela on Sunday night, with Azeezatt Oduntan scoring a late penalty in the 89th minute.

The quarter-final contest had been closely fought, with Nigeria creating several opportunities but finding Venezuela goalkeeper Valeria Rebanales a huge stumbling block. The Flamingos enjoyed much of the attacking play in the first half, but Rebanales produced a couple of saves to keep the scores level.

Midfielder Favour Nkwocha was also cautioned as Nigeria continued to press for an opening goal. Head Coach Hakeem Busari made his first change of the evening, introducing Precious Oscar for Oluwakemi Adegbuyi as Nigeria looked to find a way through.

The deadlock remained unbroken until the 88th minute, when the referee initially awarded Nigeria a penalty before being invited to the VAR monitor to review the decision. Following the review, the penalty was upheld, and Oduntan stepped forward to convert from the spot with a minute left on the clock, giving Nigeria the breakthrough.

Top scorer Oluebube Umejiaku had won the penalty for the Flamingos, setting up Oduntan to deliver the decisive moment of the contest. The victory sends Nigeria into the semi-finals, where they will face Brazil, who secured a 2-1 win over China in their quarter-final encounter.

World.title: Nathaniel Bassey becomes first African gospel artist to hit one billion YouTube views
World.content:
Nigerian gospel singer and pastor Nathaniel Bassey has surpassed one billion views on YouTube, becoming the first African gospel artist to achieve the milestone.

Bassey’s official YouTube channel, Nathaniel Bassey Main, has amassed more than 1.014 billion views and 5.24 million subscribers since its creation in 2011, according to figures displayed on the platform at the time of filing this report.

The achievement coincides with the October 2026 edition of the Hallelujah Challenge, the online prayer and worship programme

founded by the gospel minister in 2017.

The monthly initiative features midnight sessions of praise, worship and prayers, attracting participants from different parts of the world.

Initially launched as an online worship gathering, the Hallelujah Challenge has grown into an international Christian movement, with thousands of people participating in its live sessions and millions more watching recorded editions.

Bassey is known for popular gospel songs such as Imela, Onise Iyanu, Olowogbogboro and You Are God, which have contributed to his popularity among gospel music audiences in Nigeria and beyond.

The one-billion-view milestone has generated excitement among his followers, with some suggesting that the minister could explore opportunities to monetise the growing audience of his online worship sessions.

However, Bassey has maintained that the Hallelujah Challenge is primarily focused on worship and spiritual devotion rather than revenue generation.

World.title: Catholic Diocese disowns Enugu APC campaign council list
World.content:
…Bishop Obodo demands removal of his name, warns of legal action

By Anayo Okoli

The Catholic Diocese of Enugu has disowned the inclusion of the Auxiliary Bishop of Enugu, Most Rev. Ernest Anezichukwu Obodo, in the Enugu State All Progressives Congress, APC, Campaign Council, saying he was listed without his knowledge or consent.

The Diocese also demanded the immediate removal of the bishop’s name and those of other Catholic priests allegedly included in the campaign council without their authorisation.

Obodo, who is also the Enugu State Chairman of the Christian Association of Nigeria, CAN, was reportedly named Director of the Faith-Based Campaign Group in the APC campaign council.

In a disclaimer dated October 30, 2026, and signed by the Diocesan Chancellor and Secretary, Very Rev. Fr. Wilfred Chidi Agubuchie, the Diocese described the inclusion as unauthorised, misleading and a misrepresentation of the bishop’s political disposition.

The statement said the action was a “malicious act of misrepresentation and defamation,” adding that it undermined the bishop’s integrity and ecclesiastical reputation.

“The Catholic Diocese of Enugu has become aware of reports concerning the inclusion of the name of Most Rev. Ernest Anezichukwu Obodo, Auxiliary Bishop of Enugu and Chairman of the Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), Enugu State, as Director of the Faith-Based Campaign Group in the Enugu State APC Campaign Council, alongside the names of some Catholic priests.

“We categorically state that the inclusion of the Bishop’s name without his knowledge or consent is wholly unauthorised, misleading and unacceptable,” the statement said.

The Diocese stressed that the Catholic Church did not engage in partisan politics, participate in political campaigns or endorse political parties.

It said the Church remained politically neutral and committed to its spiritual mission and the promotion of peace, justice and the common good.

While acknowledging the right of individual Christians to participate in civic and democratic activities, the Diocese warned against using the name, office or identity of the Church and its ministers for partisan political interests.

“We therefore demand the immediate removal of Bishop Ernest Obodo’s name, as well as the names of all other Catholic priests included without their knowledge and consent, from the said campaign list and any related publications,” it said.

The Diocese further warned that any continued or subsequent unauthorised use of the bishop’s name, title, image or ecclesiastical office for partisan political purposes would attract appropriate legal action.

“For the avoidance of doubt, the Catholic Church is not a political campaign organisation and must not be presented as one,” the statement added.

World.title: Stop opposition politics, integrate with FG, Soludo tells South-East leaders
World.content:
Gov. Chukwuma Soludo of Anambra has urged South-East political leaders to abandon opposition politics and embrace greater integration with the Federal Government.

Soludo made the call at a stakeholders’ meeting on Sunday in Awka.

The meeting had political leaders and grassroots mobilisers from the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), All Progressives Congress (APC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and Accord Party.

The governor said that the coalition of political parties in support of President Bola Tinubu’s re-election represented a new direction for the region’s political engagement.

According to him, the era of opposition politics, which became prominent in the South-East during the 2015 general elections, should give way to active participation in governance at the centre.

He said that considerable work was required at the grassroots to change public perception of the government and mobilise support for the president.

He argued that the 5,000 votes Tinubu received in Anambra in the 2023 presidential election had contributed to attracting significant projects to the state and the region.

“If 5,000 votes could attract these projects to our state and the region, imagine what would happen if we mobilised the electorate to give him massive support,” he said.

On the economic reforms of the government, Soludo acknowledged efforts to stabilise foreign exchange availability and address fiscal challenges, noting that, although progress had been made, more work was required.

He called for structural realignment of the coalition, saying existing campaign and mobilisation structures would be streamlined during the week.

The governor urged grassroots mobilisers to adopt door-to-door campaigns, drawing lessons from successful political mobilisation strategies used during the 1983 elections.

He also advised campaign teams not to be distracted by opposition criticism and verbal attacks on social media, but to remain focused on communicating what he described as the truth.

Soludo reaffirmed his commitment to long-term governance, saying that the decisions being taken by his administration were aimed at securing a prosperous future for generations to come.

Earlier, APGA National Chairman, Mr Sly Ezeokenwa, described the gathering as a landmark in the political history of Anambra.

Ezeokenwa said that the coalition was an unprecedented political alignment involving different parties united in support of Tinubu’s re-election.

He commended Soludo for providing leadership and facilitating the alliance, assuring that APGA would fully support the governor’s political direction.

“Our party structure is ready to execute the instructions and deliver results at the polls,” he said.

Also speaking, APC Chairman in Anambra, Sen. Emma Anosike, expressed appreciation for the development strides in the state.

Anosike said that the political realignment was aimed at positioning Anambra more directly within the government’s political and developmental framework.

He called for cooperation and solidarity among political parties, irrespective of their differences, to achieve the objectives of the coalition.

World.title: 2027: Otti warns supporters against disrupting opposition campaigns
World.content:
Threatens arrest for anyone obstructing rival parties

By Steve Oko & Ugochukwu Alaribe

UMUAHIA — Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, has warned Labour Party supporters against disrupting the campaign activities of opposition parties ahead of the 2027 general elections, declaring that he has not authorised anyone to interfere with their democratic rights.

Otti said anyone found obstructing rival political parties from holding lawful rallies or other campaign activities would face arrest, irrespective of party affiliation.

The governor gave the warning on Sunday in Umuahia while flagging off the Labour Party’s 2027 campaign in the state, where he stressed that political competition must be conducted within the confines of the law.

He said opposition parties were free to use public facilities, including stadia, provided they followed the necessary procedures, obtained relevant approvals and paid the stipulated fees.

Otti added that he had directed security agencies to ensure that no political group was prevented from carrying out legitimate campaign activities.

“I have since given a public directive, and I am repeating it here, that opposition parties should not be restricted from the use of public facilities, including the stadium, once they apply and obtain the necessary approvals,” he said.

Addressing party loyalists, the governor warned that membership of the ruling party would not confer immunity on anyone who attempted to undermine the democratic process.

“You do not have my mandate to attack people or to stop people from campaigning.

“Security agencies have been mandated to arrest and deal decisively with anyone who attempts to obstruct any political group from holding their legitimate activities, even if they are Labour Party members. I hope I am heard clearly,” he said.

Beyond campaign conduct, Otti challenged opposition parties to focus their campaigns on policy alternatives and the future development of the state rather than personal attacks or issues he said his administration had addressed.

He argued that political debate in Abia should move beyond the payment of salaries and pensions, road construction and environmental sanitation to broader development priorities.

“Do not forget that in Abia we have gone past the era of campaigning on the payment of salaries and pensions, construction of roads or urban sanitation.

“The hygiene issues have been dealt with. If you are unable to raise your campaign pitch to the development realities of our state, you will definitely struggle to convince any informed voter,” the governor said.

He urged opposition parties to examine available performance data before making claims about the state, citing its ratings in the Citizen Satisfaction Index, State Performance Index and Fiscal Performance Ranking by governance-monitoring organisations.

“You should go and do your research first before coming out to open your mouth, because there are data everywhere to show what has been achieved. Evidently, the world knows that Abia is on the right track,” Otti said.

The governor also cited feedback from Abians at home and abroad, as well as development opportunities offered by multilateral institutions, as indications of progress under his administration.

“It would therefore be unthinkable that anyone will ever be allowed to return us to the old era of irresponsibility and misery,” he said.

Otti thanked residents for attending the campaign flag-off and urged Labour Party supporters to intensify grassroots mobilisation across the state.

“This is your project, and as you return to the communities, knock on every door and remind our people that we still have a job to complete. Invite them to join the campaign so that together we can conclude the journey that began 12 years ago in faith and optimism,” he added.

The event featured the presentation of party flags to Labour Party candidates for the 2027 National and State Houses of Assembly elections.

Party members, candidates and supporters attended the ceremony, chanting solidarity songs in support of their respective candidates.

World.title: NDC chieftain tackles Kalu over Obi’s four-year presidency proposal
World.content:
Benjamin Kalu

By Anayo Okoli

ENUGU — A chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Barrister Peter Agubuzu, has faulted the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, over his criticism of a proposal for the South-East to accept a single four-year presidential term.

Agubuzu described Kalu’s remarks as misplaced, urging him to focus on addressing the economic hardship and rising cost of living confronting Nigerians rather than dwelling on how long the South-East might wait to produce a President.

Kalu had reportedly criticised South-East stakeholders advocating a single four-year presidential term for the region, an arrangement attributed to the NDC presidential candidate, Peter Obi.

Speaking at an All Progressives Congress (APC) women’s rally in Enugu on Saturday, the Deputy Speaker reportedly said the Igbo could not afford to wait 60 years to produce a President who would serve for only four years.

Reacting, Agubuzu, a senior lawyer, said the immediate concern of Nigerians was the worsening economic situation and the need for leadership capable of addressing the country’s challenges.

He argued that Obi’s proposal was driven by the need to transform Nigeria’s economy from consumption to production and lift millions of citizens out of poverty.

“While Nigerians across the country are chanting ‘Tinubu Must Go’ because of the economic hardship they are experiencing and their fear of a worsening economic crisis if Tinubu is re-elected, our brother, the Deputy Speaker, is talking about 60 years.

“He forgot that Obi’s primary objective is to transform Nigeria from consumption to production to lift millions out of poverty. This is why Nigerians are chanting Tinubu Must Go,” Agubuzu said.

He maintained that the major concern of Obi was how to address the country’s economic difficulties and restore hope to millions of Nigerians struggling with the rising cost of living.

“What Nigerians are saying is straightforward: Peter Obi should come and salvage the country from the impending economic disaster they fear will follow if President Tinubu is re-elected.

“Nigerians are worried about their survival, their livelihoods and the future of their children. That is the urgent issue before us, not a speculative debate about waiting 60 years for an Igbo President,” he said.

The NDC chieftain further argued that discussions about a single presidential term should be considered within the broader context of national unity, equity and political inclusion.

He urged political leaders to pay greater attention to the concerns of ordinary Nigerians and focus on practical solutions to the country’s economic challenges rather than allow debates over regional claims to the presidency to overshadow demands for effective leadership.

World.title: Poultry Division without a hen
World.content:
One of the most funnily memorable stories I ever heard from a state governor was in 2001, when then Borno State Governor Mala Kachallah paid us a visit at New Nigerian, where I was the editor. He had left his state capital, Maiduguri in some turmoil because the state NLC branch was demanding implementation of the newly approved national minimum wage. The governor said BOSG was handicapped because it had the second largest number of civil servants in Nigeria, 30,000, so he had to retrench some workers before he could implement the new wage. NLC rejected that option. To give us an idea of the problem he faced, Kachallah said, “The Poultry Division of the Borno State Ministry of Agriculture; their last hen died in 1981, but they have 571 staffers, and every year they bring a promotion list.”

Eleven years later, I heard a slightly different complaint from Borno State Governor Kashim Shettima. In response to Boko Haram attacks, he had banned motorcycles from Maiduguri streets and instead bought 5,000 tricycles, all of which were sold to beneficiaries at a discounted price, to be paid for instalmentally. Many beneficiaries turned around, sold them at an even lower price and squandered the money. The governor was unhappy; he wondered if such attitude can happen anywhere else. I said, “Sir, take heart. I don’t know about the South, but in almost every Northern state, the same thing will happen if you sell anything on loan at a discounted price.”

The Kachallah/Shettima worry in Borno reminded me of what then Niger State Governor Musa Inuwa told me in 1993. He had proposed to retrench some skilled civil servants and instead get for them bank loans to set up businesses. They rejected the plan and threatened to go on strike. Inuwa said, “Niger State Scholarships Board has eight typists but only three typewriters. Niger State Ministry of Works has 60 skilled artisans, carpenters, electricians and plumbers who are not doing any work. They are to be found sitting in front of the ministry’s premises, and small thing they will say “Strike! Strike!”

I used to think that governors are well fed, but on two occasions I encountered a hungry governor. In 1993, Governor Musa Inuwa gave me an 8am appointment in Minna but when I arrived at his office, he had a sudden visitor in Abia State Governor Dr. Ogbonnaya Onu. I had to wait for two hours until he escorted Onu out of town. When I was ushered into his office, he apologized for keeping me waiting, said we should proceed with the interview, even though he had not eaten his breakfast. So I said, “Sir, please have your breakfast. I will wait in CPS’s office.” He was very grateful!

In 2002, Jigawa State Governor Ibrahim Saminu Turaki arrived very late for an interview at New Nigerian. An hour into the interview, he suddenly said he was very hungry, and asked if the man who used to sell roasted meat at nearby NEPA roundabout was still there. Staffers rushed out and brought hot roasted meat. The governor retreated into the MD’s office, ate his fill, and returned to continue the interview.

Most memorable was Abacha-era Works Minister Major General Abdulkarim Adisa’s press conference in Abuja. A reporter audaciously asked him why he awarded contracts only to his friends. The rambunctious Adisa said, “Those who say I give contracts only to my friends, I pray to God to make them minister so that they will give contracts to their enemies.”

In 2000AD, as Editor of New Nigerian, I accompanied my managing director Dr. Omar Faruk Ibrahim to Sokoto to pacify Governor Attahiru Bafarawa. He was very angry because, in our inside page, his picture was used to illustrate a story about a Sokoto magistrate court that convicted two homosexuals. Bafarawa was certain that New Nigerian’s Sokoto reporter planted it that way to embarrass him. We struggled to convince him that the reporter was far away from the production center and could not possibly know how a sub editor carelessly designed that page.

In 1991, very fresh into my journalism career as a Citizen magazine reporter, I was in Katsina to interview military governor Colonel John Yahaya Madaki. As we sat in the visitors’ room, Madaki saw us on a CCTV camera. He stormed out, chased away a woman and a male contractor, then came for me and said, “Who are you?” His Chief Press Secretary Abubakar Yar’adua quickly intervened and said he brought me. I was ushered into the office and sat in the conference area. Madaki left his desk, came near me and sat on the center table, his starched khaki menacingly rubbing my leg. I was young and audacious then, so I said, “Sir, please sit down on the chair.” The Jungle Expert exploded; “This is my office! I will sit down where I want! If you don’t want, pack your things and go!” But we had a rich two-hour interview.

My next explosive gubernatorial interview came 18 years later, with Adamawa State Governor Murtala Nyako in Abuja. Two of us were ushered to the dining table where the governor sat. Looking at the other man, he said, “Girigiri [Second Republic Senator Girigiri Lawan of Yobe], I asked you to come because I am going to talk to this journalist, and I do not trust him.” Turning to me, he said, “You, you hate the people of Adamawa State!” I quickly replied, “Sir, I was born in Adamawa State.” “It’s a lie!” “It is true!” “When?” “In Northern Nigeria. My father was the D.O in Mubi.” Nyako then changed tack and said, “I know why you are mischievous. It is because your family’s cattle have finished. There is no person more evil than a Fulani man whose cattle has finished.” I said, “Sir, my grandfather left behind many cows.” “How many?” I said, “Up to 30.” He said, “My father left behind 15,000 cows!”

Katsina State Governor Umaru Musa Yar’adua was one of the gentlest governors I interviewed, in 2001. I [audaciously] asked him why he drove a car with three commissioners to go on a condolence visit, why he stopped at a roadside kiosk to buy cigarettes, and why, as governor, he prayed under a Tsamiya tree instead of entering the Friday mosque to pray beside the Emir. Malam Umaru looked at me quietly and said, “I have been praying under that tree for 18 years. Why should I enter the mosque and pray beside the Emir, only to come out again one day when I am no longer the governor and resume praying under that tree? You see, all these things, my fear is for women and children. Me, any day I lose privileges, I can adjust, but when women and children are used to something, they find it difficult to adjust. It is the cause of the corruption all around.”

In 1992, I interviewed Sokoto State Governor Malam Yahaya Abdulkarim and asked him about a protracted quarrel between himself and Senator Garba Ila Gada. The governor looked at me and said, “Turn off your tape recorder.” He then said, “You know the real reason for this quarrel between me and him? It is because he wants this chair.”

I once asked former Abia State governor and then ANPP national chairman Dr. Ogbonnaya Onu about the fiasco at ANPP’s 1999 Kaduna convention, when he was nominated as presidential candidate and then substituted with AD candidate Olu Falae. Onu laughed heartily and said, “My brother, it is something you do not wish to happen even to your worst enemy.”

In 2001, Kogi State Governor Abubakar Audu invited me to Lokoja to mark two years of his administration. When I was ushered in, he said no interview until I first toured his projects. His Chief Press Secretary then grabbed a car and we charged through the state until well after dusk, inspecting roads, housing projects, the Audu Oyigi eye hospital and the then new Abubakar Audu University at Ayingba. On our way back I told the CPS that I was really impressed with what I saw. So he said, “When we go to see Oga, please praise him! My Oga likes praise. Please praise him very well, and agbada will flow!”

Small fry like me, I once found myself settling a quarrel between two governors. Former Zamfara State governor Senator Ahmed Sani came to my Abuja office in 2009 and said, “I come to report your friend [his successor, Governor Mahmud Aliyu Shinkafi].” He told me that he went to Government House to see the governor, was told that he was praying in the mosque, so he waited for him in his office. After a very long wait, he asked what was delaying the governor’s return, and the office messenger told him that when the governor heard that Yarima was waiting for him in the office, he summoned his car to the mosque and sneaked away.

I then sent a message to Governor Shinkafi and said “Sir, Yarima has reported you to me.” The very gentle Shinkafi replied that he will be in Abuja in two days and will send for me, which he did. I told him what Yarima said, and he said, “Yarima was wrong!” That there was going to be an ANPP primaries contest in Bakura LGA, and he asked Yarima who was his preferred candidate, but he said both men were the same to him. The two men went for the primaries and after one of them won, Yarima said he preferred the other one. “That was why I went away.”

For the first [and possibly the last] time in my life, I found myself scolding a sitting governor. I said, “Sir, you made a mistake by going away. As the Governor, you should have stayed and told him firmly that he was wrong. But by sneaking away, you spoilt the case.”

World.title: Our Commitment to Ndi Enugu: The Journey So Far
World.content:
GUEST COLUMNIST BY PETER MBAH

First let me begin by giving my profound gratitude to the entire Management and Staff of Godfrey Okoye University and its other collaborators for this excellent forum – and the opportunity it offers for an enriching dialogue.

My dear people of Enugu State, I want to begin today by asking you to remember something.

Think back to May 2023, when we first assumed office. Think about the condition of our state, the difficulties we faced, and the expectations we had gradually learned to live without.

I want us to be honest about that period, because unless we remember where we began, it becomes difficult to appreciate the distance we have travelled.

There was a time when Monday was no longer an ordinary working day in Enugu. Shops remained closed. Roads were deserted. Parents were afraid to send their children to school. People who depended on their daily earnings had to surrender an entire day’s income because others had decided they should remain indoors.

Consider what that meant for a woman selling food in the market. Her customers were at home, her produce was deteriorating, and the money she needed to support her family would not be earned that day.

Or the young man who had borrowed money to start a business, only to discover that one working day in every week had effectively been taken away from him.

Our children who lost a whole academic year before their compulsory external exam paper fell on a Monday. That was the reality we inherited.

Our roads were in poor condition. Public services had deteriorated. Many schools were struggling to provide the kind of education our children deserved. Our health facilities needed substantial investment.

And Enugu, a city that had once been the natural centre of commercial, political and cultural life across the region, was gradually losing that position.

Businesses were looking elsewhere. Major events were moving to other cities. Our airport had barely two incoming flights a day. Perhaps the greatest danger was that we might begin to accept these conditions as normal. Because when people live with the same difficulties for long enough, their expectations begin to change. They stop asking what is possible and concentrate instead on getting through the day. I knew we could do better.

I had spent much of my working life building businesses, dealing with challenges and making decisions about the future. I understood that Enugu possessed enormous resources, but I also knew that those resources would achieve very little unless we created the conditions for people to use them.

Our greatest resource was already here: the people of Enugu. What was missing was a clear direction, the determination to pursue it, and a government prepared to take responsibility for the results.

When I presented my original Statement of Purpose, I set out an ambition that some people considered almost impossible. We proposed to grow Enugu’s economy from approximately $4.4 billion to at least $30 billion within eight years, making our state one of Nigeria’s three leading economies.

We also committed ourselves to the long-term ambition of eliminating poverty. Those were enormous goals. I knew that. But I wanted us to understand the scale of the change required.

An economy cannot grow substantially if businesses cannot operate safely, if electricity is unreliable, if roads are impassable, or if young people leave school without the skills they need.

These problems are connected. They have to be addressed together. So, we began by identifying the foundations of a functioning state: security, education, healthcare, infrastructure, productive industries and institutions capable of delivering results.

And we made some difficult choices. We committed an unusually large share of our resources to education because we recognised that the future of Enugu would depend upon the abilities of its children.

We began restoring security and normal economic activity. We invested in roads and transport, planned improvements to healthcare and set about attracting the businesses and industries that would create employment.

I also knew that government itself had to change. For too long, public announcements had been treated as achievements. A project could be celebrated at its commencement and then disappear from public attention.

I wanted a different standard.

If we promise a school, people should be able to visit it. If we announce a road, they should be able to travel on it. If we say that public services are improving, citizens should be able to tell us whether that is true.

This is why accountability, measurable performance and public participation were written into our original Statement of Purpose. We were asking the people of Enugu to place their confidence in a programme of substantial change. We therefore had an obligation to demonstrate, through our work, that their confidence was justified.

Distinguished Guests, Today, I can stand before you and point to changes that have taken place across our state.

One of the earliest and most important was the restoration of normal activity on Mondays. I remember how deeply the sit-at-home restrictions had affected people’s lives. The fear was real, and the economic consequences were considerable.

Today, people are going about their business with a freedom that had been denied to them for far too long. A trader can plan a full working week. Children can attend school. Businesses can receive customers, move goods and keep their employees working.

It may seem strange that we should celebrate something as ordinary as being able to go to work on Monday. But anyone who lived through those years understands its importance.

Security gave us a foundation upon which other changes could begin.

We turned our attention to the condition of our roads and the movement of people around the state.

Road construction is often discussed in kilometres and contract values. Most people experience it rather differently. They know the road that used to damage their vehicles, the journey that took too long, or the difficulty of getting produce from a farm to a market.

These are the experiences that matter. We have undertaken substantial road development and begun introducing a more organised transport system, including new buses and terminals.

Our ambition is to make movement around Enugu safer, more comfortable and more dependable, while connecting communities to the opportunities being created across the state.

The same thinking informs our work in aviation. When we assumed office, Enugu had barely two incoming flights a day. In our recent review, we counted more than fifteen.

That change tells us something about the renewed interest in our state. Through Enugu Air and our wider aviation plans, we want to strengthen the connections between Enugu, the rest of Nigeria and international markets.

A businessperson should be able to reach customers and partners without unnecessary difficulty. Investors should be able to visit our state. People who have made their lives elsewhere should find it easier to return, visit family and participate in our economy.

Of course, improved air travel alone will not transform the life of someone living in a rural community. But a growing economy needs these connections, and our responsibility is to ensure that the opportunities they generate reach much further.

That brings me to education. I have always believed that the most important investment we can make is in the abilities of our children.

Consider the world into which a child entering school today will eventually graduate. Technology is already changing the way people work. Some occupations will disappear, others will be transformed, and entirely new industries will emerge. That child needs an education that prepares them to think independently, solve problems, communicate well and adapt to circumstances we cannot yet predict. This is the thinking behind our 260 Smart Green Schools, designed to bring a new standard of education to every ward in Enugu State. We want children in our rural communities to have access to the kind of learning opportunities that parents might once have believed were available only in the most privileged schools.

Imagine what that could mean for a family whose children are the first generation to receive such an education. A daughter might develop the skills to build an agricultural business using modern methods. A son might become an engineer, a software developer or a skilled technician. Another child might become a teacher or a healthcare professional and return to serve the community in which they grew up.

We cannot know exactly what each child will become. But we can give them a stronger foundation from which to choose. That is why education occupies such a central place in our development programme. And we must ensure that the economy grows alongside it. There would be little satisfaction in educating a generation of talented young people if they could find no opportunity to put their abilities to work.

Our plans for agriculture, industry, technology, energy and commerce are intended to create those opportunities.

Take agriculture: Enugu has fertile land, experienced farmers and communities with generations of knowledge about food production.

Yet many farmers still struggle with poor access to equipment, storage, processing facilities and markets. They work hard, take considerable risks and often receive too little of the final value of what they produce.

We want to build an agricultural economy in which more of that value remains here. Think of a farmer who grows cassava. If the crop can be processed locally, it creates work beyond the farm. Someone operates the equipment. Someone maintains it. Someone packages the finished product. Others transport and sell it.

The income generated by that activity can support families and create further businesses within the community. Now imagine similar opportunities developing around other crops and agricultural products across Enugu. That is the practical meaning of agricultural industrialisation.

Our plans for energy and industrial development follow the same logic. Reliable electricity can change the prospects of a small business. A tailor can work more efficiently. A food processor can preserve produce. A manufacturer can operate equipment without constantly depending on expensive alternative power.

We have set out major ambitions for increasing electricity generation and attracting industrial investment because these are essential to the kind of economy we want to build. Some of these undertakings are long-term. Their benefits will develop over several years, and we must be realistic about the work involved. But we cannot afford to postpone them.

I also want to speak about healthcare. For a parent with a sick child, the most important question is whether good medical attention is available when it is needed.

For an expectant mother, it is whether she can receive proper care during pregnancy and childbirth.

For an elderly person, it is whether treatment can be obtained without travelling an unreasonable distance or placing an impossible burden on the family.

These are the circumstances against which our healthcare investments must be judged.

We have been working to improve primary healthcare facilities and strengthen services across the state. We are also investing in the wider systems needed to make healthcare more effective.

There is still work ahead, particularly in ensuring that improvements reach every community. And I want to acknowledge that openly. I know that some people listening today are already experiencing the benefits of the changes we have made. Others are still waiting for a road to be completed, a facility to become fully operational, or a new economic opportunity to reach their community.

I understand that frustration. A government must be judged by the experiences of all its citizens, including those who have yet to see the full benefit of its work. That is why our programme must continue, and why we must remain willing to listen and make corrections.

Now consider the larger investments we are pursuing. We are working to expand Enugu’s aviation connections, develop tourism destinations, attract major hospitality investment, improve electricity supply and create new areas for business and residential development.

Some people will understandably ask what these projects have to do with their daily lives. It is a fair question. A new hotel can bring visitors and create demand for food, transport, maintenance, laundry, construction and many other services. A tourism destination can support local businesses. Better electricity can make investment in manufacturing more attractive.

But government must do more than hope that these benefits spread. We must help our people acquire the skills, access the finance and establish the businesses that allow them to participate. A large project should create possibilities for many smaller enterprises. That is how economic development begins to reach into households and communities.

We have made substantial progress in restoring Enugu’s position as a place where people want to live, work, invest and visit.

The changes are visible, and the scale of our ambition is becoming clearer. We should take pride in what has been achieved, while recognising how much remains to be done.

My fellow citizens, there is a reason I have spent time today looking back at where we began and examining the progress we have made.

I want us to understand the opportunity now before us. We are living through a period of extraordinary change. Technology is reshaping industries across the world. The way food is produced, goods are manufactured, businesses are managed and knowledge is shared is changing faster than at any previous point in our lives. The opportunities created by these changes are considerable, but they will not be distributed equally. Places that invest in education, infrastructure, skills and productive enterprise will be better prepared to benefit. Those that fail to prepare may find themselves falling further behind. This matters enormously for Enugu.

We have a young population, talented people, valuable natural resources and a long history of enterprise. We also have a generation of children growing up at a time when the possibilities available to them could be greater than anything their parents experienced.

But those possibilities depend upon the choices we make now. A young person who wants to establish a business needs more than encouragement. They need access to skills, customers, finance and dependable infrastructure.

A farmer who wants to increase production needs practical support and a market in which the additional effort can be rewarded. A community that wants better healthcare or education needs functioning institutions and a government that responds to its concerns. These are the connections we must strengthen in the years ahead.

Our Statement of Purpose was built around the ambition of creating a productive economy and improving the lives of our people. That remains our direction. The next phase must deepen the work already begun, bring projects into full operation and extend their benefits to communities that are still waiting. We must also create more opportunities for our young people to participate in the industries of the future.

The development of technology, modern agriculture, manufacturing, tourism and other productive sectors will require a workforce with new capabilities. Our schools, training institutions, businesses and government agencies must work together to develop them.

There is urgency in this work because time matters. A child who receives a poor education today cannot simply recover those years later. A business that closes because it cannot operate may never reopen. A talented young person who leaves because there is no opportunity at home may build their future somewhere else.

We cannot afford to lose another generation of potential. And this is why the moment before us is so important. The foundations we have begun to establish give us an opportunity to move faster and achieve more. The decisions we make over the coming years will determine how widely the benefits of this transformation are shared and how firmly they become established.

I believe Enugu is capable of becoming one of the great centres of economic and social progress in Nigeria. But that future will depend upon the continued effort of government, the confidence of investors, the enterprise of our businesses and the participation of our people.

Which brings me to the most important invitation I want to make today.

My dear people of Enugu, when we began this journey, I asked you to believe that our state could become something greater. Today, I am asking you to become more deeply involved in making that future a reality. Government can create the conditions for progress, but the energy that sustains it comes from the people. It comes from the teacher who takes responsibility for the children in her classroom, the business owner who trains young employees, the farmer who introduces a better method of production, and the community that comes together to solve a problem.

It also comes from citizens who ask difficult questions, demand accountability and contribute their ideas to the decisions that affect them. I want that relationship between government and citizens to grow stronger.

Our original Statement of Purpose committed us to transparent government, measurable performance and public participation. These commitments matter because people are more likely to take responsibility for something when they understand it and have a meaningful voice in shaping it.

When a new school opens in your community, I want you to regard its success as a shared responsibility. The government must provide the facilities, teachers and resources. Parents and community leaders also have an important part to play in supporting the children who attend it.

When a new road connects your community to a market, I want us to consider the businesses and opportunities that connection could support.

When an investment creates the possibility of employment, I want our young people to be ready with the skills and determination to take advantage of it.

And when government falls short, I want citizens to speak up and help us identify what needs to improve. This is how a stronger relationship between the people and their institutions is built. I am particularly conscious of the responsibility we carry towards the next generation. Our children will inherit the state we leave behind. They will live with the consequences of our decisions, our investments and the opportunities we either created or failed to recognise.

And I believe that when they look back upon this period in Enugu’s history, they should be able to say that something important happened here. That a generation of people looked honestly at the condition of their state, decided it could do better and began the difficult work of changing its future. That the progress continued because people across Enugu chose to participate.

We have already seen what can happen when a state begins to regain its confidence. People return to their businesses. Investment begins to grow. New institutions emerge. Young people see possibilities that were previously difficult to imagine.

There is a growing sense that Enugu is moving forward again. But the greatest part of this journey is still before us. I spoke earlier about the dawn. In May 2023, we stood at the beginning of a new day. There was uncertainty about what lay ahead, but we knew that the time had come to change direction.

Today, the first light has given way to morning. We can see the work taking shape around us, and we can begin to appreciate the scale of what is possible. We are now in the heat of the morning, when the real labour of the day must be done. And I want every citizen of Enugu to recognise the importance of this hour.

Because history sometimes gives a people an opportunity to change the direction of their future. Such opportunities do not remain open indefinitely.

The world is moving quickly, and we must be prepared to move with it.

This is one moment in the long history of Enugu. This is a moment of extraordinary possibility for our people. And I believe this is the moment we must seize. The work we have begun needs the commitment of all of us.

I ask you to bring your ideas, your skills, your enterprise and your experience into the life of our state. Take an interest in what is happening in your community. Help us identify problems and develop practical solutions. Encourage our young people to learn, create and build their futures here.

We have the opportunity to leave something of lasting value to those who come after us: A state with stronger institutions, a more productive economy, better opportunities for its children and communities whose people can take pride in what they have achieved together.

That is the Enugu I want us to build. And I believe we have reached the point in our history when we can begin to make that ambition real.

My fellow citizens, the morning is upon us. There is much work ahead, and I am ready to continue that work with you.

Ndi Enugu, Tomorrow Is Here.

Thank you.

Mbah, Govenor of Enugu State, presented the manifesto performance scorecard at Godfrey Okoye University, Enugu

World.title: Kwankwaso, Yusuf: South Must Retain Power in 2027
World.content:
Igbo torn between emotion and reason, declares Soludo

Says those who couldn’t defeat Tinubu out of power won’t do so now

Unites APGA, APC, PDP, Accord in Anambra for president’s re-election

Akpabio: Akwa Ibom’ll deliver South-South’s highest votes to Tinubu

Urges APC factions to unite

Deji Elumoye, Sunday Aborisade in Abuja, David-Chyddy Eleke in Awka and Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano

The Vice Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Rabiu Kwankwaso; Kano State Governor, Abba Kabir Yusuf, and Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice President), Hajya Rahma Abdulmajid, yesterday insisted that the South should retain power in 2027, warning against breaking the existing rotational arrangement between the North and the South.

While Kwankwaso warned former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) against disrupting the zoning arrangement, Yusuf and Abdulmajid argued that allowing the South to complete its eight-year tenure was necessary for national stability, reciprocity and peaceful coexistence.

Also yesterday, Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, said the Igbo were torn between emotion and reason ahead of the 2027 elections, urging them to support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election, while Senate President Godswill Akpabio assured that Akwa Ibom State would deliver the highest votes for the President in the South-South.

It’s Still Turn of South in 2027, Kwankwaso Warns Atiku, ADC

Kwankwaso has warned Atiku not to disrupt the zoning system by contesting, urging him to allow the system to continue by supporting Mr. Peter Obi to complete the remaining tenure belonging to the South.

Kwankwaso, who stated this during an interactive session with journalists at his residence in Kano, yesterday, also warned the ADC against causing confusion over the rotational presidency between the North and the South.

He said even though zoning was not enshrined in the constitution, common sense dictates that if one part of the country rules for two terms, the other region should be allowed to take over.

According to the former governor, fielding any candidate from the North would not help the country’s peaceful coexistence but will rather create confusion and disharmony among Nigerians.

“Atiku should not disrupt the system by contesting at this point in time. He should allow the system to continue by supporting Peter Obi to complete the remaining tenure belonging to the South.”

Kwankwaso recalled how he contested for president three consecutive times but decided to abandon his ambition to allow the Southern part of the country to produce Mr. Peter Obi.

“What is happening in the ADC will not help us. Some people want to create confusion by bringing a candidate from the North, knowing full well that it is still the turn of the South. After Obi presidency, it will return to the north.

“I sacrificed my ambition for Peter Obi because he is credible and from the South. We share common goals and ideology. We are strong and can manage the affairs of this country with ease,” he added.

The Kwankwasiyya leader stressed that for the Nigerian system to be balanced, Obi from the South should be given the opportunity to steer the affairs of the presidency.

Yusuf, Presidential Aide Insist on Power Rotation

Specifically, the Presidency justified the existing power rotation between the North and the South by urging the North to honour the current eight-year tenure being served by the South to completion, in the interest of reciprocity and national stability.

It said Nigeria’s national stability hangs by a slender thread, demanding that the North honour the unwritten power rotation pact and allow the South to complete its full eight-year tenure, warning that breaking this foundational trust could jeopardise the country’s unity.

Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice President), Hajya Rahma Abdulmajid, stated this in Kano during the Grand Inauguration & Strategic Media Awards Ceremony of Matan Arewa 4 Tinubu Again (MATA).

According to her, Nigeria’s power rotation arrangement was not a sectional concession but a reciprocal compact that has stabilised the Fourth Republic.

In a veiled reference to Atiku, who she recalled attended and participated in the famous Kaduna meeting where the power rotation agreement was reached, Abdulmajid argued that the North cannot sacrifice the stability of Nigeria for the ambition of one man.

Tracing the origin to Kaduna, she noted that when military rule ended, patriots negotiated a framework for unity, maintaining that, “present in that room was Atiku Abubakar himself, as later confirmed by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), George Akume.

“Chief Sunday Awoniyi, the great Northern elder, stood up in 1998 and declared that the North should not field a candidate, in order to heal the wounds of June 12 and soothe the pain of the South.”

She further listed other patriots who shaped the understanding to include Dr. Chuba Okadigbo, speaking for the South; Alhaji Abubakar Rimi, speaking for the North; Dr. Alex Ekwueme, and Dr. Okwesilieze Nwodo.

Insisting on the power rotation arrangement, the Presidency said, “In 1999, when the guns of military rule finally fell silent, this nation did not just switch governments—we made a sacred promise. Our founding patriots gathered in Kaduna with one urgent, defining question echo-chambered in their minds: How do we keep Nigeria one?

“And from that sacred deliberation came a compact: not a sectional concession, but a reciprocal agreement. This gentleman’s agreement decreed that power must rotate between North and South every eight years—an arrangement to guarantee fairness, to ensure stability, and to guarantee that no Nigerian ever feels like a stranger in his own country.”

On how the arrangement worked, Abdulmajid said it survived because it was honoured.

“This is not fiction. This is our history. And how did it work? It worked because we honoured it. In 1999, we gave it to the South—Chief Olusegun Obasanjo, eight years, from 1999 to 2007. Then we gave it to the North: Umaru Musa Yar’Adua in 2007. But death, a painful death, cut his tenure short in 2010.

“His vice, Goodluck Jonathan from the South, took over. The North felt cheated. The North said our turn was not complete, and that agitation was legitimate. What happened? In 2015, power returned to the North. The late former President Muhammadu Buhari, eight full years, 2015 to 2023! The sequence was restored! The principle survived,” she stated.

The Presidency contended that the agreement was a two-way street and the North has already taken its full benefit.

“My people, listen to me. The agreement is reciprocal; it is a two-way street. The North has already taken its full benefit after eight solid years under Buhari. You cannot eat your cake and still demand another man’s cake,” Abdulmajid said.

The presidential aide stressed that stability requires reciprocity, recalling that the current President, a Southerner, worked tirelessly for the late General Muhammadu Buhari to emerge victorious when the North demanded power must return after Jonathan’s tenure.

“That same logic applies today. You cannot abandon a principle when it becomes inconvenient. If you do, you tell the world that the agreement was never a principle at all—merely a temporary tactic. And if we destroy trust today, what will we use to negotiate tomorrow? Let us be honest. Much of this noise against the South completing its term is not a matter of principle. It is personal ambition,” she queried.

Attributing opposition to the South completing its term to personal ambition, Abdulmajid said, “Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar tells us zoning is “self-defeating.” But he participated in and benefited from zoned arrangements in 2015 and 2019 when they favored his ambition! When rotation opened the door for him, it was acceptable. When it stands in his way, it becomes “intellectually dishonest.”

“Shall we sacrifice Nigeria’s stability for one man’s ambition? The North’s genuine interest is not served by that; the North’s interest is stable inclusion. The guarantee that power will return to you only lives if we honour the compact today.”

The Presidency appealed to the North not to break the sacred promise that binds nation, urging the people of the region to rise together and complete the Southern tenure, describing it as not merely an election.

“This is for our honour. This is for reciprocity. This is for the enduring stability and peaceful coexistence of our great nation. That is exactly what the re-election of Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a second term stands for. That is the future we build today,” it added.

Also speaking, Governor Yusuf corroborated Abdulmajid’s position, saying the unity of Nigeria could only be guaranteed by fair play and inclusivity.

The Governor who was represented by his Director-General of Media and Publicity, Sunusi Bature Dawakin Tofa, argued that reversing the existing rotational arrangement would paint the North in ignoble light, even as he urged the region to maintain the status quo by re-electing President Tinubu for a second term.

In his remarks, former Governor of Jigawa State and immediate past Minister of Defence, Mohammad Abubakar Badaru, said the Renewed Hope Administration of President Tinubu has benefited the North more than any other part of Nigeria.

Badaru listed major completed road projects to include the 88km Zuba-Jere section and the 81km Abuja-Kaduna section of the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Highway commissioned in October 2026, the 77km Kaduna-Pambeguwa road, Yakasai-Badume-Damargu-Marken Zalli roads in Kano, and the Jimeta Bridge in Yola.

On social infrastructure, Badaru cited completed health facilities such as Gadon Kaya PHC in Kano, three Polio Emergency Centers in Katsina, Kano and Sokoto, pharmacy lab at ABUTH Zaria, 50-bed mental health center at UNIMAID, and infertility center at ATBUTH Bauchi, plus ongoing upgrades at Bichi General Hospital and deployment of 79 CNG ambulances.

Igbo Torn Between Emotion and Reason in 2027 Elections, Declares Soludo

Soludo has summarised the disposition of the Ndigbo ahead of the 2027 elections, saying they were torn between emotions and reason in the forthcoming presidential election, but advised that it was better to embrace reason than work on emotion.

Soludo was referring to the support being given by most Igbo people to Obi, who is from the region.

Speaking at a stakeholders’ meeting of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), All Progressives Congress (APC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and Accord Party, which he convened in Awka as the Anambra State Coordinator of the Presidential Campaign Committee of APC, Soludo insisted that those who couldn’t win Tinubu when he was not in power should not expect to win him now that he was in charge.

Speaking at the well-attended meeting which had members of the four political parties in attendance, Soludo insisted that there would be consequences for not supporting Tinubu if he won reelection next year.

He said: “This is a grand coalition for the progress, prosperity, security, and welfare of Nigeria and of course, Anambra. This is a battle for the soul of Ndigbo and Anambra, a battle between emotion and reason. Emotion will always dominate, but reason will eventually triumph.

“We have clamoured for the presidency since 1978, we have held many positions in Nigeria except president. So, how do we get there? We need partnerships. Politics is about interest, we are not doing Tinubu any favour by supporting him, rather we are doing ourselves a favour. We did not vote for him in 2023, yet he won, and some people want us to repeat the same mistake?”

Soludo said he was sure of Tinubu’s victory next year, saying, “A warrior who you couldn’t beat when he was sleeping in 2023, is it now that he is fully awake that you think you can defeat him? It can’t happen. Show me anywhere in the world that anyone has taken power from a powerful incumbent president?

“Ndigbo have been playing politics of protest and it is not in our own favour. Our brother who is running for president (Peter Obi) is my friend. We are close, our families are close and we will remain close. The only place where we disagree with each other is in politics. We cannot keep deceiving our people.

“In politics, there is not prize for second position, that is why I say we should not throw away our votes. We must remember there is consequence for running and failing. So, for Ndigbo, this is a battle between temporary emotion and reason.

“If we back Tinubu for a second term, after his tenure, power will move to the north, and when it comes to the South again, we will be able to negotiate with other regions in the South to support us because we supported them when they needed us.”

The Governor insisted that he was not supporting Tinubu’s reelection for any percuniary gains, adding that after winning a second term as governor, he was done with election contest.

He said: “I grew up in the era when we used to say – speak the truth and shame the devil. In 2023 I even wrote it down that he (Obi) will fail. I wrote that at best he would come third, and what later happened? This time, I’m saying it again that he will fail. Once you go to election with fragmented opposition, the incumbent will carry the day.

“I’m saying this truth because I care for Igbo. I’m no longer contesting any election after my second term, so I can retire to my village and be enjoying fresh palm wine, but it is the future of Ndigbo that we are fighting for. That is why I’m shouting because I know that contesting and failing has serious consequences.”

Soludo charged all parties in the coalition to go out and scout for votes to ensure a resounding victory for Tinubu on January 16, 2026.

He said parties must adopt a door-to-door campaign strategy to be able to reach undecided voters, insisting that securing victory for Tinubu in Anambra will give the state the right to negotiate for favours in his second term. He also scored the president high on projects being done in the state, saying only victory will give him the courage to complete the projects when he returns.

“Tinubu is doing many projects in Anambra State. We want to support him to ensure that he returns to complete them. There are numerous other projects that we would want him to do, but you can only ask for them if you are a member of the inner chamber.

“We need to partner the federal government for some projects. Our roads need to be motorable, there is the gas pipeline project, rail project, erosion menace. Some of these are not things a state can take on with just FAAC, and the only way the federal government can come to our aid is if we are partners,” Soludo said.

Akpabio: Akwa Ibom’ll Deliver South-South’s Highest Votes for Tinubu in 2027

The President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, has assured President Bola Tinubu and the leadership of the APC that Akwa Ibom State would deliver the highest number of votes for the ruling party’s presidential candidate in the South-South geopolitical zone in the January 16, 2027 general election.

Akpabio, according to a statement from his Media Office, gave the assurance yesterday, at a special religious service organised to dedicate the APC’s 2027 election campaigns to God at the International Christian Worship Centre, Uyo, the Akwa Ibom State capital.

The service, which had the theme, ‘We Are Well Able,’ brought together party leaders, government officials, political stakeholders and supporters to seek divine guidance for the party ahead of the forthcoming general election.

The Senate President, who called on APC members in the state to close ranks and present a united front, said the party could only translate its electoral ambitions into reality if internal divisions and disagreements were set aside.

He attributed his emergence as President of the Senate to the support of Tinubu, describing the development as an opportunity for Akwa Ibom State to demonstrate its appreciation through massive electoral support for the President.

He said, “An Akwa Ibom son, through the support of Mr. President, is today the President of the Senate and the number three citizen of Nigeria. Whether you like him or not, he is there today.

“The only way to thank Mr. President for that support is to give him all our votes. From what I have seen here today, Akwa Ibom State will give Mr. President the highest number of votes in the South-South region.”

In an address titled ‘One Family, One Destiny, One Akwa Ibom Under God,’ the statement explained that Akpabio emphasised the importance of unity, inclusiveness and peaceful coexistence among members of the APC, warning against divisions based on the length of membership or political affiliation.

He maintained that the party should operate as one family in which old and new members enjoy equal opportunities to contribute to its growth and electoral success.

He said, “In the APC family, there should be no aborigines and no newcomers; no landlords and no tenants; no first-class members and no second-class members. There should be only one big family, united by a common purpose and a shared responsibility.

“Those who were here yesterday have a history to honour, and those who arrived today have contributions to make. Neither history nor arrival should become an instrument of exclusion.”

Using a biblical illustration from John 14:2, the Senate President said there was sufficient political space for every member of the party, irrespective of when they joined.

He said, “Our Lord Jesus Christ declared in John 14:2: ‘In my Father’s house are many mansions.’ Let me borrow that beautiful imagery today. In this house, there are many mansions, enough for everyone!
