World.title: Liberia: As Boakai Launches Clean Cities Campaign, Whein Town Residents Renew Demand for Landfill Closure Amid Health Warnings from Experts
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE, Montserrado County — After sunset, when mosquitoes descend on homes in Whein Town, residents say spending time outdoors becomes almost unbearable. During the day, swarms of flies hover around food and businesses, while foul-smelling water and the presence of rodents and snakes fuel fears about what living beside a massive garbage dump may be doing to their health.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

For families in this community outside Monrovia, the struggle is not simply about living near garbage. It is about the growing cost of securing clean water, protecting children from insects and trying to maintain a livelihood in an environment they say has become increasingly difficult to endure.



The source of much of their frustration is the Whein Town Landfill, a facility established as a temporary solution to Liberia’s urban waste problem but still receiving garbage years beyond its intended lifespan.

Residents say the continued dumping has left them feeling abandoned by authorities responsible for managing the waste generated by Monrovia and Paynesville.

“We are being used as sacrificial lambs,” said Amos Moore, a resident who accused the government of failing to honour its commitment to close the landfill after its original five-year lifespan expired.

“It is a shame that the government will unleash such suffering on a large group of its people.”

Samuel Kofi Jones III, Secretary General of the Whein Town Community Leadership, said residents have complained about the landfill for years and have previously protested activities they considered harmful to their community.

For residents such as Moore, the central question is why a facility intended to provide a temporary answer to an urgent sanitation problem has become a seemingly permanent feature of their community, while promises of relief remain unfulfilled.

Their concerns have drawn renewed attention from public health and environmental experts, who warn that poorly managed landfills can expose nearby populations to serious risks, particularly when waste exceeds a facility’s intended capacity.

The Monrovia City Corporation, which manages the facility, acknowledges that the landfill has outlived its usefulness. However, it says it is taking what it describes as “immediate, aggressive action” to address the situation.

For residents, those interventions have yet to resolve their most pressing concern: ending the dumping.

The Cost of Living Beside the Dump

Samuel Kofi Jones III, Secretary General of the Whein Town Community Leadership, said residents have complained about the landfill for years and have previously protested activities they considered harmful to their community.

Residents say the continued dumping has left them feeling abandoned by authorities responsible for managing the waste generated by Monrovia and Paynesville. MCC truck being loaded with garbage for Whein Town Landfill.

Jones recalled an incident around 2012 or 2013 when authorities allegedly brought seized drugs to the area and burned them near the landfill. He said fumes spread into the community, prompting residents to protest and demand greater oversight of activities at the facility.

Following the incident, he said, a community monitoring team was established to observe activities at the landfill.

The team initially comprised eight residents who worked in shifts, including overnight, to monitor what was happening at the site.

But financial constraints eventually reduced the number of monitors to four, Jones said, adding that their stipends have not been paid consistently.

Two groups of community monitors have completed their assignments, while the latest group had worked for about two months awaiting payment, he said.

The monitoring arrangement, intended to give residents a measure of oversight, has not addressed their broader concerns about the continued operation of the facility.

“If you ask me what I want them to do, I would tell you to close the dumpsite,” Jones said.

He maintained that residents remain willing to engage the government but believe authorities have repeatedly failed to follow through on commitments made to the community.

The landfill was established in 2011 under the Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation Project as a temporary, five-year emergency waste-disposal facility managed by the MCC. It was intended to improve the collection and disposal of solid waste in Monrovia and Paynesville.

Firefighter battling a firebreak at the When Town Landfill in February, 2026.

Although accounts of the facility’s development cite both 2011 and 2012, residents agree that its continued operation has far exceeded the original period they understood it would serve.

Fifteen years later, they say, the consequences have become part of everyday life.

When Clean Water Becomes an Added Expense

For Leon Miaway, one of the most persistent problems is the mosquito population.

He said residents struggle to remain outdoors after 5 or 6 p.m., when mosquitoes become particularly troublesome, forcing many families to rely on mosquito nets to protect themselves at night.

Flies create a different problem during the day, especially in the rainy season, when Miaway said they frequently come into contact with food.

For households already struggling with daily expenses, the concerns extend to water.

Miaway said changes to the area where garbage is deposited have raised fears that liquid leaking from waste may be reaching nearby water sources. He believes the absence of adequate containment measures at the newer dumping area has worsened the situation.

The extent of any contamination has not been independently established, but residents say the uncertainty has forced some households to spend additional money on water for drinking and cooking.

“Before you prepare any good food now, it means you have to spend more, even to buy water,” Miaway said.

For families with limited incomes, the added expense can mean making difficult choices between buying water they consider safer and meeting other household needs.

Miaway also said malaria is common in the community and expressed concern about children walking barefoot around areas where stagnant water collects.

He complained that residents had not seen regular visits by government agencies or humanitarian organizations to collect household data or distribute mosquito nets and other supplies.

“It has been a long while, like, over two, three years now,” he said.

The absence of consistent assistance, residents say, has reinforced their belief that they are being left to manage the consequences of the landfill largely on their own.

Dr. Dougbeh Chris Nyan, former Director of the National Public Institute of Liberia, warned that the landfill could also be contributing to greenhouse gas emissions as organic waste decomposes, adding to the broader environmental consequences of poorly managed waste. (Fire outbreak at the landfill in February, 2026).

The residents’ renewed complaints come as President Joseph Nyuma Boakai launches the Presidential Clean Cities Initiative, a nationwide sanitation programme intended to support urban cleanliness, improve environmental health and create employment opportunities for young Liberians.

For residents of Whein Town, however, the campaign presents a troubling contradiction: while the government is mobilizing young people to clean cities and communities, their own neighbourhood continues to receive mountains of garbage from Monrovia and Paynesville, despite longstanding concerns about the landfill’s capacity and environmental condition.

They fear that unless the government addresses the continued operation of the Whein Town landfill, the clean cities campaign will fail to achieve its intended purpose for communities bearing the greatest burden of urban waste disposal.

Without addressing the conditions in Whein Town, residents fear the Clean Cities Initiative could improve the appearance of urban centres while leaving an already burdened community to continue paying the environmental price

“As long as the landfill is not closed, this cannot be a clean cities’ campaign. This is more pollution, more suffering and more sickness,” said Elijah Johnson, a student of the University of Liberia. We have complained for years that this is a death trap, yet still no solution.

‘They Are Still Dumping Every Day’

Princess Dennis, another resident, said families living near the landfill are increasingly worried about illnesses they associate with the surrounding conditions.

She cited malaria and other infections as concerns, particularly for children, and said previous mosquito-net distributions did not reach everyone.

Dennis alleged that some distributions stopped around a telecommunications junction, leaving residents in other parts of the community without nets.

But she stressed that receiving mosquito nets or other relief items would not resolve what residents consider the underlying problem.

“I’m upset about the dumpsite here,” she said, appealing to the authorities to stop the continued dumping of waste.

Dennis said garbage trucks continue to bring waste to the facility every day despite the community’s complaints.

She also operates a business along the road near the landfill, where she said flies affect customers and force her to cover her goods.

For a small business owner, the problem is both a public health concern and an economic burden: maintaining basic hygiene becomes more difficult when flies are constantly present.

Water insecurity compounds the difficulty.

Dennis said some residents sometimes consume water they consider unsafe because they cannot afford alternatives.

“When we don’t get money, we can drink the water,” she said.

Her account illustrates the difficult choices confronting households that cannot consistently pay for alternative water supplies but fear the possible consequences of using nearby sources.

Residents have raised concerns about illnesses ranging from malaria and diarrhoeal diseases to more serious conditions they believe may be associated with environmental pollution. However, establishing whether the landfill is responsible for particular illnesses requires clinical evidence and independent environmental testing.

For residents, the lack of clear information about water quality and potential exposure remains a source of anxiety.

Residents Fear Another Confrontation

Despite their frustration, some residents are reluctant to organize direct action against the landfill.

Miaway recalled previous protests during which residents blocked roads and some participants were arrested. He said the community does not want a repeat of those incidents and prefers its leadership to negotiate with authorities on its behalf.

The hesitation reflects a difficult position: residents want the dumping to stop but fear that confrontations could lead to arrests without delivering a lasting solution.

They have instead continued to press their case through community meetings, local leaders and calls for government intervention.

Their demand is not limited to mosquito control, water provision or occasional medical outreach. They want the landfill closed or relocated.

That demand has also been reflected in previous petitions to the Legislature, in which residents sought intervention over the facility’s continued operation and the lack of basic services in the community.

For them, years of complaints and temporary interventions have not delivered the change they seek.

Experts Warn of Environmental and Public Health Risks

Dr. Dougbeh Chris Nyan, a former Director General of the National Public Health Institute of Liberia and an infectious disease expert, said landfills can become serious environmental and public health hazards when they are overfilled and inadequately managed.

Dr. Nyan said the Whein Town facility has affected wildlife, may have contributed to rodent infestation and has reduced available living space in the surrounding area, contributing to community congestion.

He warned that congestion can facilitate the spread of infectious diseases, particularly when sanitation and other basic services are inadequate.

Dr. Nyan also cited findings from empirical studies conducted around 2022–2023 by public health students at the African Methodist Episcopal University. He said the studies indicated contamination of soil, streams, wells and other groundwater sources around the area.

Those findings, he said, raise concerns about possible exposure to gastrointestinal infections and other illnesses.

FrontPage Africa has not independently reviewed the studies’ methodology or results. Further investigation would be needed to establish the extent of any contamination and determine its sources.

Dr. Nyan said residents have also reported respiratory symptoms that warrant clinical documentation and investigation to determine whether exposure to polluted air is contributing to their health problems.

He warned that the landfill could also be contributing to greenhouse gas emissions as organic waste decomposes, adding to the broader environmental consequences of poorly managed waste.

His most serious concern is the possibility of a landslide or collapse at the site, which he said could result in loss of life and property.

Dr. Nyan called on the government to enforce the landfill’s closure and invest in recycling, reuse and waste-reduction programmes.

He also urged Liberia to consider stronger restrictions on plastic use as part of a broader effort to reduce the volume of waste reaching disposal sites.

For Dr. Nyan, continued dumping at a facility believed to have reached its capacity raises questions about how long the government can delay a more sustainable solution without exposing communities to additional risks.

‘The Environmental Burden Is Borne by Nearby Communities’

Mohammed W. Bah, a Liberian researcher and PhD student in Urban and Environmental Planning and Policy at the University of California, Irvine, said a landfill that exceeds its intended capacity can create serious environmental and public health problems when waste is no longer properly contained.

Bah, whose research focuses on climate adaptation, coastal vulnerability, climate-related displacement and relocation, said exposed garbage can attract flies, rodents and other disease vectors. Mohammed W. Bah, a Liberian researcher and PhD student in Urban and Environmental Planning and Policy at the University of California, Irvine, said a landfill that exceeds its intended capacity can create serious environmental and public health problems when waste is no longer properly contained.

Poorly controlled waste and leachate—the liquid that drains from decomposing garbage—can contaminate soil and surface or groundwater, while open burning and landfill fires can worsen air quality.

“These risks are particularly concerning when residential communities are located close to the site, as in Whein Town,” he said.

Bah also described the situation as an environmental justice issue, noting that communities located near waste facilities often bear disproportionate environmental and health burdens associated with services used by larger populations.

He said residents should have access to information about the landfill’s condition, environmental monitoring results, closure plans and measures being taken to protect them.

As an immediate response, Bah called for uncontrolled dumping to stop, exposed waste to be properly contained and covered, and disease vectors such as mosquitoes, flies and rodents to be controlled.

He also recommended assessments of water and soil contamination, improved drainage and leachate management, and access to safe drinking water for surrounding communities.

Given reports that the facility has exceeded its intended capacity and design life, Bah said an independent assessment should determine whether it can continue operating safely.

“If the site has exceeded its designed lifespan and can no longer be safely operated, the solution cannot merely be to continue adding waste indefinitely,” he said.

He called for a planned transition to an alternative disposal facility, accompanied by the proper closure and environmental remediation of Whein Town.

But Bah cautioned that moving the landfill would not, on its own, resolve Liberia’s wider waste-management problems.

The government, he said, must improve garbage collection, promote waste separation and recycling, encourage reuse and strengthen enforcement against illegal dumping.

“Whein Town demonstrates why environmental planning has to be proactive rather than reactive,” Bah said.

“Once a temporary solution becomes permanent without necessary infrastructure, monitoring and long-term planning, the environmental burden is often borne by nearby communities.”

MCC Acknowledges Landfill Has ‘Outlived Its Usefulness’

The Monrovia City Corporation says it recognizes the challenges at Whein Town and is pursuing measures to address them.

In a statement to FrontPage Africa, the MCC said it was taking “immediate, aggressive action” to tackle technical challenges at the facility, acknowledging that the landfill “has outlived its usefulness” and that the rainy season has compounded the situation.

“The MCC considers the health concerns of the residents as a top priority; as such, we are constantly fumigating the facility and providing routine health care interventions to the residents,” the corporation said.

The MCC also said mosquito nets had been distributed in the community and that it conducted a free medical outreach between March and April 2026. Whein Town Landfill, a facility established as a temporary solution to Liberia’s urban waste problem but still receiving garbage years beyond its intended lifespan.

Addressing allegations that garbage was being dumped directly on the ground, the corporation said it remained committed to responsible waste disposal and “would do nothing to endanger the health of the people of Whein Town.”

The corporation further disclosed that it was at an advanced stage of concluding a public-private partnership framework with a private-sector company for the joint management of the sanitary landfill.

However, the statement did not specify when the proposed partnership would be finalized, what immediate changes it would bring to waste disposal practices, or whether the arrangement would lead to the landfill’s closure.

The MCC’s acknowledgment that the site has outlived its usefulness is significant, but residents remain concerned about the continued arrival of garbage and the absence of a publicly established closure timetable.

Its claims of fumigation, medical outreach and mosquito-net distribution also contrast with residents’ accounts of inconsistent assistance and the persistence of mosquitoes, flies and concerns about water quality.

The different accounts underscore the need for transparent information about the frequency and coverage of the corporation’s interventions, alongside independent monitoring of environmental conditions.

Beyond Fumigation: A Lasting Solution

The MCC’s proposed partnership could offer a route toward improved management, but experts say the long-term solution must address the landfill’s capacity, environmental condition and eventual closure if it can no longer be operated safely.

A credible response would also require reliable access to safe drinking water, independent testing of nearby wells and other water sources, and public disclosure of the results.

For residents, such steps would provide more than reassurance. They would help establish whether the water they use is safe, clarify the health risks they face and identify which interventions are urgently needed.

The government must also explain the status of alternative waste-disposal arrangements and how it intends to prevent an indefinite continuation of the current situation.

Liberia’s growing urban population requires an effective waste-management system. But residents of Whein Town argue that the need to dispose of garbage from Monrovia and Paynesville cannot justify leaving one community to shoulder the risks without adequate safeguards.

Their experience highlights a broader challenge: waste infrastructure cannot be considered successful if the environmental costs are transferred to the people living closest to it.

For Jones, Miaway, Dennis and Moore, the immediate issue remains personal. It is about whether families can eat without flies hovering over their food, obtain water without worrying about contamination and allow children to move around their neighbourhood without fearing the conditions surrounding them.

The MCC says it is taking action. Experts say the risks warrant urgent assessment and intervention. Residents, however, say they have heard promises before.

“We are being used as sacrificial lambs,” Moore said.

For Whein Town, the test of the government’s response will not be another promise or a temporary distribution of supplies. It will be whether the dumping ends, the environmental risks are properly assessed and the community finally receives the protection and basic services its residents say they have been denied for years.

World.title: Liberia: Rural Women Wait as Corruption Case Over Money Meant for Them Stalls in Court
World.content:
A rural woman trader serves a customer at Yarkpah’s Town market in River Cess County

Summary

Women in River Cess, who were some of the intended recipients of a 2023 US$1.7 million fund that investigators say was stolen, have expressed anger at the theft of badly needed money by officials from the Weah administration.

They have also faulted the government’s transparency saying they knew nothing about the fund before the arrests made news.

Liberia’s Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force indicted seven people in April over the alleged diversion of money. There is no word on when the case will go to trial.

By Joyclyn Wea and Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon with New Narratives

TARKUN TOWN, River Cess County – Before daylight, MissionMai Sam heads for her coconut and palm farm. The mother of eight and her husband who cuts palm for a living, have spent years growing and selling what she can, hoping to make the farm bigger and earn enough to keep all of their eight children in school.



So, when Sam, 48, learned that a Weah government program had set aside money to help vulnerable rural women like her, and that it was stolen by government officials, she was angry.

“They are wicked,” Sam says. “They send their children to big big school, then we here are suffering.”

In April, Liberia’s Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force, indicted seven people over the alleged diversion of money from the 2023 Vulnerable Small Business Support Program, which was meant in part to fund the Rural Women Empowerment Fund. Those charged include former Mawine G. Diggs, Weah government commerce minister and officials connected to the ministry, the National Rural Women Structure of Liberia and the Liberia Marketing Association.

Court filings from June said US$493,000 and more than LRD 190 million (US1.2 million) was budgeted and disbursed but did not reach the beneficiaries and was instead used for personal gain. Those indicted face charges including theft of property, economic sabotage and criminal conspiracy.

The case has become the latest test of President Joseph Boakai’s anti-corruption drive. He created a Task Force in March 2024 to trace and recover stolen public assets. Since then, the Task Force has announced four rounds of indictments covering more than 60 cases and tens of millions of dollars in alleged theft. But nearly two years after it was established, it has won just one case.

In October, a jury at Criminal Court “C” found eight of 13 defendants guilty in the separate Saudi Rice corruption trial.

Those found guilty included former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf. Three defendants were acquitted and the jury reached inconclusive verdicts for two others. The case concerned 29,412 bags of Saudi-donated rice valued at about US$500,000; prosecutors alleged 25,054 bags had been diverted or misapplied. The Task Force says it would defend the verdicts against possible appeals.

Women interviewed here in River Cess say money the funds say could have helped them expand farms, keep children in school, and become less dependent on others.

In Yarkpa’s Town, Jestina Johnson has sold dry and frozen goods for 20 years, buying from Buchanan and Monrovia and reselling them to support six children. She says she heard only vague talk that money had been sent for market women. She never received any.

Johnson says she was told she needed an identification card, but she did not understand what kind. She already had a business card and nobody clearly explained what additional document was required. By the time she thought to ask again, the opportunity had passed.

She now wants justice, not just arrests. “Let’s carry them to court,” she says.

Even the county authorities tasked with distributing the funds say they knew nothing about the project. Oretha W. Carlos coordinates the Gender Ministry’s work in River Cess and serves as an official of the Rural Women Empowerment Project, the local structure through which the fund was supposed to operate.

She says she learned about the fund from this reporter, not from the government she served.

“I am the secretary; I am not aware,” Carlos says. She said she would feel bad if money intended to help rural women was sent and then kept in other people’s hands.

Saikon Johnson Hiennis works inside her small shop in River Cess County, where she has traded for more than a decade.

Even small amounts can go a long way for these women. Carlos says L$30,000 (US$176) she received through the rural women’s structure after a conference in Gbarnga, Bong County helped her expand a small shop selling rice, clothes and cooked food. With six children in school, she says properly managed support can help women pay school fees and build something their children can inherit.

Saikon Johnson Hiennis, who has traded in River Cess for more than a decade, says she heard about the fund on radio and from people passing through from other parts of the country. Her concern now is whether those arrested will lead anywhere.

“There’s a saying in this country now that when something happens after two to three days, it dies down,” Hiennis says. She wants to see justice done publicly so people can see that accountability is real.

Taskforce officials urged the community to be patient saying the indictment is only the start of a process that must move through the courts according to Liberian law before assets can be forfeited.

“Indictment is actually the beginning of the process towards conviction,” says Joseph Daniels, the Task Force’s public relations officer. “Without indictment we are heading nowhere.”

In June, Criminal Court ‘C’ denied Diggs permission to travel to the United States for medical treatment after an independent medical assessment found insufficient evidence that she needed care abroad. She remains barred from leaving Liberia. Daniels says no trial date has been set by the court.

Daniels blames the delays on an overloaded Criminal Court ‘C’, which handles corruption cases and the nine-month Supreme Court stay that temporarily froze the Task Force’s authority after a company under investigation challenged its legal standing.

Daniels points to another case as evidence that recovery efforts are still moving – the Task Force has traced about £8 million (US$10.70 million) to a British bank account and is pursuing proceedings in the United Kingdom, with support from partners in Ghana and the United States’ Federal Bureau of Investigations.

The backlog has strengthened calls for a dedicated anti-corruption court. Supporters argue that a specialized court could reduce the burden on Criminal Court ‘C’ and move corruption cases faster. President Boakai submitted a National Anti-Corruption Court bill to the Legislature in May 2026.

The proposal has also moved slowly. The Senate Judiciary Committee paused its review in May over process concerns and began consultations in June on competing versions of the bill which is also tied to a bill that would establish a war and economic crimes court. Advocates are urging the Legislature to pass both bills before Liberia takes the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council next month.

MissionMai Sam arranges freshly harvested palm fruits on her farm in Tarkun, River Cess County.

Civil society groups have welcomed the indictments but warned that prosecutions alone will not solve Liberia’s wider corruption problem. Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia, a transparency watchdog, has argued that the country also needs stronger procurement rules and public financial management.

In Tarkun, Sam is less interested in the mechanics of indictments, court motions, or legislative bills. She wants the government to finish the case and make sure rural women do not simply disappear from the story once the arrests fade from the news.

“Government should not forget about it,” she said. “Let them give our money so we can make our farms.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” project. Support for this reporting came from individual donors.

World.title: Liberia: Former NSA Official Jallah Seeks New Trail after Conviction for Statutory Rape and Kidnapping
World.content:
Monrovia – Criminal Court “E” at the Temple of Justice has scheduled a hearing for Monday, November 2, at 10 a.m. on a motion for a new trial filed by Peter Bon Jallah, former National Security Agency, NSA official convicted of statutory rape and kidnapping involving a 16-year-old boy.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

The hearing presents the next crucial test in a closely watched criminal case after Assigned Circuit Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr., sitting without a jury, found Jallah guilty of two of the three charges brought against him but acquitted him of gang rape.



FrontPage Africa has been informed by court sources that the court has received the motion and will hear arguments on Monday.

Depending on the outcome, the court is expected to proceed with a pre-sentence hearing, followed by the imposition of judgment and sentence, subject to the applicable procedures and any further orders from the judge.

Jallah’s defense is seeking to overturn the verdict, arguing that aspects of the court’s findings are inconsistent with the evidence and that legal and procedural errors warrant a new trial. The motion was filed on October 27, four days after Judge Wesseh delivered the verdict on October 23.

It asked the court to set aside the convictions and reconsider the case. The outcome of Monday’s hearing could determine whether the proceedings move toward sentencing or whether the case returns to trial.

A Split Verdict

On October 23, Judge Wesseh found Jallah guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping but acquitted him of gang rape. The ruling followed a bench trial in which the judge evaluated testimony, documentary evidence, medical findings, forensic evidence, and arguments from both the prosecution and defense.

The three charges arose from allegations involving a 16-year-old boy who reportedly performed paid domestic chores at Jallah’s residence in Monrovia.

According to the indictment, prosecutors alleged that Jallah sexually assaulted the boy on multiple occasions in late 2025 and that a subsequent incident in January 2026 involved the boy being taken to a building in the Camp Johnson Road area, where he was allegedly held for several days and sexually abused.

The indictment also named two unidentified men in connection with the allegations. Those individuals were not brought before the court during Jallah’s trial.

The court ultimately found the prosecution’s evidence sufficient to establish statutory rape and kidnapping but insufficient to sustain a conviction for gang rape. Following the verdict, Jallah was ordered remanded at Monrovia Central Prison, pending a pre-sentence and behavioral report from the Ministry of Justice’s Bureau of Probation Services. The court had not imposed a sentence when the verdict was announced.

Defense Challenged Convictions

In the motion for a new trial, defense lawyer Cllr. G. Wiefueh Alfred Sayeh advances several arguments challenging the legal and evidentiary basis of the verdict.

One central argument is that the kidnapping conviction is inconsistent with the acquittal on the gang rape charge.

The defense contends that the two charges are tied to the same alleged episode of confinement at Camp Johnson Road and argues that the court’s conclusions cannot be reconciled.

The defense also challenged Criminal Court “E”’s jurisdiction over the separate kidnapping charge, arguing that the specialized sexual-offenses court lacks authority to adjudicate that offense in the circumstances of the case.

Another major issue raised in the motion concerns the medical and forensic evidence presented during the trial. The defense argued that the evidence did not adequately establish penetration, which it said is an essential element of the rape charge.

It points to testimony concerning the complainant’s medical examination and to the limitations of the DNA findings presented by the prosecution. The motion further alleged that the defendant did not receive a fair trial.

Among other claims, the defense questions the judge’s handling of telephone records obtained during the proceedings and argues that the court improperly took steps to obtain additional evidence.

These remain arguments advanced by the defense and have not been established as findings of judicial error. Judge Wesseh is expected to consider the motion and any response from the prosecution before deciding whether the legal threshold for a new trial has been met.

Prosecution Presented Extensive Evidence

During the trial, the prosecution presented 13 regular witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses, according to reporting on the court’s written verdict. The witnesses included the complainant, police investigators, medical personnel, and Pascal Bavugirije, a forensic examiner associated with the Rwanda Forensic Institute. The prosecution also relied on DNA analysis involving four clothing exhibits.

Testimony reported during the proceedings indicated that DNA profiles from the exhibits matched Jallah’s reference sample, although the forensic findings did not establish precisely when or how the biological material was deposited.

The defense called eight witnesses, including Jallah, and subpoenaed witnesses from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Orange Liberia, and the John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

Throughout the proceedings, the defense challenged the consistency of the complainant’s account, the interpretation of the forensic findings, and the sufficiency of the state’s evidence.

The prosecution, meanwhile, maintained, during final arguments, that the evidence supported convictions on the charges. Judge Wesseh’s October 23 ruling resolved the trial at the initial level, but the defense’s motion now places the legal sufficiency and consistency of the verdict before the same court for further consideration.

Case History Marked by Delays

The case passed through several procedural stages before the verdict was delivered. Jallah was arrested on January 7, 2026, following a complaint to the police Women and Children Protection Section.

A grand jury subsequently indicted him and two unidentified men on charges of statutory rape, gang rape and kidnapping during the February 2026 term of court.

He was arraigned on June 18, 2026, pleaded not guilty and elected to be tried by a judge rather than a jury. The case was initially assigned to Criminal Assizes Court “A” for Montserrado County before being transferred to Criminal Court “E” for trial.

Proceedings were delayed after the prosecution sought a change of venue.

Following the denial of that request, prosecutors petitioned for a writ of certiorari, but the petition was denied, and the case was ordered to proceed.

The expiration of the court’s regular sitting created another interruption before the matter was reassigned for trial on August 5, 2026. After the prosecution and defense completed the presentation of their cases and delivered final arguments on October 22, Judge Wesseh reserved his ruling for the following day.

The October 23 decision resulted in convictions on statutory rape and kidnapping, alongside an acquittal on gang rape.

Monday’s hearing will determine whether the court upholds its original decision or grants the defense’s request for a new trial. If the motion is denied, the court may proceed toward sentencing after considering the required pre-sentence report and hearing any submissions relevant to the sentence.

If the motion is granted, the case could return to trial in accordance with the court’s order.

The defense has also indicated its intention to appeal the verdict to the Supreme Court of Liberia, although the timing and procedural requirements of any appeal will depend on the court’s subsequent actions and applicable law.

For now, Jallah remains subject to the court’s remand order while the proceedings continue. The November 2 hearing is therefore expected to be a decisive moment because of the defendant’s former position within the country’s national security establishment and the seriousness of the offenses at issue.

The hearing is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Monday, November 2, at Criminal Court “E,” Temple of Justice, Monrovia.

World.title: Liberia: AML Reaffirms Support to Liberia’s Future, Says Country Ready for Global Mining Boom
World.content:
Unification Town, Margibi County— ArcelorMittal Liberia, one of the country’s largest investors in the mining sector, has reaffirmed its commitment to Liberia’s development agenda, highlighting its investments in iron ore production, railway infrastructure, and industrial expansion as key drivers of economic growth.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The company’s Chief Executive Officer, Michiel van der Merwe, said ArcelorMittal Liberia is helping position the country as a strategic supplier of premium iron ore to global markets while creating opportunities for industrial development and long-term economic growth.



Speaking at the Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Expo (LIMEC), held at the Farmington Hotel, van der Merwe stated that Liberia has the mineral resources, strategic location, and investment potential needed to compete in the global mining and energy sectors.

The conference marks the return of a major mining and energy gathering in Liberia after approximately 15 years.

Mining and Energy as Drivers of Economic Growth

Van der Merwe told the gathering that the future of Liberia’s economic growth depends partly on the country’s ability to capitalize on its natural resources while building strong partnerships among government, investors, industry players, and local communities.

He noted that countries capable of providing stable investment conditions, strong partnerships, and high-quality mineral resources are better positioned to attract investment and compete in international markets.

According to him, Liberia possesses many of these advantages but must strengthen collaboration and demonstrate sustained commitment to translate its potential into lasting prosperity for its citizens.

He also emphasized the importance of developing Liberian talent, saying investments in human capital would help ensure that future generations can lead and sustain the industries being established today.

Phase II Expansion Positions AML for Growth

Van der Merwe explained that ArcelorMittal Liberia’s experience demonstrates the benefits of long-term partnerships built on trust, commitment, and a shared development vision.

He pointed to the company’s Phase II Expansion Project as evidence of its long-term commitment to Liberia, describing the investment as a major transformation of the country’s iron ore industry.

He recounted that the commissioning of Liberia’s first large-scale iron ore concentrator represents a significant milestone for both the company and the country.

“It enables Liberia to move higher up the value chain by producing premium iron ore concentrate for international markets for current steel mills as well as the next generation of steel mills with lower carbon emissions technology.”

For him, the project demonstrates Liberia’s ability to attract and execute large-scale industrial investments capable of creating jobs, building local capacity, and strengthening national infrastructure.

US$800 Million Invested in Railway and Port Infrastructure

Beyond its investment in the concentrator, the AML chief threw light on the rehabilitation and expansion of the railway linking the company’s mining operations at Tokadeh to the Port of Buchanan.

Although the railway and port facilities are government-owned assets, van der Merwe maintains that ArcelorMittal has invested approximately US$800 million to date in rehabilitating the railway and expanding its capacity to accommodate the company’s planned growth.

He described the railway as critical infrastructure for supporting future mining operations and creating opportunities for other investors to transport minerals through the corridor.

The company’s investment, he asserted, has laid the groundwork for a multiuser railway system intended to support broader mining development in Liberia.

AML Targets More Than 20 Million Tons in 2027

Van der Merwe revealed that ArcelorMittal Liberia is preparing to increase its iron ore exports to more than 20 million tons in 2027, up from less than five million tons exported in 2024.

The projected increase follows the introduction of the company’s new concentrator and the expansion of supporting infrastructure.

“That’s a quadrupling of tonnage exported from Liberia,” he declared.

He added that the company is also planning to increase production capacity at its mines to 30 million tons, noting that the current railway expansion already accommodates this anticipated growth and could allow other users to access surplus capacity in the interim.

The planned expansion is expected to strengthen Liberia’s position in the international iron ore market while increasing demand for supporting services and infrastructure.

Government Reaffirms Multiuser Railway Commitment

Van der Merwe reiterated ArcelorMittal Liberia’s commitment to working with the Government of Liberia to ensure that the Tokadeh-to-Buchanan railway remains accessible to other mining companies.

He indicated that the company supports the position maintained by successive presidential administrations that the railway should operate as a multiuser asset, allowing other investors to benefit from the infrastructure.

The Third Amendment to the company’s Mineral Development Agreement, ratified earlier this year, provides for the railway to be open to other users, with the Government of Liberia determining which additional companies may access the corridor.

He told the gathering that prospective users would be responsible for financing their own expansion requirements, while benefiting from the foundational investments already made by ArcelorMittal Liberia.

“The recent Third Amendment to our Mineral Development Agreement, that was ratified earlier this year ensures that this is a railway open to all users, with the Government of Liberia deciding who else can utilize this infrastructure.”

Van der Merwe further disclosed that the operating framework for the multiuser railway, discussed by three successive administrations over the past decade, is being formalized through the Rail Systems Operating Principles (RSOP).

He accentuated that the principles provide for the railway to be operated by an independent company beginning in 2030.

Calls for Independent Railway Operator

The AML chief called for the establishment of an independent railway operator, describing the move as an important step toward transforming Liberia’s economy and expanding access to critical infrastructure.

He intoned that the cooperation among the government, investors, and industry could create the conditions necessary for sustainable economic growth.

“More importantly, it lays the foundation for a truly shared infrastructure platform that can unlock new mining opportunities, attract further investment, and accelerate national development,” van der Merwe said.

He added that the vision of shared infrastructure and prosperity extends beyond mining and rail transportation, requiring a collective commitment to national development.

Van der Merwe also disclosed that ArcelorMittal Liberia is in agreement with the government on the establishment of a National Rail Authority that would eventually oversee the development and management of additional railway corridors across the country.

The AML CEO clarified that the company wants the operating principles governing the Tokadeh-to-Buchanan railway to be recognized when the proposed authority is established.

AML Pledges Long-Term Partnership

, van der Merwe informed the conference that Liberia’s development ambitions could not be achieved by any single company, government institution, or investor acting alone.

At the same time, he is of the conviction that sustained cooperation could help create an environment in which investment flourishes, industries expand, and communities benefit from economic opportunities.

“ArcelorMittal Liberia remains committed to playing its part in that journey. We’ve played this part for the last twenty years and we are ready to do so for another forty years or more.”

World.title: Kanyelele Bridge completed
World.content:
The newly constructed Kanyelele Bridge in Mpika District, Muchinga Province, is set to permanently resolve the severe transport and logistical challenges that have long affected local residents and motorists.

This follows the successful completion of the multi-million-kwacha Kanyelele bridge.

The bridge was constructed by the Zambia National Service (ZNS) and funded through the National Disaster Risk Management Division (NDRMD).

The completion of the bridge was confirmed by the Division’s Director for Disaster Humanitarian and Operations Management, Amos Mumba, during a site inspection visit conducted to assess the quality of works ahead of the bridge’s official commissioning.

Mr Mumba said the bridge is a strategic piece of infrastructure that directly connects the district to the Kanyelele Gold Mine, thereby enhancing access to the area and supporting economic activities.

He stated that the Kanyelele and Sasubele bridges, together with several other crossing points being constructed across Muchinga Province at a total cost of over 9,098,255 kwacha are fundamentally transforming the lives of local communities.

Mr Mumba, however, cautioned that while the permanent infrastructure is capable of supporting heavy mining machinery, proactive control measures must be implemented immediately to regulate traffic and safeguard the bridge’s long-term durability.

Meanwhile, for local motorists, the completion of the bridge marks the end of a perilous and frustrating chapter, as they will no longer have to contend with the challenges and risks previously associated with crossing the Kanyelele River.

Jackson Sichula, a local motorist, expressed his gratitude to the government for delivering on its promise.

He recounted the challenges drivers faced prior to the construction, noting that accessing neighbouring areas was often an impossible task.

“We used to get cut off completely,” Mr. Sichula explained. “Driving through this area was a nightmare, especially during the rainy season.”

“Vehicles would get stuck, and sometimes we had to cancel trips entirely, which crippled our business. This bridge is a lifesaver,” he added.

Mr Sichula said the lack of a proper crossing point previously paralyzed daily life in the district, directly impacting agriculture, education, and healthcare.

He noted that before the ZNS intervention, farmers, school-going children, and community members could not cross to either side of the river whenever water levels rose.

Mr Sichula also highlighted that farmers watched their produce spoil as they failed to reach markets, while pupils routinely missed classes for days due to the dangerous currents.

And Frezer Ndaba, a resident of Mpika, thanked the government for the development, describing the construction of the bridge as a turning point for the community.

“For a long time, our children risked their lives trying to get to school, and simple errands across the river were impossible. This bridge restores our dignity and opens up our area for real growth,” he stated.

The Kanyelele Bridge is now undergoing final assessments and is expected to be officially commissioned soon, permanently restoring safe, year-round connectivity to Mpika District.

World.title: ZRA Trains Journalists in Taxation
World.content:
Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) Senior Tax Consultant Taxpayer Services and Education, Adrian Saluti says paying taxes plays a major role in the country’s development process.

Mr Saluti notes that revenue collected helps Government finance various sectors and progammes such as health, education, road works, pay salaries, CDF and infrastructure development among many other essential services.

He explained that taxation has played a significant role in the development of many countries, where citizens pay higher taxes than in Zambia, and that this is why Zambians should comply with their tax obligations.

Mr Saluti was speaking during a media workshop for Lusaka Province-based journalists in Chongwe District, when he explained how the construction sector has benefited from these taxes.

“The construction sector plays a vital role in Zambia’s economic development through infrastructure development, job creation and the growth of businesses across the country,” Mr. Saluti said.

He added that sustainable business growth goes beyond delivering quality projects, as it requires tax compliance hence ZRA’s promotion of a culture of voluntary tax compliance that supports business sustainability, fair competition and national development.

Mr Saluti said that funding public service expenditure through tax revenue helps reduce the country’s dependence on foreign aid.

Meanwhile, ZRA Senior Corporate Affairs Officer Robert Zawe explained that a well-informed media will be able to give the nation accurate and timely information on taxation, which the public can use to make informed decisions.

Mr Zawe said interactions between ZRA and different media organisations helps to identify gaps, find solutions and help in asking the right questions which will be beneficial to everyone including the public.

He stated that some people get scammed at border posts by people purporting to be agents because they lack basic information on how certain operations are done.

He encouraged the public to take advantage of online platforms by the institution where information on ZRA matters are well explained through accurate information.

World.title: Government to continue pursuing coordinated mental health responses
World.content:
Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security Permanent Secretary, Dickson Matembo, says government will continue to pursue a stronger and more coordinated mental health response for the correctional sector by deepening collaboration between the Zambia Correctional Service and health sector.

Mr Matembo says mental health cannot be left at the margins of the health system alone, adding that people including inmates experiencing mental health conditions must be cared for rather than excluded from society.

The Permanent Secretary stated that mental illness particularly among inmates is a health condition that must be approached through compassion, professional assessment, treatment, psychosocial support and where appropriate rehabilitation and reintegration.

ZANIS reports that he said this during the 2026 International Day of Prayer and Action for Inmates at Mwembeshi Remand Prison and Correctional Centre in Chilanga district.

And Mr Matembo noted the government’s concern particularly about the relationship between mental health and substance abuse, saying that incarceration measures alone cannot adequately address the challenges.

“Accountability must be accompanied by prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and reintegration. This is why the national response initiative programme increasingly brings together professionals, communities, families, religious institutions and other stakeholders, ” he said.

Mr Matembo implored the Zambia Correctional Service to strengthen the evidence based mental health programmes, stating that a good mental health policy requires reliable information on the needs of inmates and officers, the services available to them and outcomes of interventions.

“To every inmate who is struggling with mental illness, remember that you are not forgotten, your condition does not define the whole of your life. There is still room for treatment, growth, reconciliation and hope,” he encouraged the inmates.

The Permanent Secretary noted the need for the International Day of Prayer and Action for Inmates to bring renewed commitment to Zambia where mental health is treated as a matter of public health, human dignity and shared commitment.

Meanwhile, Zambia Correctional Service Deputy Commissioner General, Bwalya Kuyomba, explained the theme, a mentally ill inmate is also a patient: a call for compassion reminds every one of the physical, emotional and spiritual needs of inmates that require attention.

Mr Kuyomba revealed the mental illness has increasingly taken centre stage in the correctional health agenda, as psychological wellbeing is integral to rehabilitation and successful reintegration.

“With support from the government we continue to build a correctional environment where seeking help is encouraged. An inmate who is supported can participate meaningfully in rehabilitation and an officer whose wellbeing is protected can serve professionally and compassionately,” he said.

He also thanked the government for policies s7ch as the free education and skills training, disclosing that for the first time in history over 7500 inmates and former inmates have obtained TEVETA certificates over the past five years.

Mr Kuyomba said this has equipped them with practical skills for livelihood and economic independence upon release.

“We have also seen increased enrolment of inmates in general certificates of education examinations and through partnerships with universities, access to tertiary education in both humanities and natural sciences. Facilities are becoming places of learning, personal development and renewed opportunity, ” he added.

Giving homily, an inmate Winfred Mapapayi stressed the need to treat mentally ill inmates with compassion and a sense of restoration in that they are also humans that need care, restoration, love and not isolation.

Mr Mapapayi explained mental illness comes about due to a number of psychological trauma that requires treatment.

Meanwhile, another inmate Hope Nyirenda thanked the government, religious organisations among other stakeholders for the continued support towards the inmate’s spiritual, emotional wellbeing and overall welfare.

World.title: Mweetwa dismisses speculations of why he is not in new cabinet
World.content:
Choma Central Member of Parliament, Cornelius Mweetwa has dismissed social media speculation that his exclusion from the new Cabinet and that of other former ministers is due to political misalignment or working with the opposition.

Speaking at a press briefing in Lusaka, Mr Mweetwa, who is also a UPND National Management member, said his non-inclusion alongside other former ministers is a normal exercise of presidential prerogative.

The Choma Central law – maker, who served as Minister of Information and Media in the 2021-2026 administration, expressed gratitude for his five years of service.

He emphasised that under Articles 173 and 259 of the Republican Constitution, the President has the exclusive power to determine Cabinet composition based on national interest, regional balance, ethnicity and gender.

“The President has absolute jurisdiction regarding appointment or termination of any individual within his administration. No individual has an inherent right to a Cabinet position and all Members of Parliament are considered equal,” he said.

ZANIS reports that Mr Mweetwa explicitly refuted claims that he was dropped for working with a former UPND MP or the opposition, explaining that a new term following a general election necessitates a fresh team with new skill sets and energy rather than a direct carryover from the previous administration.

He noted that there are about 237 Members of Parliament available to serve, adding that no one can therefore claim entitlement to appointment.

The parliamentarian reaffirmed his unwavering loyalty to President Hakainde Hichilema and the UPND, describing himself as a disciple of the President with whom he shares a history of political struggle.

Mr Mweetwa said he is not personally disturbed by being left out and will continue to serve as MP for Choma Central, as a national management member of the party and as a patriotic citizen.

He further pledged full support for President Hichilema’s “Grow Zambia Agenda” aimed at economic growth and improved livelihoods.

Mweetwa also urged fellow UPND members, to guard against propaganda intended to cause disunity within the party and government and to remain steadfast against opposition attempts to sow division

World.title: Vice President to grace world’s leading Global Child Nutrition forum
World.content:
Vice President, Mutale Nalumango, will tomorrow grace the world’s leading Global Child Nutrition Forum on behalf of President Hakainde Hichilema.

The Forum, which will attract over 65 countries worldwide, is being hosted by Zambia in collaboration with the Global Child Nutrition Foundation.

The event aims to foster learning, collaboration, and provide technical support for countries implementing school feeding programmes such as Zambia.

Speaking during a pre-forum briefing meeting, Permanent Secretary in the Office of the Vice President Lillian Kapusana, announced that Mrs Nalumango would be representing President Hichilema at the forum.

ZANIS reports that Mrs Kapusana highlighted the importance that President Hakainde Hichilema attaches to this initiative, aimed at supporting countries in their efforts to implement effective school feeding programmes.

She underscored President Hichilema’s keen interest and passion in good nutrition in the country, citing that the country’s nutrition coordinating office was placed under the Vice President’s office to ensure the establishment of good policies as well as governance in the matter.

Mrs Kapusana, who is also the Deputy Chairperson of the Committee of Permanent Secretaries on National Food and Nutrition Security, highlighted that over eight thousand schools are benefiting from the school feeding programme in all the 116 districts in the country.

And the Global Child Nutrition Foundation Executive Director, Arlene Mitchell praised Zambia for being a good model for countries to learn from, citing the progress in school meals programme.

Ms Mitchell expressed that where other countries struggle to fund school meals programmes, Zambia is implementing the programme with impressive action.

“I am impressed with Zambia and I can not wait to share this with the rest of the visiting countries during the forum,” she said.

The Global Child Nutrition Forum unites representatives from governments, businesses, international organisations, NGOs, and academic institutions to share knowledge as well as strategies for improving school feeding and child nutrition worldwide.+

World.title: Nkana sanctioned over ilampi chants
World.content:
Nkana Football Club says it respects the ruling issued by the Football Association of Zambia -FAZ- Disciplinary Committee dated 30th October 2026.

The ruling follows a complaint lodged by the Zambian Premier League -ZPL- concerning the chanting of political slogans by a section of supporters during the MTN Super League fixture against Makeni All Stars FC at Nkana Stadium on 10th October 2026.

In a statement issued by Media and Communications Manager Mike Mubanga, the club says it was asked to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken and subsequently submitted its response expressing regret and outlining measures to prevent recurrence.

In its ruling, the Disciplinary Committee found the club guilty and imposed a fine of K100,000 alongside a sanction requiring the club to play its next five home matches at a neutral venue situated at least 300 kilometres from Nkana Stadium without spectators.

The Committee however, having considered the club’s remorse and remedial measures, ordered the partial suspension of the implementation of the five-match sanction to provide the club an opportunity to demonstrate improved conduct for the remainder of the season.

Nkana FC says it is committed to complying with the directives and will continue engaging relevant football authorities to ensure similar incidents do not recur.

The club notes the ruling has significant financial, logistical and sporting implications and would deprive the Kalampa faithful of the opportunity to support their team at home.

The club has therefore appealed to supporters to exercise restraint, respect football rules and refrain from chants or conduct that could expose the club to further disciplinary action.

World.title: Nkana content with derby draw against Power
World.content:
Nkana coach Elijah Tana has expressed satisfaction with the goalless draw against Power Dynamos in the Kitwe derby played at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Saturday.

Near misses were the hallmark of the derby as Nkana keeper William Mtonga denied Power a win with crucial saves in both halves.

It was a match Super League champions Power dominated with Nkana showing flashes of brilliance.

Power striker Andy Boyeli came close to opening the scoring when he missed from inside the box with keeper Mtonga off his line after 14 minutes.

There were also misses from Boyeli’s teammates Joshua Mutale and Ismael Ankobo in the first half before the crossbar denied Power.

Nkana striker Lazarus Kambole will go home kicking himself after misdirecting a shot within the box when set up by winger Charles Zulu.

In a post-match comment, Tana said he was happy with the one point Nkana earned from the derby.

“I’m happy with the clean sheet. Credit to the boys for getting one point from the derby,” Tana said.

“I told my boys at half time to be cautious. This is a new team with energetic boys so I will keep pushing on the boys,” he said.

Tana further saluted the conduct of the usually controversial Nkana supporters.

“Our fans should continue conducting themselves well like they did today. I’m happy with the conduct of our fans and they must continue,” he said.

Meanwhile, Power assistant coach Linos Makwaza lamented the missed opportunities in the derby.

“It was a very tough game. Nkana played with positive energy and as Power Dynamos we created a lot of chances,” Makwaza said.

Nkana are third in Stream A with ten points and Power are placed fifth on the table with seven points after five matches played.

New Minister of Youth and Sport Likando Mufalali was among thousands of spectators who thronged Levy Mwanawasa Stadium for the biggest match on the local football front.

World.title: Energy expert welcomes splitting of ministries
World.content:
An energy expert, Bornface Zulu, has described the creation of the Ministry of Petroleum and Ministry of Electricity as a strategic governance reform.

Mr Zulu says the decision to split the Ministry of Energy into the two ministries reflects the growing complexity of Zambia’s energy sector and the need for specialised leadership, accountability and policy focus.

Speaking in an interview with the media Mr Zulu says Electricity and Petroleum have evolved into distinct industries with different technical demands, investment requirements and national security implications.

He said managing both under one ministry increasingly risked diluting attention and slowing critical decision-making.

Mr Zulu added that one ministry was expected to simultaneously address load shedding, generation planning, transmission investment, fuel security, storage infrastructure and international petroleum market developments which became unsustainable in the long run.

“For many years, the Ministry of Energy was responsible for electricity generation, transmission, power trading, renewable energy development, fuel procurement, petroleum storage, strategic reserves, and broader energy policy. While this structure worked historically, the rapid expansion of both subsectors created what can be described as a governance capacity challenge,” he said.

Mr Zulu further commended the decision saying it is in line with regional best practices citing Angola and South Africa.

He said Zambia is not alone in adopting specialized approaches to energy governance stating that as the energy sector becomes larger and more complex, governance structures must evolve accordingly.

“South Africa restructured aspects of its energy governance framework to provide greater attention to electricity security and power sector reforms. Angola similarly maintains separate institutional arrangements for petroleum and electricity oversight, recognizing the unique strategic importance of each sector,” Mr Zulu said.

Government recently increased the number of ministries from 24 to 30 with the Ministry of Energy among those that were split into the Ministries of Petroleum and Electricity.

World.title: Zim’s abortion information gap puts vulnerable women at risk
World.content:
Local News

VANESSA GONYE · October 31, 2026

SEXUAL and reproductive health rights (SRHR) activists have decried the information gaps pitting the poor against other vulnerable groups that are at the bottom of the information food chain.

In an interview with NewsDay Weekender, health policy expert at the Health Law and Policy Consortium, Tinashe Mundawarara, said the information gap is resulting in impaired and fettered access to SRHR services, particularly on safe abortion, due to myths and misconceptions of what is legal or permissible.

“The information gaps noted relate to criminalisation, wherein the law is often portrayed as a dragnet, an umbrella provision covering every element and mischief around abortion,” he said.

“Resultantly, access becomes difficult even for women who qualify for legal abortion as they are either afraid of prosecution or are discouraged by the procedural requirements to access legal abortion.”

He said access to safe abortion is disproportionately affecting the poor, rural and socially excluded groups of people, and yet the well to do and financially able individuals are procuring abortion in neighbouring countries or practising self-managed abortion.

This results in grave health inequities, Mundawarara said, and debilitating health outcomes for the most vulnerable in our communities.

“Official pathways to safe and legal abortion are quixotic and hidden under a mountain of red tape.

“They are time consuming, financially taxing and not purposive in a right to health jurisdiction like Zimbabwe.

“The pathways fly in the face of access to justice and are anathema to gender transformative reproductive health.”

Stakeholders have maintained that access to lawful, safe abortion care depends on more than the existence of a statute but requires accurate information, qualified providers, privacy, timely referrals and respectful services across the health system.

Contrary to beliefs, safe abortion care is delivered with methods and clinical support appropriate to the pregnancy and the patient’s circumstances, by qualified health workers operating within the law and applicable clinical guidance.

It includes accurate information, voluntary informed consent, privacy, respectful treatment, appropriate follow-up and referral when a facility cannot provide the required service.

The word “safe” describes more than a medical technique.

It also points to a system in which a person is not misled about eligibility, exposed unnecessarily to disclosure, sent from facility to facility without guidance or denied post-abortion care because of stigma.

Lunia Centre for Youths executive director Tjedu Moyo, however, said it should be known that in Zimbabwe abortion is not illegal in all circumstances.

She said there is a need for more awareness on the subject, to cover the information gap.

She explained instances allowing for safe abortion and also decried the fact that getting access/approval was difficult, a scenario leading to more unsafe and clandestine abortions as people would try to evade the “difficult” and sometimes disappointing process.

“The Termination of Pregnancy Act allows it on three grounds — risk to life/physical health, serious foetal anomaly, and unlawful intercourse (rape/incest). But in real life the pathway is almost unusable.

“It needs two doctors, superintendent permission and in rape cases a magistrate certificate,” she said.

“Many women don’t know this law exists, and designated facilities are few. That’s why we still see thousands of unsafe abortions and why post-abortal care remains critical.

“If we want fewer deaths, we need to make the lawful pathway actually accessible and make information available at community level.

“It is not about legalising abortion for now, it’s about ensuring the existing pathway works for those that need it, because they do need a working pathway.”

Zimbabwe’s Termination of Pregnancy Act establishes a narrow legal route for termination rather than unrestricted access.

Women and Law in Southern Africanational director Isheanesu Chirisa highlighted worrisome statistics on unsafe abortions in the country.

She revealed that studies from 2019 show that 219 abortions occur daily in Zimbabwe, with 80 000 abortions recorded that year.

“Of these abortions, about 185 occur among adolescents,” Chirisa said.

“Without safe abortions being allowed under the law, adolescents often resort to backstreet procedures, which are unsafe and life-threatening.

“This is often due to the medical costs involved.”

Further studies show that between 2016 and 2017, 40% of pregnancies in Zimbabwe were unintended, with 25% of those resulting in unsafe and illegal abortions.
