World.title: Allies fear Trump will target NATO in case of midterm loss
World.content:
“Usually what happens to lame duck presidents is a mix of venting frustrations and adventurism in foreign policy,” said one senior European defense official. And attacking NATO “seems to be a consistent part of [the] Trump worldview.”

White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told POLITICO that “President Trump has done more for NATO than anyone else,” citing his successes in securing agreements by allies to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, bolster U.S. military presence in Greenland, and efforts to end Russia's all-out war in Ukraine.

Yet he “remains firm that our NATO allies should have been there for the United States” over the war in Iran, she said, adding: “The President will never settle for the West’s managed decline and will continue to unapologetically advance our interests at home and abroad.”

Democrats are widely expected to win the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate, while Trump’s personal approval ratings have fallen to his lowest on record.

The worries underscore growing transatlantic tensions after a U.S. cutoff of Starlink satellite services for Ukraine and a fresh rapprochement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin weeks before the midterms. Further attacks would deal a fresh blow to NATO, just as Russia steps up its sabotage campaign and so-called hybrid war across Europe.

“He could be very pissed off,” said one of the NATO diplomats. If so, “he’ll be very harsh.”

World.title: EU and Canada’s 6-month test of commitment
World.content:
The test of that plan comes in six months, when the European Commission will meet with the Canadian government to see what progress has been made. One diplomat involved in the talks, granted anonymity to speak freely, said the meeting, which will be held in March before next year’s EU-Canada summit in Brussels, should make clear how far the relationship can develop and whether Ottawa is really on track for associate membership.

In the months ahead, there will be plenty of issues that could distract EU leaders. Governments must negotiate the bloc’s next seven-year budget, amid deep divisions over its size and spending priorities. Plus, a series of elections in some of the EU's biggest countries, including Spain, France, Italy and Poland, will make concentrating on Canada a tall order.

Deal first, definition later

The joint declaration signed in Montreal commits both sides to defining the concept of “associate membership” by their 2027 summit. In the meantime, they have a slate of agreements and work plans to put into practice.

Carney speaks during an interview with POLITICO at the Port of Montreal Tower in Montreal, Canada on Oct. 30, 2026. | Adil Boukind for POLITICO (@adilboukind on IG)

That includes a digital trade agreement and a competition deal signed in Montreal, plus Canada’s participation in the EU’s high-performance computing partnership. They also agreed on a new framework for cooperation between EU border force Frontex and the Canada Border Services Agency. Ottawa said it intends to join the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan facility.

The declaration sets out further work on critical raw materials and energy, including a feasibility study into long-term liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and exploring ways to jointly stockpile strategic resources. It also calls for cooperation on subsea cables, artificial intelligence and research, closer financial links, Arctic security, and disaster response. Canada and the EU will begin talks on deeper Canadian participation in Erasmus+, the EU’s education and youth program.

The summit also saw the launch of the Alliance for the Future, a broader partnership plan that could eventually include Japan, South Korea and Australia. It aims to build resilient supply chains and coordinate on economic security, so partner nations do not inadvertently harm one another with trade measures as they respond to Chinese overcapacity and U.S. tariffs.

World.title: Russian strikes leave thousands without power in Ukraine, says Zelenskyy
World.content:
Zelenskyy’s comments came as Russian authorities reported a “massive” Ukrainian drone strike overnight on an industrial facility in the Nizhny Novgorod region.

“A massive drone attack occurred overnight and this morning in the Nizhny Novgorod region: more than a hundred drones were destroyed,” Gleb Nikitin, the region’s governor, wrote on Telegram on Sunday.

“According to preliminary reports, there were no casualties,” he said, adding that an industrial facility in the Kstovsky district sustained “significant damage.”

“During the restoration process, temporary power outages and reduced hot water and heating services are possible in certain sections of the utility networks supplying residential buildings,” he wrote.

Nikitin did not specify which industrial facility had been attacked. The NORSI oil refinery is located in the region.

On Friday, the local governor of Russia’s Samara region blamed Ukraine for an early morning drone attack that struck an oil refinery in Novokuibyshevsk city.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Kyiv agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries until after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump.

Ukraine paused drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for 72 hours when Trump announced an energy ceasefire in October, but the Kremlin continued to bombard Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

World.title: Commission backs Tusk as he vows no compromise in court showdown
World.content:
The Commission said it was closely monitoring developments and, in a carefully worded statement to POLITICO, appeared to show support for Tusk’s position.

“The Polish Constitutional Tribunal needs to be able to function in accordance with the Polish constitution and the case law of the Court of Justice of the EU,” Commissioner for Democracy, Justice and the Rule of Law Michael McGrath said.

“This matters for every Polish citizen, and it is for the Polish authorities to ensure that,” McGrath added, stating that “the Venice Commission has been clear that appointing the new judges lies within the power of the Sejm [Poland’s lower house of parliament].”

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk vowed Saturday night not to back down on the dispute. “In some matters there can be no compromise,” Tusk said in an address to the nation, comparing calls for reconciliation to a thief demanding to keep half the contents of a stolen handbag.

“We have waited too long for the treasure of an independent, democratic Poland to be frightened into retreat,” Tusk said.

The prime minister also targeted Nawrocki, who turned his plane around mid-flight en route to Senegal and returned to Warsaw, where he pushed his way into the Tribunal shortly after midnight Saturday, confronting judges challenging its leadership.

World.title: UK’s future lies in EU, says Rachel Reeves
World.content:
Reeves added that while she believes “Britain’s future lies in the European Union”, it was “incumbent on supporters of our re-entry to make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right.”

Last week, Burnham expressed an openness to restarting free movement between the U.K and the EU. He also said he’d like to see Britain rejoin the bloc in his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament.

At the last election, Labour’s manifesto — which Reeves helped to draw up — said a Labour government would stay outside the EU.

But at the Labour Party’s conference in September, Burnham called for closer links with the bloc.

Reeves’ intervention comes ahead of a leaders’ summit later this month where she said “at a minimum” she hoped to see confirmation of a youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for.

At the Nov. 20 summit, the EU and the U.K. hope to sign off on a set of agreements ranging from trade to climate regulations.

World.title: How Merz’s five-day Asia trip ended up being mostly about Europe
World.content:
The remarks concluded a tour of Singapore, Japan and South Korea, where the chancellor was challenged by Asian capitals over security and trade cooperation — and often reminded of how the region's turmoil are intertwined with Europe's precarious moment.

'Collective security'

One only has to look across the border. Shortly before Merz arrived in the demilitarized zone, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan. The chancellor's greatest security concerns at home — Russia’s war against Ukraine and Moscow’s threat to Europe — are increasingly becoming problems in the Asia-Pacific region as well.

The fact that Pyongyang is able to launch so many ballistic missiles, testing and expanding its long-range strike capabilities, is directly linked to its cooperation with Russia. North Korea has been sending soldiers to the Russian front in Ukraine for two years and in return benefited from combat experience and technology transfers.

North Korean state television on Thursday showed leader Kim Jong Un with new military drones, including a potential stealth drone, underscoring the great strides the country is also making in drone development. These are serious security issues that other countries in the region, including Japan, cannot ignore.

Besides provocations from Pyongyang, there is China, which is not only becoming increasingly dominant in trade but also casting its eye toward Taiwan, making far-reaching territorial claims in the South China Sea and putting strong pressure on critics such as Japan. And there is Russia, which is forging close military ties with Beijing and carrying out joint bomber flights with the Chinese air force near the Japanese border.

“Russia’s war against Ukraine is ever-present here in the region,” Merz told reporters following his visit to the border. “There is no longer such a thing as unilateral security in the world, only collective security,” he added, underscoring his call to “work closely” with Japan, South Korea and Singapore “on security policy issues” and in the defense industry.

World.title: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s food fight is coming to Brussels
World.content:
“I welcome the US - including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. - putting a stronger spotlight on this agenda including the #eatrealfood campaign,” Várhelyi wrote on LinkedIn after his appearance at the USA-EU Transatlantic Business Summit in Brussels earlier this year.

But sharing an ambition is the easy part. Deciding what ultra-processed food is — and whether or how it should be regulated: not so much.



At the heart of the debate is a growing body of research linking UPFs to conditions such as obesity and diabetes, risks everyone says they want to reduce. But the challenge is translating that evidence into public health policy without dictating what people eat.

An ashtray and lit cigarette sit beside a cigarette pack with a warning label on a café terrace in Lorient, France, on Oct. 19, 2019. | Maud Dupuy/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

For industry, the priority is protecting personal choice. For public health advocates, the problem is systemic. What appears to be an individual choice is often the result of inequality, they argue — influenced by income, education and a food environment that can make healthier options harder to access.

The issue has been pitting health advocates against Big Food companies on multiple continents for years now — but global momentum is moving toward regulation as the World Health Organization prepares to unveil new tools to help policymakers this week.

The “million dollar question,” as health activist Liz Arnanz put it, is how to define ultra-processed foods.

The term might bring to mind salty chips, preservative-filled pastries and sugary drinks, but that category can also include whole-grain bread or fortified yogurt.

World.title: Britain and Germany’s defense cooperation plans face tough choices
World.content:
Streeting will meet his German counterpart, Boris Pistorius, as the countries discuss the development of long-range missiles together, even as Berlin weighs whether to join Britain’s next fighter-jet program or pursue a different European partnership.

"The defining test is not where every single component of a piece of kit or equipment was made," Streeting said on Oct. 22 at the opening of a British artillery factory by German arms giant Rheinmetall. His message: Allies must prioritize delivering weapons over competing industrial interests.

Building Europe's next missiles

At the heart of the partnership is a plan to develop weapons capable of hitting targets more than 2,000 kilometers away. Known as Deep Precision Strike, or DPS, the project aims to give European forces the ability to strike far behind enemy lines without relying on American missiles.

The internal briefings reveal how Britain and Germany intend to divide the work.

Britain will lead development of a missile designed to fly low and evade enemy radar, known as the High-End Cruise Missile. The first version is expected to be ready for military use in 2032.

Germany will take charge of a different weapon, designed to travel several times the speed of sound. A rocket would carry this so-called hypersonic glide vehicle high into the sky before releasing it toward its target. Berlin aims to have it ready for military use by 2035.

World.title: Bulgaria's acting President Yotova leads in exit polls of runoff election
World.content:
According to the exit polls, the run-off election for the Bulgarian presidency appears to result in a majority for the incumbent, Ilijana Yotova. Initial projections suggest that Yotova, the candidate of the ruling centre-left party Progressive Bulgaria (PB), could secure 52% of the vote. If confirmed by official results, she would become Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state.

 

Former interim Prime Minister and challenger Andrey Gyurov, backed by reformist pro-Western opposition parties, is said to be trailing with around 45%.

The war in Ukraine, not far from Bulgaria, has played a significant role in the election in this country on NATO’s eastern flank. Throughout the election campaign, Yotova repeatedly advocated for a peaceful solution for Ukraine through negotiations with Russia. She said she wanted to be a Bulgarian "President of Peace".

During the campaign, Gyurov signalled a closer alignment with Western partners and stronger support for Ukraine in the face of Russia’s war of aggression.

The vote was the first major test for Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party, which has endorsed Yotova. The 62 years old politician took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament. Observers expect her to stick to Radev’s policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path, while at the same time supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions.

The election in this south-eastern EU country was overshadowed by the conflict in Ukraine. In the Bulgarian economic zone in the Black Sea – and also in that of neighbouring Romania – drone attacks on merchant ships have become increasingly frequent in recent weeks.

Bulgaria’s presidency is primarily ceremonial. The head of state has no executive powers, and all major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.

Presidents in Bulgaria are elected directly for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 1st, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Heidi Klum's 2026 Halloween party costume: a giant bloody replica of her own hand
World.content:
When Heidi Klum announces her annual Halloween party, her guests know one thing for certain: her costume is going to be elaborate.

 

But with her latest edition in New York, the model still managed to exceed expectations, appearing as a gigantic, bloody hand.

Anyone who ever hesitates over a handshake has not yet seen Heidi Klum's Halloween costume. 2026 Invision

And the costume was not just any hand, but an enlarged copy of Klum's own left hand.

According to Vogue_,_ body scans were used to create it. Her engagement ring, wedding ring and the tattoo with her husband Tom Kaulitz's name were all there.

Klum reportedly got the idea for the costume last year.

“I looked at my hand and I thought, ‘Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,’” Klum said, per the Associated Press.

Behind the transformation was once again special effects make-up artist Mike Marino, who has already brought several of Klum's costume artworks to life.

Family affair

Klum's husband has been a key part of her Halloween bashes for years, often turning out in equally spectacular outfits. He has appeared as an egg to match her peacock, a fisherman to her giant worm, and a petrified counterpart to her Medusa.

This time, he was absent due to a concert in Germany, however.

“Of course I would have loved to hold hands with Tom,” Klum told Bunte magazine. “But you can’t be in two places at once.”

Her daughter, Leni Klum, came as Miss Piggy, with pig ears, XXL eyelashes and a purple feather boa.

Other guests included actors Kyle MacLachlan and Neil Patrick Harris, who appeared with his husband David Burtka as a creepy twin team.

Neil Patrick Harris (left) and David Burtka at Heidi Klum's 25th annual Halloween party. 2026 Invision

On the eve of the event, Klum also invited a small group to her pizzeria in the New York neighbourhood of Soho. There, she appeared without the monster hand, donning an orange dress and black boots for the occasion.

It seems the "Queen of Halloween," who has also appeared as E.T. and Fiona from the animated film Shrek, has no intention of giving up the title any time soon.

World.title: Russia arrests minor after US embassy warns of 'credible threat of a mass casualty event'
World.content:
Russian authorities have arrested a minor in connection with an alleged terror threat against the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow, according to Russian media.

 

The US embassy in Russia had issued a security alert on Saturday warning of a "credible threat of a mass casualty event" at the site.

According to the embassy, Washington was coordinating a response with Russian authorities.

While it did not provide specific details, the embassy advised people to "avoid the area, stay alert, and avoid crowds."

Russian state media published a statement from the Federal Security Service (FSB) on Sunday announcing that a minor had been detained in relation to the threat.

"As a result of the operation, a minor Russian citizen was detained; he had posted photographs of himself on the short-video platform TikTok wearing tactical clothing, a balaclava, a cap, sunglasses, headphones and an object resembling an automatic weapon, as well as photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, captioned: 'I found a place,'" it said.

On Saturday evening, the grounds of the Tsaritsyno museum and park were closed "for technical reasons" and visitors were evacuated. It reopened as usual on 1 November, per Russian media reports.

The German embassy in Russia also reportedly issued a warning about a possible security threat at the museum reserve.

In March 2024, the US embassy in Russia issued a similar alert about a threat a few days before a terrorist attack at the Crocus City Hall concert venue near Moscow. The attack took place on 22 March and left more than 150 people dead and hundreds injured.

In the days leading up to the attack, Russian President Vladimir Putin described warnings from “a number of official Western bodies regarding the possibility of terrorist attacks in Russia” as "provocative." At the time, he stated that “this amounts to outright blackmail” and “an attempt to destabilise society."

World.title: University of Cambridge scientist among victims of deadly Spain train crash
World.content:
A researcher at the University of Cambridge has been named as one of at least 69 victims of a deadly train crash in Spain earlier this week.

 

Marta Shahbazi had been travelling to receive a prize for scientific excellence from the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology when the train she was on collided with another service near Urda in the province of Toledo on Wednesday.

Shahbazi was a group leader at the Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) and an affiliate assistant professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute.

In a statement, the LMB said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic death of our colleague Marta Shahbazi, Group Leader in the Cell Biology Division."

"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist. Her death is a profound shock and a huge loss. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time," it added.

News of her death was confirmed by the CiMUS research centre in Santiago de Compostela, which called her a "brilliant young researcher."

"The CiMUS community would like to express its support and deepest sympathies to our dear PI María José Alonso, following the death of her niece, Marta Shahbazi, in the railway accident that occurred on 28 October," the centre said in a post on social media.

Shahbazi had been due to arrive in El Rompido, Huelva, to collect the 2026 José Luis Gómez-Skarmeta prize for her "outstanding contributions to the study of the early stages of human development."

According to the Society of Developmental Biology, her research focused on "understanding how the human embryo organises itself during early development and how cells make decisions that determine their fate," while her laboratory work centred on embryonic implantation.

The train collision occurred when a high-speed Renfe service slammed into a stationary Iryo train outside of Urda, south of the Spanish capital Madrid.

World.title: Swiss foreign minister makes first North Korea visit since 2003 as diplomatic office reopens
World.content:
Switzerland has formally reopened its diplomatic office in North Korea as Ignazio Cassis became the first Swiss foreign minister to visit the country since 2003.

 

Cassis visited Pyongyang on 29 and 30 October before travelling to Seoul. In a statement issued on Saturday, the Swiss foreign ministry said the trip aimed to restore direct political dialogue with North Korea as it looks to maintain contact with both sides of the divided peninsula.

The office restarted operations on 19 October. It falls under the Swiss embassy in Beijing, which remains responsible for diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. Switzerland’s previous office in Pyongyang handled humanitarian cooperation and closed in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The two countries have maintained diplomatic relations since 1974, but regular political consultations stopped after 2019.

Bern said the office would allow Switzerland to deal directly with North Korean authorities and follow developments in the region.

Talks in Pyongyang

During his visit, Cassis met with North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui and Jo Yong Won, secretary of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Central Committee.

His discussions with Choe covered restoring political dialogue, security on the Korean Peninsula and wider security challenges in Europe and Asia.

Speaking to Swiss news agency Keystone-ATS on Saturday, Cassis said he had offered Switzerland’s help in facilitating dialogue to ease tensions on the peninsula. He said the proposal appeared to have been well received.

North Korea’s state news agency KCNA said on Saturday that the two ministers discussed diplomatic cooperation and international issues in a "friendly atmosphere." It did not provide a detailed account of the discussions.

Asked by Euronews whether the office could support wider European dialogue with Pyongyang, a Swiss foreign ministry spokesperson said the department had nothing to add to Saturday’s statement.

Seoul hopes for renewed engagement

Cassis also made a trip to Seoul on 30 and 31 October, meeting National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac and senior foreign ministry official Jeong Yeon-du.

He briefed Jeong on his Pyongyang talks. Jeong expressed hope that the Swiss office would help South Korea engage with the North, according to Seoul’s foreign ministry.

The visit came amid renewed military tensions. North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, according to South Korea’s military, a day after Seoul renewed its call for military talks to prevent accidental border clashes.

In a separate statement on Sunday, South Korea’s foreign ministry said Foreign Minister Cho Hyun had urged support for dialogue between the two Koreas at a G20 meeting in Atlanta.

Switzerland has helped monitor the armistice that halted fighting in the Korean War since 1953 through the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission, based at Panmunjom. Cassis also met the head of the Swiss delegation to discuss the security situation.

World.title: Looted shops, burning barricades as riots erupt in Frankfurt
World.content:
Police remained on duty in central Frankfurt on Sunday, 1 November, after riots broke out following a demonstration the previous day. Footage shows smashed shop windows, looted stores, burning barricades and debris scattered across the streets. Police used water cannon to extinguish fires and clear obstacles from the roads.

 

Several protesters and police officers were injured, while 30 people were detained. The situation had calmed by early Sunday morning after police cordoned off parts of the city centre.

Hesse state premier Boris Rhein condemned the violence, saying he was shocked by the events and that those responsible would face consequences.

Violence was also reported in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse crowds, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked officers with bottles and pyrotechnics.

World.title: Heidi Klum turns herself into a giant severed hand for Halloween
World.content:
Celebrities gathered in New York on Saturday, 31 October, for the 25th anniversary of Heidi Klum’s famous Halloween party, with guests showing off an array of elaborate and unusual costumes.

 

Klum once again made headlines with an elaborate transformation, appearing as a giant, gruesome severed hand. The costume featured dangling ligaments and tendons, with only her eyes and mouth visible, while blood appeared to drip from her mouth. She was accompanied by helpers dressed in blood-stained hazmat suits.

The idea came to Klum last year, when she looked at her left hand and wondered whether she could fit her entire body inside a giant version of it.

Among the guests was actor Kyle MacLachlan, who brought back his evil Cliff Vandercave costume from the 1994 film The Flintstones. He arrived with his wife, Desiree Gruber, and their son, Callum Lyon MacLachlan.

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

Editor’s note: This story was updated at 13:25 on 30 October 2026 to include a statement from lawyers for Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron, sent to us by counsel for Macron's legal team. It responds to the court’s ruling on Candace Owens’ motion to dismiss the case against her.

In the statement, lawyers for the Macrons said: “We are pleased that the Court rejected Mrs. Owens’ attempt to remove the case from Delaware, where her companies continue to publish and monetize her defamatory falsehoods. As for Mrs. Owens personally, we are keeping all options open to ensure that, in addition to the liability she still faces through her companies, she is held accountable personally.”

***

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Ukraine, Russia report hacking attacks on emergency alert apps
World.content:
Skip next section Zelenskyy says Ukraine will stop refinery strikes if US sends Patriot missiles

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.

Speaking to US broadcaster Fox News, Zelenskyy said he had had "different and several" conversations with Trump and his team on the issue.

"We asked that we can't not respond after Russia's attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything," he said.

"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid," Zelenskyy added.

The Ukrainian leader said if Washington provided the missile systems for one month Kyiv would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same period.

Asked if he was concerned that this would be seen as trying to "leverage" Trump, Zelenskyy said: "I don't have any concerns when I share the truth between partners."

Ukrainian authorities have been warning for weeks that their supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles were dwindling.

World.title: German police investigating after needles found in Halloween candy
World.content:
German police said they received phone calls with reports about sharp objects concealed in Halloween candy.

Needles or other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets that children collected while trick-or-treating for Halloween, German police said Sunday.

Police believe most or all of the objects, which also included metal screws, were placed intentionally to cause harm.

Incidents were reported in Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Lower Saxony, and Rhineland-Palatinate, among other locations, police said.

In one of the cases in the southern city of Nuremberg, police said a child had bitten down on a needle while eating a piece of chocolate. The child was unharmed.

In two separate cases in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg, police said the needles had been concealed as such that they were not visible from the outside.

In several of the cases, police have opened investigations into attempted aggravated assault.

No suspects have been identified.

World.title: Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO
World.content:
Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.

The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility – each more than 500 meters long – look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers, allowing Moscow to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.

The radar near Gvardeysk would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications, detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles Image: Planet Labs

The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," he added.

Mass surveillance system

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals – citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.

"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.

"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.

"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.

Russia ramps up drone war with new launch megabase To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Electronic warfare hub

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.

"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.

The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

This satellite image shows what might be another large circular antenna complex near the city of Chernyakhovsk Image: Planet Labs PBC

ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

With airfields like Chkalovsk, Russia is beefing up its military presence in Kaliningrad Image: Planet Labs PBC

"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."

Motivation for the West

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.

"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."

Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.

The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

World.title: Serbia: Police chief arrested after election for abuse of office
World.content:
Marko Kricak, an Aleksandar Vucic loyalist, is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into a gangland murder. Prosecutors say the arrest is not linked to Vucic's recent election defeat.

The head of Serbia's criminal police directorate has been arrested and charged with abuse of office, state media reported on Sunday.

Marko Kricak is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into the murder in May of a suspected criminal underworld figure in a Belgrade restaurant.

Serbia: who is police chief Marko Kricak?

The 42-year-old was seen as a supporter of defeated Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, whose right-wing populist camp was defeated by the opposition Student List in parliamentary elections on October 25.

Indeed, he has also been accused by student groups of "brutality" in the police response to peaceful anti-Vucic demonstrations.

The removal of Kricak and other Vucic loyalists in Serbia's police and intelligence apparatus was one of student leaders' demands.

But Belgrade's chief prosecutor, Nenad Stefanovic, denied a connection between the student movement's demands and Kricak's arrest.

"This arrest has no link with ... the result of the legislative elections," he told journalists.

Against all odds: How Serbia's students took on Vucic To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Serbia: Vucic system dismantled

Nevertheless, the arrest of a senior police officer regarded as close to the former regime is being seen as an example of the strongholds of the Vucic system slowly eroding.

Kricak worked as a car salesman before being recruited into Serbia's domestic intelligence agency, the BIA, and was a loyal supporter of Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

In July 2023, he was appointed commander of the Serbian police's personal protection unit (JZO).

It was in this position that he is alleged to have personally led the abduction of a group of university students, allegedly assaulting one female student and threatening to rape her in the basement of a government building in Belgrade.

At the end of 2025, he was appointed head of the Serbian Criminal Police.

World.title: France opens attempted murder probe after protest attack
World.content:
Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation after a Molotov attack on police. France reported 779 arrests during nationwide protests and Halloween night, fewer than on previous weekends.

Paris prosecutors opened an attempted murder investigation Sunday after a Molotov cocktail was thrown at security forces during a demonstration in the French capital.

Prosecutors said explosive projectiles targeted about 15 gendarmes as well as police officers. No suspects have been arrested over the attack, and investigators were still establishing the number and severity of injuries.

What happened in Paris?

The attack took place at Porte de Charenton, where Saturday's march ended. Photographs and video from the AFP news agency showed an incendiary device exploding at a gendarme's feet and setting his protective equipment alight.

Prosecutors said reported injuries included second-degree burns and tinnitus, although those details remained provisional. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez described the attack as an attempted murder.

How many people were arrested?

The Interior Ministry reported 779 arrests nationwide during the demonstrations and Halloween night. The figure includes both events, updating Saturday evening's provisional total of 565. Authorities said the later part of the night passed without major incidents.

Paris prosecutors separately reported 105 arrests in the capital: 88 linked to the demonstrations and 17 to Halloween night. They said 89 people remained in custody, including at least 22 minors.

A protester holds a placard calling for French President Emmanuel Macron to work in a mine and billionaires in factories Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

The protests focused on high living costs and government policies. The ministry put nationwide turnout at 320,000, while unions estimated nearly 500,000 participants.

The nationwide arrest total was below the 1,314 recorded during the previous Saturday's mobilization and the 2,628 on October 17, when widespread rioting and looting broke out. Authorities had increased security ahead of Halloween amid online calls for violence.
