World.title: Sherlock Holmes Exhibition Lets Visitors Play Detective in Prague
World.content:
Visitors can test historical investigative techniques, examine crime scenes and follow clues at a new interactive Sherlock Holmes exhibition in central Prague.

The exhibition, located on the third floor of the Bílá labuť department store, covers more than 2,000 square metres and features over 200 exhibits.

Rather than simply moving between display cases, visitors take on the role of an investigator and work through a series of tasks inspired by the methods used by detectives more than a century ago.



Each visitor receives a detective’s notebook to record observations and clues. The notebook guides them through the exhibition as they investigate evidence, solve puzzles and gradually build their own picture of the case.

One section focuses on the history of criminal investigation around the turn of the 20th century. It includes authentic objects loaned by the Police Museum, ranging from historical fingerprinting equipment and tools used by safecrackers to more disturbing evidence connected with violent crimes.

The exhibition also explores the development of forensic science. Visitors can make footprint impressions, examine insects found at a crime scene, send messages by telegraph and learn how investigators studied bullets and other evidence. Several interactive stations test whether visitors can identify clues and apply the techniques used by detectives of the period.

The literary side of the exhibition looks at the life and work of Arthur Conan Doyle. Visitors can see early editions of the Sherlock Holmes stories and learn more about the author behind one of literature’s most enduring fictional detectives.

A reconstruction of Holmes’s famous Baker Street apartment is among the main attractions. The exhibition then moves into a series of crime scenes where visitors search for evidence and attempt to connect the clues. Some puzzles draw on well-known Sherlock Holmes stories, while others require close attention to details hidden throughout the exhibition.

Period newspapers are also part of the investigation, and visitors are encouraged to look carefully: a coded message may be concealed within the reports.

The final section examines Sherlock Holmes’s lasting influence on popular culture, including books, comics, films and television adaptations. Vintage Sherlock Holmes comic books are also on display.

A scavenger hunt for younger visitors has been added for the current school year, with children asked to find objects hidden throughout the exhibition. The format also works well for school groups, which can divide into smaller teams and compare their discoveries.

Visitors are allowed to take photographs without flash. A full visit typically takes between 90 minutes and two hours, and booking a timed entry is recommended.

Opening hours: Daily from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Duration: The exhibition is scheduled to run at least until January 10, 2027.

Admission: Adult tickets start at 380 CZK, while family tickets start at 980 CZK.

World.title: Czech Billionaire Strnad Offers €30 Billion for Ray-Ban Family’s Firm
World.content:
Czech billionaire Michal Strnad has offered €30 billion to acquire Delfin, the investment vehicle of Italy’s Del ​Vecchio family and the key shareholder in eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica.

News of the offer, which was first reported by Italian newspaper Il Domani, comes amid growing tensions within Delfin, whose investment portfolio includes also large holdings in Italy’s ​financial sector.

Il Domani published a copy of a letter dated October 20 ​outlining the offer.



“I am looking for long-term investment opportunities in companies ⁠operating in, or investing in, businesses positioned at the top of their value chain,” ​Strnad said in the letter said, according to the newspaper.

Delfin “perfectly fits my investment approach and ​strategy,” the letter added.

Jan Osuch, a spokesperson for AKIPIA, which oversees some of Strnad’s investment activities outside the defence sector, said the group did not comment “on market speculation or potential business negotiations.”

Strnad earlier ​this year bought a 14% stake in Italian tyre maker Pirelli, opens new tab from China’s ​Sinochem.

Strnad, 34, heads the family’s defence company Czechoslovak Group (CSG) which listed in Amsterdam earlier this year.

Delfin shareholder Leonardo ‌Maria ⁠Del Vecchio, one of the six children of the late Ray-Ban billionaire Leonardo Del Vecchio, confirmed he had been recently informed of an offer for the company received from a foreign investor.

“The work of a lifetime by my father must remain part of ​Italy’s heritage”, he said in a ​statement.

The late Luxottica ⁠founder built his business empire from scratch having grown up in a Milan orphanage.

Delfin’s ownership is divided equally among Del Vecchio’s ​eight heirs: his six children, his widow Nicoletta Zampillo and her ​son from ⁠a previous marriage.

A sale would require a virtually unanimous decision from the heirs, who have become increasingly at odds with one another.

In addition to its stake in EssilorLuxottica, Luxembourg-based Delfin holds stakes in ⁠Italian ​insurer Generali and lenders Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) and ​UniCredit, for a combined current market value of €43 billion.

Delfin declined to comment. A representative for Strnad was not ​immediately available for comment.

World.title: Prague’s Only Christmas MINT Market to Take Place on November 28–29
World.content:
Don’t leave your Christmas shopping until the last minute this year.

On the weekend of 28–29 November, head to Hall 13 at Holešovice Market and discover original gifts directly from the people who made them.

MINT Market will bring together more than a hundred carefully selected brands from across the Czech Republic, offering a relaxed alternative to the pre-Christmas rush in shopping centres.



On Saturday from 10 am to 6 pm and Sunday from 10 am to 4 pm, visitors can look forward to independent fashion, designer jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations, original accessories and plenty of Christmas gift inspiration.

And, of course, there will be the relaxed and friendly atmosphere that has become an essential part of MINT Market. The event is suitable for all generations and admission is free.

The youngest MINT Market visitors and their families can enjoy the beautiful NOOK Family Lounge, featuring high-quality wooden toys, a creative play area, a quiet zone with books and space to relax, as well as facilities for babies and parents, including a changing table and a peaceful place for breastfeeding.

There will also be Christmas-themed creative workshops.

MINT Market has been active for sixteen years. During that time, it has become an important platform for small and emerging creators, often directly from Prague, who are given the opportunity to present their products to a wide audience.

Residents of Prague and the surrounding area thus have several opportunities each year to purchase quality products that are literally made by their neighbors – locally, sustainably, and with an emphasis on honest craftsmanship.

MINT Market is not just about shopping. Since 2010, the project has been run by a team of people who systematically support small and local brands and are the only ones bringing high-quality Czech design to more than twenty cities across the country.

What started as a small project has gradually grown into a community of more than 1,500 creatives and a platform that has hosted over 450 events and welcomed more than 1.3 million visitors.

World.title: Czech Government Proposes Voluntary TV and Radio Fees Without State Budget
World.content:
People in the Czech Republic could soon be allowed to decide whether they want to pay television and radio licence fees under a new funding model being prepared by the government.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said the Finance Ministry is working on a system that would make contributions to Czech Television (ČT) and Czech Radio (ČRo) voluntary while ensuring the two public broadcasters receive a guaranteed level of funding.

The proposal is expected to be discussed by the coalition council on Monday.



For now, however, the existing system will remain in place. Although the government had initially hoped to introduce changes at the beginning of 2027, Babiš said the legislative timetable makes that unlikely.

Under parliamentary rules, the bill requires a 60-day review period before moving forward. That means its second reading would fall during the Christmas period, delaying further debate until at least January 2027.

The proposed changes have already sparked political and public opposition.

On October 24, the Chamber of Deputies approved in its first reading a proposal to abolish television and radio licence fees. The governing coalition, made up of ANO, SPD and the Motorists party, added the measure to its priority legislative agenda. The vote took place early in the morning after a lengthy parliamentary debate.

Opposition parties have warned that changing the funding system could expose public broadcasters to greater political pressure. Government representatives have rejected those concerns, saying the planned reform does not threaten democratic standards.

Babiš has said the final model must comply with European requirements concerning the independence of public media and predictable funding.

The issue has also prompted demonstrations. On October 25, thousands of people gathered in Prague’s Old Town Square for a protest organised by the Million Moments for Democracy movement.

Participants expressed concern that changes to the financing of Czech Television and Czech Radio could increase political influence over the broadcasters.

World.title: Prague Welcomes a Week of Polish Films and Culture
World.content:
Prague will host a week of Polish cinema and culture from November 9 to 15, as the 3Kino – Polish Film Festival Prague returns for its 13th edition.

The festival will screen 13 feature films representing contemporary Polish cinema, with a program that also includes theater, stand-up comedy, exhibitions, music and events for children.



This year’s festival opens with The Doll (Lalka), directed by Maciej Kawalski. Based on the classic novel by Bolesław Prus, the film is among the most expensive Polish productions ever made and takes audiences to 19th-century Warsaw.

The story explores love, ambition and social divisions, with Marcin Dorociński, one of Poland’s best-known contemporary actors, in a leading role.

Freedom will be the central theme of this year’s edition. The festival will explore the idea through historical events as well as everyday life, personal relationships and decisions that can alter a person’s future.

The program extends beyond the cinema. Visitors can attend theatrical performances, stand-up shows and exhibitions, while this year’s edition will also put a special focus on Poland’s Lower Silesia region.

Among the accompanying events is the opening of photographer Rafał Pawłowski’s exhibition Shadows of Sounds. Another exhibition will mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda, featuring a selection of Polish film posters.

The festival aims to bring Polish culture to audiences across Prague, with screenings and accompanying events taking place at several venues throughout the city.

Ticket sales are now open, and the full program is available on the festival’s official website.

World.title: The intersection of sleek design and modern wellness brands
World.content:
Explore how modern consumer brands are elevating their aesthetic appeal by investing in highly customized and visually striking product hardware.

Discover how deliberate styling and tactile materials redefine daily customer routines.

You probably remember when health tools hid inside bathroom cabinets, kept out of sight because their clunky plastic shells felt purely clinical. Today, wellness tools serve as personal fashion statements that you proudly display on living room tables and office desks.

Modern customers want daily items that mirror their curated tastes and fit their personal spaces. When your brand treats hardware design as an artistic craft, you turn simple wellness routines into meaningful daily rituals.

Why Are Wellness Tools Becoming Lifestyle Statements?

Your customers no longer separate wellness routines from their broader aesthetic choices. They curate their living rooms, nightstands, and carry bags with items that express their taste. When you produce clean hardware with balanced silhouettes, you invite buyers to keep your products in plain view.

Visibility drives regular daily use. A handsome object sitting on a counter prompts natural engagement, while an awkward gadget gets shoved into a dark drawer. By focusing on intentional shapes, you build products that seamlessly merge into home decor.

Thoughtful design also influences how customers perceive product quality and long-term value. Smooth finishes, understated colors, and ergonomic details create a premium experience that extends beyond basic functionality. When wellness tools complement personal spaces and individual preferences, they become desirable everyday accessories rather than purely practical devices.

How Do Color and Material Guide Consumer Choices?

Color establishes an immediate emotional connection with your audience. Earthy neutrals, muted pastels, and soft cream tones communicate calm and relaxation before a buyer even reads your ingredient list. If you choose harsh neon finishes, you risk sending mixed signals about serenity and health.

Material choices reinforce that visual promise. When people lift a device made with weighted aluminum or a soft-touch matte shell, their hands register quality. Thoughtful finishes create an impression of quiet sophistication that plain plastic cannot deliver.

How Do You Align Product Hardware with Brand Identity?

Customers judge your company within seconds of unboxing a new device. When you source sleek empty disposable vape pens that match your signature visual tone, you give customers an experience that feels deliberate and luxurious. That visual harmony bridges the gap between everyday utility and curated luxury. Your audience notices when physical hardware matches the graphic polish of your outer box.

Mismatched components break customer trust. You lose credibility when premium outer cartons hold generic items that clash with your voice. Consistent colors, unified fonts, and matching tactile surfaces establish a unified identity from the moment the package arrives.

Why Does Outer Presentation Drive Buying Decisions?

Your retail box acts as an interactive introduction to your brand story. According to data shared by the Forbes Business Council, roughly 72% of shoppers say that package styling directly impacts their purchasing decisions. That finding confirms that visual presentation carries just as much weight as product features.

Shoppers form split-second opinions based on packaging textures, embossing, and typography. If your exterior box looks rushed, shoppers assume the interior hardware lacks care as well. Investing in bespoke packaging signals that you prioritize quality across every single detail.

What Steps Create a Seamless Product Experience?

Building an unforgettable product requires harmony between visual appeal and reliable mechanics. You need a structured approach that guides your production decisions from concept to final delivery.

Structuring Your Hardware Design Strategy

Practical Manufacturing Benchmarks:

Standardize finish specifications: Pick a distinct surface texture like anodized metal or matte coating across all hardware runs.

Synchronize print colors: Match your Pantone shades across cardboard packaging, printed guides, and physical device shells.

Test hand ergonomics: Check device grip and balance to guarantee that the unit feels comfortable during daily handling.

Following these benchmarks keeps your production tight and reliable. Your buyers receive hardware that looks cohesive, feels comfortable, and performs reliably during routine use.

How Does Responsible Material Selection Support Growth?

Modern consumers care deeply about how companies manage resources. Guidance from the Environmental Protection Agency highlights that analyzing how packaging components are manufactured and discarded shapes sound business investments. When you integrate thoughtful materials into your supply chain, you satisfy conscious shoppers while reducing unnecessary waste.

Sleek presentation does not require excess plastic or non-recyclable wraps. By choosing compact paper boxes and recyclable device housings, your brand displays environmental integrity. Customers respect businesses that balance elegant design with mindful stewardship.

Style and practical functionality walk hand in hand across the modern self-care market. When you treat your hardware as an extension of personal taste, you build genuine customer loyalty that outlasts fleeting market trends.

Focus on thoughtful colors, premium materials, and cohesive packaging to make your brand an unforgettable part of your audience’s daily lives. By consistently delivering attractive designs and dependable performance, you strengthen emotional connections with customers and encourage lasting engagement with your products.

World.title: Czech Citizen Confirmed Dead After High-Speed Train Collision in Spain
World.content:
A Czech citizen has been confirmed among the victims of a deadly train collision in Spain, the Czech Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday.

Spanish authorities identified the victim as a young Czech national who had been travelling on one of the trains involved in the accident near Toledo.

The Czech Embassy in Madrid is in contact with the person’s family and is providing consular assistance, the ministry said.

The collision occurred on Wednesday shortly before 9 a.m. near the town of Urda, in the province of Toledo. Two high-speed trains were involved in the crash, with about 540 people on board.



Sixty-nine people died and around 100 others were taken to hospital, according to the information available from Spanish authorities. Local media reported on Friday that about 40 people remained hospitalized.

Investigators are still examining the circumstances of the crash. According to local reports, one of the trains struck another train that was stationary and may have been travelling at between 160 and 200 kilometres per hour.

The Spanish Foreign Ministry said that more than 40 foreign nationals from at least seven countries were among those killed or injured. The victims included citizens of Mexico, Italy and Japan.

Czech officials had initially said on Wednesday that a Czech citizen might have been aboard one of the trains. Relatives and acquaintances had contacted the ministry’s emergency hotline with concerns about the passenger.

Spain is observing the second day of a three-day period of national mourning following the disaster.

The accident is among the deadliest rail disasters in Europe in recent decades. Earlier this year, another major train accident in southern Spain claimed 46 lives after a train derailed and collided with an oncoming service.

The investigation into Wednesday’s collision is continuing.

World.title: Prague to Begin Winter Maintenance of Roads and Sidewalks on November 1
World.content:
Prague will begin its annual winter road maintenance programme on November 1.

Until the end of March, the Technical Administration of Communications (TSK) will be responsible for keeping roads, sidewalks and other public routes accessible to vehicles and pedestrians.

Maintenance priorities are determined by the importance of individual routes for traffic and local residents. Roads and pedestrian areas are divided into several categories, each with specific deadlines for snow and ice clearance.



Residents can check the designated maintenance routes and the type of work planned for each area through the city’s online Winter Maintenance application (Zimní údržba).

Road maintenance is divided into three priority categories. The first covers 1,399 kilometres of the city’s busiest roads, which must be treated within two to four hours of maintenance crews being deployed.

The second category includes 519 kilometres of roads, with a clearance deadline of 12 hours. The third covers another 346 kilometres, where maintenance must be completed within 48 hours after the first- and second-priority routes have been treated.

Sidewalks, cycle paths and other pedestrian routes follow a separate schedule. The first category includes 1,063 kilometres, which must be serviced within 12 hours. The second covers a further 693 kilometres, with work required by 5 p.m. on the day after maintenance of the first category has been completed.

Altogether, Prague’s winter maintenance programme covers 2,264 kilometres of roads and 1,756 kilometres of sidewalks and other pedestrian routes.

From December 1 to March 31, temporary workers will help clear sidewalks in parts of Prague 6 that are more difficult to reach with standard maintenance equipment.

These include Hanspaulka, Baba, Sedlec, the Šárecké Valley and parts of Ořechovka.

World.title: Hungary should look beyond its traditional export markets
World.content:
A trade agreement signed thousands of kilometres from Budapest may carry a lesson worth considering for Hungarian businesses. On October 27, the United Arab Emirates and Canada signed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement intended to expand trade, investment and cooperation across several strategic industries.

By Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi, MIoL

Hungary was not a party to the agreement, and it would be misleading to suggest that Hungarian exporters will receive any of its preferential trade benefits. Yet the development raises an important question for a country whose prosperity is closely connected to international manufacturing and European supply chains: how prepared are Hungarian businesses for a world in which established commercial relationships can change rapidly?

Hungary has built a substantial industrial economy through its integration into European production networks. Automotive manufacturing, electronics, machinery and related activities have connected Hungarian factories with customers and suppliers across the continent.

These relationships remain valuable. Germany, in particular, is a major destination for Hungarian exports. Data published by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office demonstrate the importance of this commercial relationship and the wider European market.

There is nothing inherently wrong with concentrating business activity where demand, infrastructure and established partnerships already exist. In fact, geographic proximity and participation in the European single market provide Hungarian companies with significant advantages.

The challenge appears when commercial concentration becomes excessive dependence.

A manufacturer that relies on a limited group of customers may experience serious difficulties when orders decline. A supplier whose production schedule depends heavily on one industrial sector may struggle to respond when that industry slows. Even a financially healthy company can face disruption if important transport routes, components or markets become temporarily unavailable.

These are not uniquely Hungarian problems. They are features of an international economy built around highly interconnected systems.

The new UAE-Canada agreement offers an interesting comparison because it illustrates how countries are developing commercial relationships beyond their traditional geographical and economic circles.

The agreement was negotiated in 47 days and is expected to enter into force in 2027, following the required procedures. Once fully implemented, it is expected to reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99 percent of current Canadian exports to the UAE.

Canada is seeking greater access to markets outside its established trading relationships, while the UAE continues expanding its position as an international investment and commercial centre.

For Hungary, the relevant lesson is not the speed of negotiations or the precise terms of the agreement. It is the importance of creating additional economic options before external developments make diversification urgent.

Hungary’s opportunities in this area deserve serious consideration.

The country has industrial capabilities and technical expertise that could be relevant to markets beyond Europe. Hungarian companies involved in manufacturing equipment, food technology, water management, healthcare products, engineering services and specialised industrial systems may find opportunities where international demand matches their capabilities.

If you missed it – Big shake-up for Budapest public transport: capital and suburbs to get one transport system

The Gulf region is one potential area of interest.

The United Arab Emirates already maintains economic relations with Hungary, while the European Union and the UAE have been negotiating a free trade agreement since May 2025. The negotiations cover goods, services, investment and areas of strategic cooperation.

If concluded and implemented, such an agreement could create additional opportunities for businesses across EU member states, including Hungary. However, it remains under negotiation, and companies should not assume that proposed trade provisions are already in force.

That distinction matters.

International commercial opportunities are frequently discussed in terms of political announcements, investment commitments and future projects. Business decisions, however, must be based on conditions that can be verified.

A Hungarian manufacturer considering expansion into the Gulf needs to understand the actual demand for its products, customs requirements, certification standards, distribution arrangements and payment risks. A promising market becomes valuable only when a company can serve it competitively and consistently.

This is particularly important for smaller businesses.

Large multinational corporations often have the financial resources and international networks to explore new markets. Smaller Hungarian manufacturers may possess excellent products but lack the overseas contacts, regulatory knowledge or resources required for expansion.

Chambers of commerce, export-support institutions and industry associations can help bridge this gap by providing reliable market information and facilitating introductions to suitable partners.

Nevertheless, export diversification should not become an exercise in pursuing every available destination.

A company producing highly specialised components for European manufacturers may achieve greater resilience by developing additional customers within the same industry. Another business may benefit more from entering a new geographical market. A third may need to strengthen its supplier network before seeking international growth.

The appropriate strategy depends on the company’s actual vulnerabilities and operational capabilities.

In my view, this is where economic diversification and risk management should become part of the same business discussion.

Governments often evaluate diversification through changes in export destinations or investment flows. These indicators are useful, but businesses also need to examine the reliability of their commercial relationships and their capacity to maintain operations during disruption.

A company with customers in several countries may still depend on a single supplier for an essential component. A manufacturer may gain a new export contract while creating new exposure to currency fluctuations or unfamiliar regulatory requirements.

Diversification does not automatically eliminate risk. Poorly managed expansion can simply replace familiar vulnerabilities with less visible ones.

Hungary also occupies a distinctive position because its businesses operate within the European Union’s trade framework. This provides access to a substantial single market, but it means that international trade negotiations with third countries generally take place at EU level.

Hungarian businesses can still develop new commercial relationships, investment partnerships and export strategies within that framework. The task is to make better use of existing capabilities while identifying opportunities consistent with applicable European trade rules.

The UAE-Canada agreement should therefore be viewed as an illustration of a broader international trend rather than a model Hungary can reproduce directly.

Countries are increasingly reassessing the concentration of their commercial relationships. They are exploring new markets, alternative suppliers and partnerships involving energy, logistics, technology and industrial development.

For Hungary, the important question is how its companies can participate in these changes without weakening the strengths that have supported their existing success.

Read also: Hungary Airlines flight returns to Budapest Airport after mechanical issue in the air

European manufacturing relationships will remain essential. The objective should not be to replace them, but to ensure that Hungarian companies possess enough flexibility to respond when markets change.

That begins with practical decisions: understanding customer concentration, identifying realistic export opportunities, evaluating supply-chain dependencies and investing in the capabilities needed to operate internationally.

A strong industrial economy should not be judged only by how effectively its factories serve existing customers. Its longer-term strength also depends on whether those businesses can adapt when demand shifts and new commercial opportunities emerge elsewhere.

The agreement between the UAE and Canada may not alter Hungary’s trade position directly. But it offers a timely reminder that countries and companies capable of developing credible alternatives are often better prepared for uncertainty than those that discover their dependence only after a disruption occurs.

About the Author

Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi, MIoL, is a UAE-based author and independent researcher specialising in security, risk management, operational resilience and institutional governance. His work examines the relationship between international developments, organisational decision-making and economic resilience.

World.title: Turkish Republic Day in Budapest: Torchlit march celebrates 103 years of the republic – VIDEO
World.content:
Turkish flags, burning torches and a festive celebration brought the spirit of Türkiye’s Republic Day to the streets of the Hungarian capital. Turkish Republic Day in Budapest was marked by a commemorative march and a special ball, celebrating the legacy of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk while highlighting the strong cultural, historical and diplomatic ties between Hungary and Türkiye.

Turkish Republic Day in Budapest brings the community together

Members of Budapest’s Turkish community came together to celebrate the 103rd anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Türkiye, established on 29 October 1923.

The celebrations were organised by the Hungarian Turkish Solidarity Network (Macaristan Türk Dayanışma Ağı, MATDA), which held a Republic March through the streets of Budapest.

Carrying Turkish flags and flaming torches, participants commemorated the founding of the modern Turkish republic and honoured its first president, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

According to an Instagram statement shared by MATDA, the procession was followed by a Republic Ball, bringing the community together for an evening of celebration and remembrance.

The organisers expressed their gratitude to the Yunus Emre Turkish Cultural Institute and Asım Öksüz for their hospitality and support, as well as to the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) for helping ensure the event’s safety.

They also thanked the organising team and everyone who participated in the celebrations.

In their message, MATDA emphasised that the ideals of the republic established by Atatürk 103 years ago continue to inspire Turkish communities around the world.

Turkish Embassy in Budapest hosts official Republic Day reception

The 103rd anniversary of the Republic of Türkiye was also celebrated at an official reception hosted by the Turkish Embassy in Budapest.

According to the Embassy’s Facebook post, the event brought together prominent Hungarian officials, diplomats and representatives of the Turkish community. Among those attending were József Jelencsik, President of the Hungarian Parliament’s Hungarian–Turkish Friendship Group, Hungary’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Chief of the Hungarian Defence Staff, and representatives of various government institutions. Members of the diplomatic corps and Turkish civil society organisations were also present. The reception highlighted the diplomatic dimension of the anniversary celebrations and the close relationship between Hungary and Türkiye.

If you missed it: Hungary and Türkiye restart structured diplomatic cooperation after government change

Why 29 October is so important to Türkiye

Republic Day is one of Türkiye’s most significant national holidays, commemorating the proclamation of the republic on 29 October 1923 following the Turkish War of Independence.

As explained in the official history of the Turkish Grand National Assembly, the proclamation fundamentally transformed the country’s political system, with Mustafa Kemal Atatürk becoming the republic’s first president.

The new political order paved the way for sweeping reforms in education, legislation, government and public life, laying the foundations of modern Türkiye.

For Turkish communities living abroad, Republic Day is more than a historical anniversary. It provides an opportunity to celebrate national identity, maintain cultural traditions and strengthen connections between generations.

The Turkish Republic Day celebrations in Budapest reflected these values, bringing a major Turkish national commemoration into the public spaces of the Hungarian capital.

Hungarian–Turkish friendship has deep historical roots

The Budapest celebrations also highlighted the close relationship between Hungary and Türkiye, two countries whose modern friendship has developed despite a complicated shared past.

While Ottoman rule shaped parts of Hungary’s history for approximately 150 years, modern relations have increasingly focused on cooperation, mutual cultural interest and political dialogue.

Diplomatic relations between modern Hungary and the Turkish republic date back to the early years of Atatürk’s presidency. A friendship treaty was signed between the two countries on 15 December 1923, as recorded by Türkiye’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism.

The relationship has strengthened considerably in recent decades.

According to the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Hungary and Türkiye established a strategic partnership in 2013, which was upgraded to an enhanced strategic partnership in 2023.

Both countries are NATO members, while Hungary also maintains observer status in the Organisation of Turkic States, reflecting Budapest’s growing engagement with the Turkic world.

Economic cooperation has also expanded. Turkish official statistics show that bilateral trade reached approximately USD 5.16 billion in 2025, compared with USD 3.95 billion in 2023.

Read also – Türkiye’s road to COP31: From Ankara’s zero-waste ambitions to a greener Black Sea – Video

Cultural cooperation brings Hungary and Türkiye closer

Cultural diplomacy has become another important pillar of Hungarian–Turkish relations.

The year 2024 was celebrated as the Hungarian–Turkish Cultural Year, marking the centenary of the entry into force of the friendship agreement between the two countries.

According to Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications, Hungary organised 160 cultural, artistic and scientific events in 17 Turkish cities during the programme, attracting nearly 1.5 million visitors.

The Yunus Emre Turkish Cultural Institute in Budapest also plays an important role in maintaining these connections by promoting Turkish language and culture among Hungarian audiences.

Events such as the Republic March demonstrate how these bilateral relations extend beyond official diplomacy. They provide opportunities for Turkish residents in Hungary to celebrate their heritage while sharing their traditions with the wider Hungarian public.

The torchlit celebrations in Budapest were therefore not only a tribute to Türkiye’s republican history but also a visible expression of the growing cultural connections between the two nations.

As Türkiye celebrates 103 years of republican history, the Budapest gathering serves as a reminder that national identity and cultural traditions can remain vibrant far beyond a country’s borders.

World.title: Inside Esterházy Palace: An exclusive interview about its past, present and future – VIDEO
World.content:
One of Hungary’s most magnificent Baroque landmarks, Esterházy Palace in Fertőd, has witnessed centuries of aristocratic splendour, musical innovation and dramatic historical change. But what does the future hold for this remarkable royal residence? Daily News Hungary visited Eszterháza to speak with the palace’s director about its fascinating past, its role today and the opportunities and challenges ahead.

Often described as the “Hungarian Versailles”, Esterházy Palace is far more than an architectural masterpiece. It is a symbol of Hungary’s cultural heritage, a place closely associated with the great composer Joseph Haydn, and a destination that continues to attract visitors interested in history, art and music.

Esterházy Palace: A brief history of Hungary’s Versailles

Located in Fertőd, close to the Austrian border in north-western Hungary, Esterházy Palace is one of the country’s most impressive historic residences. Its story dates back to the early 18th century, when a hunting lodge was established on the site.

The palace owes much of its present appearance to Prince Nikolaus Esterházy, also known as Miklós “the Magnificent”, who transformed the estate into an extraordinary Baroque and Rococo residence during the second half of the 18th century.

Inspired by the great European royal courts, the prince created a cultural centre renowned for its lavish celebrations, theatrical performances and musical life. The palace even welcomed Empress Maria Theresa in 1773.

One of the most important figures associated with Eszterháza was Joseph Haydn, who worked for the Esterházy family for decades. The composer spent considerable time at the palace, where he directed musical performances and composed works that contributed to his international reputation.

Following the death of Prince Nikolaus in 1790, the palace gradually lost its former prominence. Later periods of revival were followed by the destruction and disruption of the Second World War. Restoration work began in the 1950s, with further major reconstruction projects undertaken in the 21st century.

Today, Esterházy Palace remains an important monument to Hungary’s aristocratic and musical heritage, welcoming visitors to discover its historic interiors, gardens and cultural legacy.

Exclusive interview: Discovering the past, present and future of Esterházy Palace

What does it take to preserve a historic palace while keeping its remarkable story alive for new generations?

The interview brings together three perspectives: the palace’s extraordinary history, its place in contemporary Hungary and the future of this nationally significant landmark.

For international audiences, the conversation offers an opportunity to learn more about a historic destination that may be less familiar than Budapest’s celebrated attractions, but holds an important place in Hungary’s cultural identity.

Eszterháza’s connection with European aristocratic life, classical music and architectural heritage makes it a fascinating subject not only for history enthusiasts but also for travellers seeking to discover another side of Hungary.

Source: Daily News Hungary

Through the interview, viewers can explore the relationship between the palace’s historical legacy and its contemporary role, while gaining a broader understanding of why preserving places such as Esterházy Palace matters.

Watch our exclusive interview from Esterházy Palace

Join Csilla for this special Daily News Hungary interview, filmed at Eszterháza, and discover the story behind one of Hungary’s most remarkable historic landmarks.

The full interview is available in Hungarian with English subtitles.

Whether you are planning a cultural trip to Hungary, interested in the world of the Esterházy family or simply curious about the future of one of Central Europe’s outstanding palaces, this conversation offers a compelling introduction to Eszterháza.

The palace’s history is a reminder that cultural heritage is not simply about preserving beautiful buildings. It is also about keeping alive the stories, artistic achievements and traditions that connect the past with the present – and ensuring they remain accessible to future generations.

World.title: All Saints’ Day in Hungary: Why millions light candles for their loved ones – and how it differs from Halloween
World.content:
Every autumn, cemeteries across Hungary are transformed into seas of flickering candlelight as families gather to remember those they have lost. All Saints’ Day in Hungary, observed on 1 November, is one of the country’s most deeply rooted traditions. But what exactly do Hungarians commemorate, why do they decorate graves with flowers and candles, and how does this solemn occasion differ from Halloween?

What is All Saints’ Day in Hungary?

Known in Hungarian as mindenszentek, All Saints’ Day falls on 1 November and is a national public holiday. Originally a Christian feast honouring all saints, including those without individual feast days, it has also become closely associated with remembering deceased family members.

The following day, 2 November, is halottak napja, or All Souls’ Day, traditionally dedicated to praying for the dead.

Although the two occasions have different religious meanings, they are closely connected in everyday Hungarian life. Many families visit cemeteries on 1 November, while others spread their commemorations across both days.

All Saints’ Day is an official public holiday in Hungary, while All Souls’ Day is not. In 2026, 1 November falls on a Sunday.

Why do Hungarians light candles and decorate graves?

One of the most recognisable Hungarian traditions is visiting the graves of deceased relatives, often travelling considerable distances to return to family burial places.

In the days leading up to All Saints’ Day, families clean gravestones, remove fallen leaves and arrange fresh flowers, particularly chrysanthemums, which have become strongly associated with remembrance.

As darkness approaches, they light candles and small memorial lanterns, known as mécsesek.

The flames traditionally symbolise remembrance, eternal light and hope. According to older folk beliefs, they could also help guide the souls of the departed.

If you missed it: Best Hungarian comfort dishes for cold weather

The result can be an extraordinary sight. Large cemeteries in Budapest and smaller village graveyards alike glow with thousands of lights, creating an atmosphere that is peaceful rather than frightening.

For many Hungarians, the occasion is not necessarily about religion. Even non-religious families maintain the custom as an expression of respect, affection and family continuity.

All Saints’ Day in Hungary. Illustration. Source: depositphotos.com

Forgotten Hungarian folk traditions

Hungarian remembrance customs once extended well beyond the cemetery.

According to the Hungarian National Digital Archive, older folk beliefs held that deceased relatives could return home during this period.

In some communities, families left food, bread or water on the table for visiting souls. Others kept a candle burning at home to welcome the departed.

Certain regions also had traditions of baking special bread or sharing food with those in need.

Although most of these practices have largely disappeared, they reveal how Christian observances became intertwined with Hungarian folk culture over the centuries.

All Saints’ Day vs Halloween: What is the difference?

For foreigners, the proximity of Halloween and All Saints’ Day can be confusing.

Halloween, celebrated on 31 October, combines historical Celtic and Christian influences with modern customs popularised particularly in North America. Today, it is widely associated with costumes, pumpkins, parties and trick-or-treating.

Hungarian All Saints’ Day, by contrast, traditionally focuses on reflection, remembrance and family visits to cemeteries.

Interestingly, the word Halloween derives from All Hallows’ Eve, meaning the evening before All Saints’ Day. The occasions therefore share historical connections despite their very different modern expressions.

Halloween has become increasingly popular in Hungary, especially among younger generations. Costume parties, pumpkin carving and themed events are now familiar features of late October.

Pumpkin carving. depositphotos.com

However, Halloween has not replaced the older traditions. A Hungarian family might attend a Halloween party on Saturday and still visit relatives’ graves on Sunday.

The two customs increasingly coexist, although some Hungarians consider the quieter atmosphere of remembrance more appropriate for this period.

What should foreigners know about All Saints’ Day in Hungary?

Visitors spending early November in Hungary may notice unusually busy cemeteries, flower stalls and an increased demand for candles.

Those wishing to observe the tradition can visit a cemetery respectfully, keeping noise to a minimum and avoiding intrusive photography of grieving families.

Budapest’s historic Fiumei Road Cemetery is particularly notable for its elaborate mausoleums and the graves of prominent figures from Hungarian history.

For foreign residents, understanding All Saints’ Day offers a glimpse into an important aspect of Hungarian culture.

While Halloween often turns the supernatural into entertainment, the Hungarian tradition gives remembrance a visible place in everyday life.

And as thousands of candles illuminate the November darkness, the message remains remarkably simple: those who have died are still remembered by the people they leave behind.

World.title: Fit enough to run, but what about your blood pressure?
World.content:
Hundreds of runners and visitors stopped for a quick health check-up during the 41st SPAR Budapest Marathon Festival at the FirstMed tent, on the weekend of 10-11 October. People passing through had their blood sugar and blood pressure checked, while colleagues from FirstMed’s Budapest, Rome and Milan clinics were out on the course running and walking different distances.

Collaborative content

At first glance, a marathon might seem an unusual place to think about high blood pressure or blood sugar. After all, many people there were active enough to run 10, 21, or even 42 kilometers. But being physically active, or simply feeling healthy, doesn’t guarantee these numbers will always stay within the expected range.

That is one reason a routine blood pressure check matters, even when nothing appears to be wrong.

Why can you feel healthy and still have high blood pressure?

High blood pressure, or hypertension, often has no noticeable symptoms. The World Health Organization (WHO) notes that many people with hypertension don’t know they have it. They may exercise regularly, work, travel, and carry on with everyday life without realizing their blood pressure is elevated. That’s why measuring it is particularly useful.

A blood pressure test is simple and usually takes only a few minutes, but it can pick up a reading that may need rechecking or discussion with a doctor.

However, a single high measurement does not necessarily mean you have hypertension. Blood pressure changes throughout the day. It can be affected by various factors such as physical activity (for example, a measurement taken after running), stress, and caffeine.

If a reading is high, a healthcare professional may recommend repeating the measurement, monitoring your blood pressure at home, or using a 24-hour monitor before making a diagnosis.

The important point is: don’t wait for symptoms to get it measured.

What about blood sugar?

Blood glucose is another number that may change before you notice anything unusual.

Prediabetes and type 2 diabetes can develop without symptoms, which is why screening is important even if you feel well. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) explains the blood tests used to identify them.

A quick (random) blood sugar measurement, such as those offered during the marathon weekend, can provide a snapshot of your glucose level at that particular moment. But don’t treat it as a diagnosis.

If a result raises concern, a doctor may recommend a laboratory test. Tests used to screen for diabetes include FPG (fasting plasma glucose) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1C), which shows average blood glucose over a longer period.

This distinction matters: treat an unexpected reading as a reason to investigate further, not a diagnosis on its own.

Who should have their numbers checked?

Blood pressure becomes more important to monitor as we get older. At 40 or over, pay particular attention to regular checks, while those with certain risk factors may need to start earlier or have their blood pressure measured more frequently. The main risk factors include:

a family history of hypertension,

smoking,

excess weight, and

a diet high in salt.

Your doctor may also monitor blood pressure more closely if you have another medical condition or take certain long-term medications.

How often should you have a blood pressure check?

No single schedule fits everyone. If you are 40 or older and haven’t had your blood pressure checked in several years, it is worth getting it measured. People with known hypertension or increased risk may need more frequent monitoring.

You can also monitor blood pressure at home. Pay attention to the proper technique: Sit relaxed, with your feet flat on the floor and your arm supported. For a more reliable picture, it’s best to repeat the measurement after a short time.

If your doctor has asked you to monitor your blood pressure at home, follow their recommended schedule rather than relying on occasional readings.

Blood pressure measurement at the FirstMed tent at the SPAR Budapest Marathon in Budapest. Photo: FirstMed

When should you get blood glucose screening?

For someone with normal blood glucose results, current recommendations (such as the American Diabetes Association’s 2026 Standards of Care) suggest starting blood glucose screening at age 35 and then repeating it at least every three years.

Although the right interval depends on risk factors, earlier or more frequent testing may be appropriate based on weight, family history, and other health conditions.

Rather than following a general screening schedule, a routine appointment with your GP is a useful opportunity to discuss which checks make sense for your age, medical history, and lifestyle.

Where can English speakers get these health checks in Budapest?

For foreigners living in Hungary, knowing what to check may be easier than knowing where to go, especially if discussing medical history or test results in Hungarian is difficult.

You can have your blood pressure measured in various healthcare settings. Private healthcare providers in Budapest also offer blood glucose screening and laboratory testing.

FirstMed Budapest provides primary care and health screening in English at its clinic in Hattyúház, near Széll Kálmán tér. An annual health exam includes a review of medical history and lifestyle factors, a thorough physical examination, blood pressure measurement, and a range of lab tests.

For patients who need blood glucose testing, lab tests help a doctor assess glucose levels and determine whether further investigation or follow-up is necessary.

Having consultations, testing, and results explained in English can make routine preventive care easier to navigate for internationals living in Budapest.

What should you do with an unexpected result?

Try not to interpret one number on its own. A higher-than-expected blood pressure or blood glucose reading may need follow-up, but a single result is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis. The circumstances in which the measurement was taken also matter.

This is especially important to know at an event like the Budapest Marathon, where participants may have recently exercised, eaten, consumed caffeine, or experienced the normal excitement and stress of a race day.

If you get an unexpected result, discuss it with a healthcare professional. They may help interpret it, decide whether to repeat the test under standardized conditions, or determine whether additional assessment is appropriate.

The hundreds of quick checks carried out during the Budapest Marathon weekend offered a simple reminder: preventive healthcare is not only for people who feel unwell. Knowing a few basic numbers can be a useful starting point for understanding your health, whether you have just completed a marathon or your running shoes have been sitting untouched for years.

For more about FirstMed’s health activities at the 2026 SPAR Budapest Marathon Festival, read the full story on firstmed.hu.

I exercise regularly. Do I still need health checks? Yes. Regular physical activity is a significant part of maintaining good health, but it doesn’t eliminate every risk factor. For example, high blood pressure often causes no symptoms. Age, family history, and other health factors can also increase your risk. Can I tell if my blood pressure is high from how I feel? Usually not. Many people with high blood pressure feel completely well. Measuring it is the only way to know whether your number is elevated. Does one high blood pressure reading mean I have hypertension? Not necessarily. Blood pressure varies, and diagnosis usually requires additional measurements. Depending on the result, a healthcare professional may suggest repeat clinic readings, home monitoring, or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring. At what age should I start checking my blood sugar? Current diabetes guidelines recommend screening adults from age 35, unless other factors indicate earlier testing. Testing may be appropriate sooner for people with certain risk factors, including overweight or obesity combined with factors such as a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, or cardiovascular disease. How often should I have a blood sugar test if my results are normal? For people without diabetes or prediabetes, repeating screening at least every three years is generally considered reasonable. However, more frequent testing may be recommended depending on your risk factors or changes in your health. Where can I arrange an English-language health check in Budapest? FirstMed Budapest provides English-language medical care, health screening and in-house laboratory services at its clinic in Hattyúház, Hattyú utca 14, near Széll Kálmán tér.

This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Please consult a qualified healthcare professional.

World.title: Big shake-up for Budapest public transport: capital and suburbs to get one transport system
World.content:
Budapest’s General Assembly has approved agreements paving the way for the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) to become a regional public transport organiser, with the new system scheduled to launch on 1 January 2027.

The proposal, submitted by Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony, was passed on Friday with 17 votes in favour and 11 abstentions, according to the Hungarian news agency MTI.

The decision follows an agreement reached between the Hungarian government and the capital. At a meeting of the Council for Metropolitan Development on 1 October, the parties approved plans for shareholder and cooperation agreements involving the Budapest Municipality, the Ministry of Transport and Investment, the state-owned National Transport Centre (OKK) and BKK.

Under the arrangement, OKK will acquire a 50% stake in BKK through a capital increase, making the state an equal shareholder alongside the municipality.

Don’t miss this: Budapest drivers to face weeks of disruption as major junction undergoes renovations

One transport organiser for the capital and its suburbs

From 1 January 2027, the company will operate under the name BKK Budapest Metropolitan Transport Centre Plc. It will act as a joint transport organiser, commissioning public transport services across the capital and the surrounding region.

Its responsibilities will include services operated by the capital, suburban railway lines, suburban rail services and regional bus routes terminating in Budapest. The aim is to bring the organisation of transport across the metropolitan area under a more coordinated system.

The reform could affect almost three million people living in Budapest and its surrounding settlements, who rely on a network of urban and suburban transport services for commuting and other journeys.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Politicians welcome the decision

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy welcomed the vote in a post on Facebook, describing it as approval of the regional BKK concept.

He said the state would become a 50% owner alongside the capital and that BKK would gain commissioning rights across the entire suburban region.

“The biggest winners are the passengers,” Vitézy wrote.

Mayor Gergely Karácsony also praised the decision, saying that from January, the BKK would organise public transport throughout the region. He described the residents of Budapest and its agglomeration — nearly three million people in total — as the main beneficiaries of the agreement.

World.title: Leading Czech magazine portrays Viktor Orbán in handcuffs
World.content:
A leading Czech political magazine has depicted former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in handcuffs next to Péter Magyar on its latest cover as it examines Hungary’s political transformation following his departure from power.

Popular magazine depicts Viktor Orbán handcuffed

The cover of Reflex, a popular Czech public affairs weekly, features Orbán handcuffed alongside Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar. The issue contains extensive coverage of the new government’s efforts to dismantle the political structures established under Orbán and restore the rule of law.

Magyar bought a copy of the magazine during a brief visit to Prague, where he also met Oliver Adámek, a journalist specialising in Hungarian politics. Adámek presented the prime minister with a copy of his newly published book, Világoš, which examines the collapse of Orbán’s political system after 16 years in power.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Book explores Orbán’s electoral defeat

Founded in 1990, Reflex is widely regarded as a right-wing libertarian publication. Adámek is among the Czech media’s best-known experts on Hungarian domestic politics and speaks Hungarian fluently.

An extract from his book appears in the latest issue, recounting the final days of the election campaign, including US Vice-President JD Vance’s visit and Orbán’s closing rally in Budapest. Adámek recalls sensing that the election had been decided when a large crowd gathered to welcome Magyar in Ráckeve early on the morning of 7 April, coinciding with Vance’s arrival.

The book’s title is a play on the Czech expression dostat világoš, meaning to suffer a beating or a heavy defeat. The phrase is believed to derive from the Hungarian surrender at Világos in 1849 and is used here to refer to Fidesz’s electoral defeat.

Stay up-to-date: Viktor Orbán reported to police over controversial speech about ‘handing out appropriate tools’

Questions over Hungary’s democratic reforms

A second major article by Adámek examines the Magyar government’s record in dismantling the former ruling party’s political structures. It discusses changes to state institutions, efforts to replace officials appointed under Orbán, and plans to introduce an age limit for Constitutional Court judges.

However, the journalist also questions whether the government’s reforms risk concentrating power rather than restoring democratic checks and balances. He asks whether voters gave Magyar a mandate for such far-reaching constitutional changes.

Adámek argues that Magyar must now demonstrate tangible improvements in people’s lives and prove that the political transition represents more than symbolic revenge against his predecessors. The Reflex coverage reflects wider Czech media interest in Hungary’s political direction, with other publications also examining the government’s reforms and the future of Hungarian democracy.

World.title: Tragedy that Led to Change: Serbia Marks Two Years Since Canopy Collapse
World.content:
Novi Sad, Serbia’s second city, was in shock and mourning on November 1, 2024.

Since Sunday, the grief and anger once so palpable in this Danube city and the country as a whole has given way to hope for a better future and talk of ‘liberation’ following a bruising election defeat suffered by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, at the hands of a student-led protest movement.

On November 1, 2024, Serbia and Novi Sad were firmly under the rule of the SNS and its founder, then President Aleksandar Vucic. At 11.52 that morning, everything changed.

That was the moment the outdoor canopy of Novi Sad’s newly renovated railway station collapsed. Fourteen people, including children, were killed instantly, buried under tonnes of concrete. Three others fought to stay alive, but ultimately only one did not succumb to their injuries, taking the death toll to 16.

World.title: The Anatomy of Forging Freedom: Lessons from Serbia’s Students
World.content:
An avalanche of small acts

Through the same painstaking, often exhausting practice of direct democracy, faculty assemblies distributed quotas to select 250 parliamentary candidates, ensuring representation across the country. Every name then underwent nationwide scrutiny, with faculties able to challenge and collectively veto one another’s choices. Finally, they chose a parliamentary list reflecting the breadth of Serbian life they had encountered on foot, from workers and farmers to academics, doctors and judges: Student List – Students Are Winning.

On September 9, 492 days after the students first called for early elections, Aleksandar Vucic finally yielded and called the vote. Eighteen days later, he resigned the presidency to run for prime minister.

From that moment, the fruits of the students’ long democratic struggle began to show. Student working groups, established months earlier, launched the campaign, backed by a formidable infrastructure of civic self-organisation, with millions of citizens contributing whatever time, skills and resources they could. Recognising the circumstances, most opposition parties stepped aside. By election day, there was hardly a corner of Serbia where students and citizens had not organised to safeguard the vote against fraud and manipulation.

Turnout reached a historic high. The Student List secured 52.71 per cent of the vote against 39.17 per cent for the then-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, winning an outright parliamentary majority. So decisive was the victory that even a regime determined to hold on to power at any cost had no choice but to concede defeat.

At the beginning, these young people had little more than imagination and the stubborn hope that their country could be different. Through two years of determined work, courage and sacrifice, they brought millions alongside them. Most had wanted nothing more than a democratic Serbia, a country where they might finally imagine a future of their own.

And yet, by bringing down a regime that had long fuelled tensions across the Western Balkans, maintained close ties with Putin’s Russia and presented itself to Europe as a guarantor of stability, they accomplished something far beyond a change of government.

They loosened the grip of a politics that had held the region’s future hostage for far too long, inviting the Western Balkans and the EU to finally begin building the future they had spent so many years waiting for.

Milan Vujić currently works at the Erste Foundation in Vienna, and is also a lawyer and former student activist from Novi Sad in Serbia.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Week in Review: Big Changes, Bigger Challenges
World.content:
Many in Serbia are still pinching themselves after Sunday’s parliamentary elections. Not only did Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party lose the election, they did so in a landslide. Contrary to many expectations, they also quickly conceded defeat.

The extent of the swing away from the long-time ruling party surprised many observers. Our analysis takes stock of the elections and their outcome as both Serbia and the region digest the results.

World.title: New Exhibition Features Italian Photojournalist’s Work from Wartime Sarajevo
World.content:
Mario Boccia was among the many journalists and photojournalists that covered the siege of Sarajevo. “Many were better than me,” he said, humbly.

But few others, he believes, held their first exhibition of Sarajevo photos in the city itself while it was still under siege.

In September 1994 he took some photos of a class in Ciglane, a neighbourhood in Sarajevo, where instructors were teaching children how to use a computer. “In January 1995 I brought those pictures back, glued them on cardboard and hung them on the wall and the children came to see them,” he said. “It was something quite unique.”

World.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Race Heads to Runoff as Russia Divides the Two Candidates
World.content:
On Sunday, Bulgarian voters head to the polls again for the second round of geopolitically charged presidential elections.

In the first round on October 25, current acting President Iliana Iotova won 34.7 per cent to opposition candidate and former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov’s 31.9 per cent.

The elections were marked by record low turnout. The Central Election Committee reported that only 22.98 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot.

Iotova and Gyurov are both running as independents, but they are supported by opposing factions and represent opposing foreign policy approaches and political alignments.

Iotova has been endorsed by the ruling party Progressive Bulgaria, the Bulgarian Socialist Party (which she is a former member of) and the nationalist party VMRO. Her potential victory would represent a consolidation of power by Progressive Bulgaria and Prime Minister Rumen Radev, whom Iotova served as vice president when he was president from 2017 to early 2026.

Gyurov has been supported by the pro-EU opposition parties Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change, of which he was formerly a member. However, his campaign has tried to present him as independent of party dynamics.

During a TV debate on October 29, Iotova positioned herself as the candidate who can guarantee peace in the region and maintain more balanced diplomatic relations with Russia.

Among her criticisms of her opponent is that as interim Prime Minister, Gyurov signed a 10-year agreement with Ukrainian President Zelensky. She also disapproves of his past association with the party We Continue the Change, particularly the party’s work on gas diversification in 2022 after Russia’s Gazprom cut off supplies to Bulgaria.

The opposition has recently criticised Iotova for pardoning five people sentenced for drug dealing since 2022, at least one of whom was later arrested again for the same crime.

For both candidates 2026 brought major changes. Iotova became acting president after Rumen Radev stepped down and ran successfully in the April snap elections with his Progressive Bulgaria party. Before Radev took over as prime minister, Gyurov led the caretaker cabinet.

The presidential campaign coincided with increased drone attacks in the Black Sea which stoked public debate and divisions over the government’s reluctance to name Russia as the aggressor. Both Radev and Iotova remain elusive about Russia’s potential role in the security risks in the Black Sea region.

Shortly after the first round, the government was criticised for using official communication channels to promote Iotova and for domineering language directed at journalists who cover the elections. On October 30, the government issued a statement saying that the Central Election Committee found no wrongdoing but has deleted the Iotova-related posts if Gyurov’s team is “so sure this would help them in their campaign”, in an atypically ironic tone for an official statement.

Opposition figures have also accused Radev’s government of meddling with social media. Three popular satirical social media pages – often targeting political figures through memes and jokes but occasionally appearing supportive of Gyurov and the pro-EU opposition parties – were taken down and restored repeatedly.

World.title: Mourning Day Declared in Bosnia’s Brcko Following Deadly EUFOR Helicopter Crash
World.content:
The mayor of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s semi-autonomous administrative unit Brcko District, Sinisa Milic, declared a day of mourning on Friday following the deaths of four EUFOR personnel from the Italian armed forces.

The deaths occurred when a helicopter operated by the European Union Force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, EUFOR, crashed on Thursday during a routine operation near Brcko in northeastern Bosnia.

Milic said the victims were members of the force deployed to maintain peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

“This is a symbolic way of expressing solidarity with the victims’ families and the entire Italian people,” Milic said.

He emphasised that special recognition should go to the helicopter pilots, who tried to keep the aircraft airborne and prevent it from crashing into populated areas, thereby avoiding civilian casualties.

EUFOR confirmed on Thursday night that two of the four people killed in the helicopter crash were members of the Italian armed forces, while the other two belonged to the Italian Red Cross Military Corps.

Another 11 people were injured, all of whom are in stable condition, according to EUFOR. Two were transferred to the Tuzla Clinical Centre for treatment, while the remaining nine are receiving medical care in Brcko.

“EUFOR is deeply saddened by this tragic loss of life and extends its deepest condolences to the friends and family of those who lost their lives in the service of peace,” a EUFOR statement said.

Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto announced on Thursday that those killed in the crash were Sergeants Simone Ruggia and Claudio Marchesi of the Italian armed forces, and Lieutenant Franco Adriano Zecchillo and Sergeant Laura Procacci of the Italian Red Cross Volunteer Military Corps.

EUFOR reiterated its appeal to the public not to spread disinformation or speculate about the circumstances of the crash, urging the public to rely exclusively on official sources for information.

They reported that no civilian infrastructure, property or vehicles were damaged in the incident and that no civilians were injured, adding that the investigation into the accident is currently ongoing.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her condolences, saying the news had caused deep sorrow.

“The news of the tragic crash of an Italian EUFOR helicopter in Bosnia and Herzegovina is a cause of deep sorrow. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and everyone involved in the mission to maintain peace and stability in the region who are now going through hours of uncertainty,” Meloni said.

The European Union Force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, EUFOR Althea, is an EU-led military operation established in 2004 to help maintain a safe and secure environment in the country.

Operating under a United Nations mandate, EUFOR supports the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement and is headquartered at Camp Butmir in Sarajevo. A total of 24 countries take part in the mission, including some non-EU countries, with the commanding structure rotating on an annual basis.

World.title: Moldova Steps Up Border Security Amid ‘Unprecedented’ Threats
World.content:
From airspace violations to cyber attacks, Russia’s war in Ukraine has confronted Moldova with “unprecedented” threats, forcing the country to upgrade its defences with new surveillance systems, drones and anti-drone technology, border police chief Ruslan Galusca has told BIRN.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Moldova has registered more than 100 drone incursions, 65 of which occurred this year.

In recent weeks, Russia has targeted border crossings between Ukraine and Moldova that it claims are being used to resupply the Ukrainian military despite Moldovan denials.

On October 5, one of Galusca’s officers was wounded in Russian drone strikes near the Palanca-Maiaki-Udobnoe crossing.

“The risk is real,” Galusca said in an interview.

World.title: New Rules are Coming for Road Users in Croatia
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – New rules are coming into force for road users across Croatia, with higher penalties and significant amendments to the Road Traffic Act.

The Ministry of the Interior has now released for public consultation a draft of amendments to the Road Traffic Safety Act. Index reports that it will introduce significantly stricter penalties for dangerous behaviour in traffic, new parking rules and easier removal of vehicles by tow truck, as well as special registration plates for taxis and electric cars.

higher fines for those filming and posting dangerous driving

One of the key novelties concerns drivers who film their own dangerous driving in order to post it on social media, which the legislator now treats as a significantly more serious offence. While such behaviour was previously punished as ordinary mobile phone use while driving with a fixed fine of 130 euros, the new proposal introduces fines of 800 to as much as 2,000 euros for anyone who uses a mobile phone or other device while driving to record their own unlawful behaviour and then makes it publicly available. The explanatory notes state that such posts have additional social harm because they encourage others to imitate them and normalise dangerous driving patterns.

police no longer need to attend minor collisions

For the first time ever, the law defines the concept of a “minor traffic accident,” which means an accident involving only material damage that does not impair the technical soundness of essential parts of the car and allows it to be easily removed from the road. Under the new Article 182, police officers are no longer obliged to go to the scene of such an accident if the participants are able to exchange details with each other or complete the European Accident Statement. Drivers who nevertheless refuse to immediately move their cars off the carriageway and continue to block traffic while waiting for the police will be fined 200 euros, whereas the fine until now was 60 euros.

a total ban on parking on squares

The draft also introduces the concept of a restricted traffic zone into the law, together with significantly stricter rules for stopping and parking in city centres. The previous practice whereby drivers, especially delivery vehicles, parked in city squares and pedestrian zones while invoking the rule about leaving a 1.60-metre passage for pedestrians will no longer apply. Article 82 introduces an absolute ban on stopping and parking in squares, in cultural-historical complexes and on surfaces that local authorities have designated exclusively for pedestrians, regardless of how much free space remains. At the same time, the rules for the operation of the tow-truck service are also changing. A tow truck will be legally able to lift an improperly parked vehicle from the pavement if the free passage between the car and any obstacle is less than one metre. An obstacle is no longer considered only a building, but also bollards, waste bins, outdoor café terraces or any other physical obstacle on the sidewalk.

special registration plates for taxis and electric cars

The law also introduces the obligation to issue special registration plates for two categories of vehicles — taxis and electric-powered cars. While in the case of taxis this is about easier control and alignment with market rules, for electric cars the reason is directly linked to the safety of emergency services. Lithium-ion batteries in electric and hybrid vehicles, in the event of a collision and fire, generate extremely high temperatures, release toxic gases and require completely different firefighting tactics from classic petrol and diesel engines. Special plates will enable firefighters, already upon arrival at the scene of a traffic accident, to recognise electric propulsion and immediately apply the appropriate extinguishing and rescue procedure.
