World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Cyber attacks hit Russia, Ukraine after truce ends
World.content:
Russia said its emergency warnings app came under a “massive cyberattack” on Monday, hours after Ukraine reported a hack in an apparent exchange of blows between the foes, as their longest truce came to an end.

Moscow’s emergencies ministry said hackers posted “false information” on the app, which is designed to warn the public of incoming drone attacks and other threats.

Hours earlier, Ukraine said it suspected its air raid alert system had been compromised, after baseless alerts of a radiation threat appeared on the app.

World.title: Poland’s Tusk says he won’t back down in top court standoff
World.content:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk vowed to press on with changes at the top court and accused the opposition of stirring up violence in an attempt to destroy the rule of law as the political crisis continued to spiral.

Tusk said in a TV address on Saturday that the Constitutional Tribunal in its current format isn’t independent and his government’s attempts to fix it have been sabotaged by the Law & Justice party and President Karol Nawrocki.

He spoke hours after riot police were deployed in front of the court, and two of its top judges were suspended. Nawrocki turned back his plane en route to Senegal and returned to Warsaw to hold consultations with parliamentary parties on Saturday, which Tusk’s ruling Civic Coalition didn’t attend.

World.title: Japan-supported Grand Egyptian Museum marks first year of operations
World.content:
The Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM), built with Japanese support on the outskirts of Cairo, marked its first anniversary Sunday.

During its first year of operations, the museum attracted over 5 million visitors despite the deteriorating situation in the Middle East.

The museum in the city of Giza houses over 100,000 ancient Egyptian artifacts, including the golden mask and other funerary items from the tomb of King Tutankhamun.

To commemorate its first anniversary, the GEM will host a special nighttime show from this month through the end of April next year. Using lighting and music, the show recreates scenes from ancient Egyptian life, including the flooding of the Nile and crop harvesting.

GEM CEO Ahmed Ghoneim told reporters that the museum had achieved its goal of attracting more tourists to the pyramid area, highlighting its contribution to local tourism.

Located near the three pyramids in Giza, which are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site, the GEM is one of the world’s largest archaeological museums. Japanese experts have assisted in restoring excavated artifacts and training local technicians.

“I couldn’t see all the exhibits even after spending three and a half hours,” said Hideyuki Ninomiya, a 52-year-old company employee from Tokyo who visited the museum. “Tutankhamun’s coffin and golden mask were particularly impressive.”

World.title: Arsenal reaffirms status with win over Liverpool to move into first place
World.content:
If Arsenal’s title rivals thought its humbling penalty shootout defeat against fourth-tier Fleetwood Town in the League Cup might have shaken the confidence of Mikel Arteta’s side, Sunday’s gritty 1-0 win at Liverpool was sobering viewing.

Being knocked out by a team 84 rungs lower on the ladder was not the best way for Arteta’s Premier League champion to prepare for a trip to Anfield, especially with Andoni Iraola’s team beginning to click.

Four days later, however, Arsenal’s armor-plating looked fully restored as it held Liverpool at bay and sealed its first league win at Anfield in 14 years to move three points clear of Manchester City at the top of the table.

World.title: Honma, astronomer behind black hole image, named for autumn honor
World.content:
The government said Monday that it would award Medals of Honor to 736 people and 25 organizations this autumn, including astronomer Mareki Honma, who participated in the project that captured the first image of a black hole.

Honma, 55, professor at the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, will be awarded the Medal with Purple Ribbon, which honors those who have achieved outstanding academic, sports or artistic results.

He headed the Japanese team for the Event Horizon Telescope international research project, which succeeded in photographing a black hole by linking radio telescopes around the world.

Other awardees of the same medal include contemporary artist Yoshitomo Nara, 66, known for his depictions of girls with large, cartoon-like eyes and works featuring dogs. The government recognizes his contribution to the development of contemporary art in Japan.

Contemporary artist Yoshitomo Nara is known for his depictions of girls with large, cartoon-like eyes and works featuring dogs. | AFP-JIJI

The medal will also be awarded to Yuko Kitagawa, 66, vice president of Keio University and a specialist in surgical medicine, and Takao Someya, 58, professor of electronic engineering at the University of Tokyo.

Among those selected for the Medal with Blue Ribbon in recognition of their contributions to the promotion of industry and social welfare was Naoki Iimori, 64, head of sake producer Fukuchiyo Shuzo, known for its Nabeshima brand.

Of the 736 awardees, 160 are women. Thirteen people, including one woman, are set to receive the Medal with Purple Ribbon, while the Medal with Blue Ribbon will go to 443 people, including 132 women.

The Japan Times, a member of our group, as Japan’s leading and historic English-language media outlet, possesses strong information dissemination capabilities and an exclusive network reaching global leaders and international readers both domestically and abroad. World.title: Long-distance flights can interfere with the internal clocks of seabirds
World.content:
People who travel across many time zones, like a trip from London to Tokyo, may experience jet lag, with the body’s internal 24-hour clock — the circadian rhythm — thrown out of sync with the local time at the arrival location. A new study shows that birds that fly long distances may experience a similar phenomenon that causes them to drift off course.

Research involving seabirds called Manx shearwaters found that crossing the Atlantic at speed can throw their internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing errors in the strategy they use to navigate their way home.

Birds can use several cues to find their way, including having the sun serve as a compass. A bird flying south sees the sun on its left at sunrise and on its right toward sunset, so it must keep adjusting its heading as the sun moves across the sky.

World.title: India’s protest movements unite in New Delhi to challenge Modi
World.content:
Tens of thousands of protesters poured into central New Delhi on Sunday in a largely peaceful protest that represented a show of unity among disparate opposition groups, in one of the biggest rallies against Prime Minister Narendra Modi since he took power in 2014.

Opposition supporters marched toward Ramlila Maidan — a sprawling area in the heart of the capital that has hosted some of the nation’s biggest political demonstrations — as part of a series of protests over a voter roll scandal. The rally began to disperse at about 5 p.m. local time.

Modi had earlier accused the opposition of conspiring to divide the country and obstruct its development, underscoring the political tensions surrounding the weekslong dispute. It centers around a sweeping voter-roll revision that critics allege is disenfranchising legitimate voters after millions of names were excluded from draft lists. The Election Commission denies any wrongdoing.

World.title: What can Cambridge teach Hong Kong about building university towns?
World.content:
Strong government-industry partnership and interdisciplinary education are what make a university town financially viable and successful, the head of a University of Cambridge college has said, sharing the UK’s experience as Hong Kong develops its Northern Metropolis plan.

In an interview with the South China Morning Post, Professor Girish Menon, president of Lucy Cavendish College, said Hong Kong’s cosmopolitan character made it “best placed” to place young people at the heart of its university town.

“A successful university town has to think about what young people need to survive and thrive – a strong pastoral community, recreation and opportunities to engage with enterprise, the public sector and civil society,” he said.

World.title: Drug maker Rohto plans clinical trials in Hong Kong as OASES’ first Japan partner
World.content:
Top university research, cross-border data exchanges and access to mainland China’s large market have attracted Japanese firm Rohto Pharmaceutical to conduct clinical trials in Hong Kong, making it the first company from the country to partner with the city’s government under a flagship investment initiative.

Rohto, known for its over-the-counter eye care and skincare products, is among the latest batch of 18 firms recruited by the Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises (OASES), a government unit under the Financial Secretary’s Office tasked with attracting companies of strategic importance to Hong Kong.

Kunio Yamada, chairman and representative director of Rohto, told the South China Morning Post in an exclusive interview that Hong Kong’s top research capabilities and proximity to the mainland attracted the firm to expand in the city.

World.title: Former Apple Daily publisher joins mainland China tour for rehabilitated offenders
World.content:
A former publisher of the now-defunct Apple Daily newspaper has joined a Hong Kong government-organised mainland study tour for rehabilitated offenders, telling a state-owned broadcaster he felt “very proud” as a Chinese national after experiencing the country’s technological advances first-hand.

Cheung Kim-hung, a key prosecution witness in former media boss and Apple Daily founder Jimmy Lai Chee-ying ’s national security trial , pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign or external forces to endanger national security.

He was sentenced to six years and nine months in prison and had been expected to remain behind bars until 2028.

World.title: ‘Less than a minute’: Hong Kong travellers praise Japan’s new tax refund at airports
World.content:
Hong Kong tour groups returning from Japan have praised a smooth roll-out of the country’s new tax refund arrangement that requires travellers to complete refund procedures at airports or ports rather than at shops.

Under the “pay first, refund later” scheme, which took effect on Sunday to curb illicit domestic reselling and tax evasion, international tourists must now pay the 10 per cent consumption tax upfront at the counter.

Travellers are now required to complete customs verification before checking in their luggage, either at self-service airport kiosks or via the website Visit Japan Web. After verification, most will be cleared automatically, while some may be selected for customs inspection and asked to present their purchases.

World.title: Clarify crime thresholds and immunity in bid-rigging law: Hong Kong Bar Association
World.content:
The Hong Kong Bar Association has called on the government to clearly define criminal thresholds and resolve whistle-blower immunity rules under its plan to outlaw bid-rigging following the deadly Tai Po inferno.

A task force formed by the association, which represents the city’s barristers, spent 10 months reviewing four key areas of law and released a 140-page report on Sunday in the hope of providing direction to address the shortcomings that led to the deadly Wang Fuk Court blaze last November.

While its suggestion to criminalise bid-rigging, which was put forward in May, was adopted by the government as part of a basket of reforms unveiled last week, the association stressed the elements of the crime, including the definition of bid-rigging, the burden of proof and mens rea, must be clearly defined.

World.title: High Court redevelopment plan ‘not workable’, Hong Kong Bar Association warns
World.content:
The Hong Kong Bar Association has warned that a proposed phased redevelopment of the High Court, which could span more than a decade, is “not workable” and risks deterring legal practitioners from joining the bench.

The association, the professional body for barristers, urged the government to consider faster alternatives, such as repurposing the existing District Court building.

In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post on Sunday, association chairman Jose-Antonio Maurellet SC also said the authorities should consider offering judges an ex gratia pay rise, on top of keeping salaries in line with inflation, to attract top-tier practitioners from the private sector.

World.title: How could a single gene-editing injection treat inherited eye diseases?
World.content:
In the third of a four-part Health Matters wellness series on frontier medicine in Hong Kong, Fiona Sun examines how a local start-up is testing a gene-editing therapy that could tackle a group of inherited eye diseases at their genetic source and what it will take to turn it into a treatment patients can access.

For 15 years, Professor Zheng Zongli has worked to make gene-editing therapies safe enough to treat diseases with limited treatment options.

His path has taken him from a PhD in medical epidemiology at Sweden’s Karolinska Institutet to postdoctoral training at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School – and, ultimately, to Hong Kong, where he co-founded the gene therapy start-up GenEditBio.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.title: Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.content:
Breast milk from mothers with postpartum depression may negatively impact infants’ brain development, a Chinese study has found.

The study, published Oct. 27 in the top academic journal Cell Metabolism, was led by a team at Nanjing University, in the eastern Jiangsu province. Through a mouse model, it shows, for the first time, how depression-related changes in levels of microRNA, a type of gene-regulating molecule, contained in structures called extracellular vesicles in breast milk can affect offspring brains.

Between 10% and 20% of mothers worldwide experience postpartum depression. Children of affected mothers are more likely to face challenges in cognition, language, behavior, and school performance, and are at a higher risk of developing depression themselves.

Past research has implicated genetics and the way mothers with postpartum depression bond with, and care for, their infants as contributing to this phenomenon, but the broad and long-lasting effects of postpartum depression on child development remain unclear, according to the researchers.

Because breast milk is increasingly viewed as a “signaling system orchestrating infant development,” the researchers wrote, they looked at the relationship between milk-based microRNAs and extracellular vesicles, key parts of this signaling. Because babies’ blood-brain barrier is more permeable than adults’, these vesicles can enter the brain during nursing, making its development more sensitive to diet.

The researchers compared the breast milk of 40 human mothers clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression, and 51 without, finding that those with depression had elevated levels of three types of microRNA implicated in psychiatric illness. The same was true of the breast milk of depressed mice.

To test nursing’s role in brain development, swapping mouse pups between healthy and depressed mouse mothers. Pups born to healthy mice but nursed by their depressed counterparts showed worse cognitive and emotional behavior than pups born to depressed mothers but nursed by healthy ones.

They also found that neurons in pups nursed by depressed mothers had shorter dendrites and fewer branches in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, a part of the brain believed to play a role in memory development and depression. The problems arose mainly as the neurons matured, were detectable by day 21 after birth, and persisted into adulthood, suggesting that early nursing-environment effects can last into later development.

Giving milk from depressed mothers to healthy pups was also enough to cause cognitive impairment after weaning, while milk where the vesicles had been removed had no such effect, the researchers found.

When the team inhibited Rab27a, a protein and key factor in vesicle secretion, in the mammary glands of depressed mothers, vesicle secretion fell by 58%, and the cognitive and neurodevelopmental deficits in their pups improved significantly.

The researchers also found that microRNA in milk vesicles from depressed mothers blocks a “brake” receptor called mGluR8 in pups’ brains. Without this brake, brain regions can become overstimulated, impairing the development of neural connections. As a result, new brain cells are more active overall but respond more weakly to memory tasks, helping explain the cognitive problems seen in pups nursed by depressed mothers.

The study offers the key findings of both a new communication pathway and a microRNA-based mechanism of inheritance between mothers and babies, according to the researchers.

Breastfeeding is widely seen as good for babies’ brain development, but this study also suggests that breastfeeding by mothers with postpartum depression may have a “double-edged effect on offspring health,” the researchers wrote.

“Elucidating the molecular mechanisms linking maternal postnatal depression to offspring neurological outcomes therefore holds considerable public health value and underscores the urgent need for targeted maternal mental health interventions during lactation,” they added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.title: 90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.content:
Chinese prosecutors have exposed an invoice-trading network that illegally traded special value-added tax (VAT) invoices totaling more than 7.4 billion yuan ($1.1 billion) over three years.

Under the guise of a Shanghai-based advertising business, the group profited by issuing and charging service fees for fake invoices from shell companies it registered to customers seeking to illegally claim tax deductions — which can be claimed for special tax invoices, but not ordinary tax invoices in China — domestic media reported Tuesday.

The case has exposed major weaknesses in business-registration oversight, tax monitoring, and financial regulators’ ability to detect suspicious fund flows between affiliated company accounts, according to experts.

From June 2025 to June 2026, more than 90 criminal suspects on the case were processed by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Procuratorate, some of whom were ordered to return their illegal gains. Processing of the case is ongoing.

The group’s ringleaders, surnamed Cui and Shen, first had employees register over 70 shell companies in their own names. Invoices were then handled via three steps: a sales team first connected with customers, who transferred money to the group in order to receive invoices; then a team obtained invoices from both the operation’s registered shell companies or legitimate businesses with unused invoicing quotas; before another team returned funds to customers following invoice-fee deductions. Customers were charged a service fee of between 7% and 13% of the invoice value.

Chinese tax law requires contracts, fund transfers, invoices, and movement of goods to align. Falsely issuing invoices can result in fines of up to 500,000 yuan, while tax dodgers may be fined up to five times the underpaid tax. Both carry risks of criminal prosecution.

To circumvent the law, customers transferred the full invoice amount to the group, which then transferred the remaining funds back to the customer through a separate, third account.

The group illegally traded over 7.4 billion yuan in VAT invoices, involving more than 420 million yuan in VAT. It also conducted illegal foreign-exchange transactions totaling 420 million yuan.

“The scale of the crimes, the degree of organization, and the length of time over which they were committed were all relatively unusual,” Li Huaisheng, a professor at the School of Criminal Justice at China University of Political Science and Law, told state media outlet CCTV.

Similar cases involving companies that obtained invoices through intermediaries have made national headlines in recent years. Last year, a group allegedly used 15 shell companies to falsely issue almost 3,500 special VAT invoices totaling 300 million yuan, domestic media reported. The defendant, surnamed Li, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison and fined 500,000 yuan.

According to the State Taxation Administration, such companies often disguise themselves as consulting, advertising, or other business services in industries with low fixed-asset requirements, long industrial chains, and large transaction values, such as recycling, road freight transport, and information technology consulting.

Li Huaisheng recommended that market regulatory authorities establish early-warning models to flag suspicious company registrations, and tax authorities improve big-data checks on invoices, capital, contracts, and goods.

In an interview with CCTV, Zhou Xianbao, a lawyer at BZW Law Firm in Beijing, also recommended establishing a system requiring real-name authorization for invoice issuance and formal tax-compliance commitments.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.title: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.content:
When most Chinese people think of World War I, they think of it as a “European war.” This is not simply an oversight. It is the result of a century of forgetting.

Few people are aware that between 1916 and 1918, Britain and France recruited around 140,000 Chinese laborers from Shandong, Hebei, Guangdong, Hong Kong, and other regions to work on the Western Front. They dug trenches, built defenses, and transported ammunition. After the fighting ended, they stayed on to help with reconstruction, clearing battlefields and filling in shell craters. Some did not return home until 1922.

Sending laborers overseas was not simply a matter of supplying manpower. It was also part of a carefully considered political strategy. Politicians such as Liang Shiyi — an influential adviser to then-President Yuan Shikai — believed that Germany and Austria-Hungary were unlikely to defeat Britain and France, and advocated a “laborers-as-soldiers” strategy that would allow China to participate indirectly in the war and break its diplomatic isolation. Meanwhile, figures associated with the New Culture Movement, an early 20th-century intellectual and cultural reform movement, saw sending laborers overseas as an opportunity to develop China’s working class. They included Li Shizeng, a French-educated anarchist and organizer of the Diligent Work-Frugal Study Movement, and Cai Yuanpei, a leading educator and president of Peking University.

Yet China’s participation in the Allied war effort did not bring the diplomatic gains its leaders had hoped for. At the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, the victorious powers agreed to transfer Germany’s former rights in Shandong province to Japan rather than return them to China, a decision that helped spark the May Fourth Movement, a wave of student-led protests that became a turning point in modern Chinese history.

The contributions of the Chinese laborers themselves also received little recognition. When they returned home in the 1920s, they found a country gripped by political upheaval and were often met with indifference or even suspicion.

The result was a double erasure. The West forgot their contributions, while China forgot their sacrifices.

In July 2019, a delegation from Belgium’s In Flanders Fields Museum visited Shanghai University. The two institutions agreed to jointly investigate, excavate, study, and exhibit the remains of Chinese labor camps on the Western Front during World War I. By then, scholars from the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Germany, Canada, and other countries, led by Professor Nicholas J. Saunders of the University of Bristol, had spent nearly a decade systematically surveying the physical remains and landscapes of the Western Front. Yet the Chinese labor camps remained a missing piece of the puzzle. Although frequently mentioned in historical records, they had never been systematically investigated or excavated by archaeologists.

In May 2023, Shanghai University officially launched the Chinese Labour Corps (CLC) Camp Project, in collaboration with the In Flanders Fields Museum, Ghent University, and Howest University of Applied Sciences. A non-invasive geophysical survey was completed in April 2024, and excavation began in February 2025. The project concluded in March 2026.

Before we began digging, information about the Chinese labor camps could be found in historical documents, but it was fragmented. Official military archives paid little attention to these noncombatants from China, while local records offered a more vivid picture. One example is the diary of Belgian priest Achiel Van Walleghem. In August 1917, he recorded the presence of two Chinese labor camps in the village of Reningelst, near the Belgian town of Ypres, a major battleground during World War I. In January 1918, he noted that some shop owners had begun learning Chinese to attract the laborers. And on the night of April 13, 1918, when one of the camps came under German artillery fire, he recorded 10 deaths and more than 30 injuries. In fact, the threat of shelling had already prompted strikes and protests among Chinese laborers in late 1917. British military records provided another crucial detail: the 75th Company of the Chinese Labour Corps was stationed there from August 1917 to April 1918. Gu Xingqing, an interpreter for the Chinese laborers, also described the night of the bombardment in his memoirs.

Historical records also reveal differences in how the British and French treated Chinese laborers. Those recruited by the French worked alongside locals under relatively loose supervision, making the remains of their camps difficult to identify. By contrast, British-recruited laborers — organized into the Chinese Labour Corps — were subject to military-style discipline and housed in enclosed camps surrounded by barbed wire. The camps followed a military organizational structure. Initially, each battalion consisted of 1,031 men, with 10 to 12 sharing a tent. Each camp had just one iron gate, which was locked at night. To leave, the men had to obtain permission and travel in groups, and they were forbidden from venturing more than 3 miles away.

Documents even record how the laborers died and were commemorated. The leading causes of death were tuberculosis and the 1918 influenza pandemic, rather than artillery fire. However, the death tolls vary considerably: British records put the figure at around 2,000, French records at approximately 1,500, while Chinese figures suggest that at least 20,000 did not come back to China. Chinese laborers recruited by the British were buried in military cemeteries. Their headstones followed the same style as those of British soldiers, but bore inscriptions in both languages, including the laborers’ names and places of origin in Chinese, alongside English epitaphs such as “Though Dead, He Still Liveth” and “A Noble Duty Bravely Done.”

After the war, returning French and Belgian residents sometimes blamed the surviving Chinese laborers for social unrest. Yet the laborers were still bound by their contracts and remained to clear the battlefields. Some stayed in France to work in mines until 1929, while others married and settled there permanently.

In June 1921, the British military issued a total of 93,357 commemorative medals at its Chinese labor base in Shandong’s port city of Qingdao. Some were presented in person, while others were mailed to the laborers’ homes. Even today, these medals can occasionally be found in remote villages across Shandong and Hebei.

If historical records tell us so much, why was archaeological excavation necessary? Because documents can tell us where the camps were and what happened there, but they cannot fully reveal what the camps looked like. Their layouts were never systematically recorded, and the sites had long since been cleared and leveled after the war. This is where archaeology comes in.

The non-invasive geophysical surveys of the site we commenced in spring 2024 used high-resolution electromagnetic induction and magnetic survey techniques. The data revealed numerous anomalies at depths of 1 to 1.5 meters, including fragments of artillery shells of various calibers. This was consistent with local farmers’ accounts of still unearthing shrapnel when plowing their fields.

The two intersecting trenches excavated in February 2025 covered 512 square meters. We uncovered two ash pits with traces of burning at their bases, eight shell craters ranging from 1 to 5 meters in diameter, foundation stones from barracks, tent pole bases, and clusters of communication cables. For the first time, we were able to reconstruct the layout of a camp whose physical arrangement had never been documented, identifying its barracks, tent area, and main road.

We also unearthed more than 520 artifacts that offered glimpses of everyday life: belt buckles, Royal Engineers and Royal Artillery cap badges, surgical forceps from a field hospital, piles of bullet and shell casings, and nearly intact British army-issued rum jars and lemonade bottles. If historical documents help us understand the Chinese labor camps, archaeology brings us closer to the people who lived in them.

The significance of the project extends beyond the discoveries themselves. For a long time, World War I archaeology was mainly the preserve of metal detectorists, while professional archaeologists generally avoided the subject. This began to change with archaeological investigations conducted ahead of construction of Belgium’s A19 highway in 2002, which helped establish the field as a serious area of academic research.

Our excavation of the Chinese labor camp was the first of its kind to be led by a Chinese academic institution.

The project also opened up new avenues for Chinese archaeological research in two fields. The first is conflict archaeology, which looks beyond weapons and battlefields to examine entire societies caught up in war. The second is industrial archaeology, which can shift attention away from industrial achievements alone and toward the people and human efforts behind them. At its heart, this approach is about focusing on people rather than objects.

The Chinese laborers were not merely supporting characters in World War I. They found themselves caught up in a conflict involving Eastern and Western societies, working and dying amid misunderstanding and hostility. Yet even in the face of constant danger, they found ways to express themselves, creating trench art engraved with dragon motifs and landscape scenes.

Even the idyllic scenery of Flanders today was partly shaped by Chinese laborers, who filled in many of the trenches and craters left by the war. The experiences of these 140,000 ordinary Chinese men lie at the intersection of 20th-century Chinese and world history, reflecting the interactions and tensions between different societies.

“In Flanders fields the poppies blow / Between the crosses, row on row,” wrote John McCrae in his poem “In Flanders Fields.” Today, the poppies still bloom every year. But among those fields and crosses, Chinese laborers once lived and worked. Archaeology cannot bring them back to life, but it can give the soil a voice and remind the world that they were here.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A British soldier and a Chinese laborer examine written identification ribbons during a roll call at a Chinese Labour Corps camp in Samer, France, May 26, 1918. From the collection of the Imperial War Museums)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.title: China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.content:
China’s popular chili sauce brand Lao Gan Ma has drawn public scrutiny for adopting AI-driven production, allegedly at the expense of hundreds of jobs.

The controversy began after multiple domestic media outlets reported that Li Xin, Lao Gan Ma’s executive vice general manager and chief quality officer, touted the company’s use of AI at a provincial business conference last month in China’s southwestern Guizhou province, where the sauce originates.

Li reportedly said the number of workers on one production line fell from over 600 to just 48 after the company introduced an AI-powered pepper inspection system last year. He added that the company’s 2025 revenue reached a record 5.4 billion yuan ($810 million), crediting AI with reducing production errors to almost 0%. Li’s full remarks are not publicly available online.

The company’s history of touting its dedication to working people has drawn particular criticism over the potential layoffs, according to a commentary by Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper. Lao Gan Ma’s founder, Tao Huabi, whose portrait adorns the brand’s jars and is known across China, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before founding the brand in 1997.

As of Wednesday, a hashtag related to the scandal has garnered more than 120 million views on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users said automation is a standard part of industrial upgrading that can help improve efficiency and ensure consistent product quality. Others argued that the company should consider its responsibilities to workers.

“If everything is done by AI and robots, and people have no jobs or income, they won’t be able to afford to consume. What’s the point of producing so much, then?” one highly upvoted Weibo comment read.

Many also called for a boycott of the brand, reposting one user’s comment: “If you lay off workers, we’ll get your products pulled from the shelves.”

Responding to the controversy, Lao Gan Ma human resources representatives stated in an interview with domestic media on Oct. 26 that Li had not referenced staffing figures in his remarks.

In response to the company’s denial, users scrutinized its social insurance enrollment figures, which often reflect a company’s workforce size. Corporate filings disclosed by business data platforms Tianyancha and Qichacha show that the number of employees insured by the company fell from nearly 3,000 in 2022 to 740 in 2025 — a roughly 75% decline.

However, changes in social insurance enrollment do not prove AI use drove the layoffs, as other factors such as retirement and employee turnover also affect employment figures.

The debate comes as China seeks to expand AI adoption while curbing its potential negative impacts on employment. On Oct. 23, the State Council issued guidelines calling for “maximizing AI’s potential to create jobs, empower workers in traditional occupations, improve job quality, and stimulate innovation” while “slowing down the impact of AI-related job replacement.”

The guidelines also urge companies to deploy AI with caution in labor-intensive industries. They encourage employers to provide transition periods for displaced workers, give advance notice before large-scale AI rollouts, and offer retraining and support for locating new jobs.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019174/Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.title: Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019174/Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.content:
When glimpsing the Terracotta Army for the first time, almost everyone is awestruck by its sheer scale: thousands of armored clay figures standing in perfect formation, their gray earthen bodies stretching rank upon rank. At first glance, the ghostly 2,000-year-old soldiers look as if they were cast from a single mold.

But look closer, and the impression of uniformity begins to dissolve. No two faces are exactly alike: brows thick or faint, eyes wide open or slightly narrowed, cheekbones high or low, jawlines rounded or square. When viewed individually, each warrior is far more than a figure: it is a work of art as intricate as many Renaissance statues.

Zhao Hui (Steve Zhao) has spent much of the past 25 years trying to capture this hidden artistry. A veteran photographer who trained under cinematographer Peter Levy in the 1980s, Zhao became well known for his portraiture. His 1996 project “China Story” has toured more than 30 countries.

Since 2001, he has applied his talent for portrait photography to the Terracotta Army, amassing images of more than 2,000 figures. The works offer a striking new perspective on the warriors, often zooming in close enough to highlight the carved stroke of an eyebrow, the turn of a cheekbone, or even faint fingerprints left in the clay by a Qin dynasty artisan.

For Zhao, the project is also about more than changing perceptions of the Terracotta Army; it’s part of a wider effort to document, classify, and analyze it. The vast photo archive helps researchers understand the production processes, craftsmanship, and organization behind the relics — and, most importantly for Zhao, the anonymous master sculptors who carved them.

In this interview, Sixth Tone sat down with Zhao to discuss how his project began and how it has shaped our understanding of the Terracotta Warriors. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: The Terracotta Army has long been a research focus for archaeologists and historians, but what led you to study them through high-definition photography?

Zhao: At first, it was just a routine assignment. In 2001, the China National Tourism Administration approached me to photograph the Terracotta Warriors. It was a rare opportunity, of course.

My task was to capture the warriors in the finest possible detail. That is far harder than most people imagine: heritage photography is not simply pointing a lens at an object. Every click of the shutter is a repeated negotiation with light, angle, material, and patience. The warriors are massive and their preservation conditions special, so every shoot requires meticulous preparation and on-site coordination.

After taking enough high-definition images, I began to notice striking details — the rise and fall of a brow ridge, the hooked line at the corner of an eye, the marks left by the sculptors’ hands. Perhaps it’s because I’m a portrait photographer, trained to observe people.

Looking at all those warrior faces, I noticed not only the differences between them but couldn’t stop wondering how those differences came about. Behind them lie the techniques and aesthetics of their makers. That is how I began studying the craftsmanship of the Terracotta Warriors — 25 years ago now.

Sixth Tone: You have said the creation of the Terracotta Army was not just a feat of manufacturing, but an artistic process. Why do you believe that?

Zhao: You have to distinguish between three separate steps in the production process. First, the rough cores of the heads, hands, and torsos were made separately; then a layer of fine clay was applied over the cores, and the details refined; finally, the parts were assembled and joined, air-dried, fired in kilns, and painted.

The key point is that the heads and torsos were made separately and joined only at the end. The torsos were mainly the work of craftsmen. They coiled strips of clay round and round to build up the body, tapering gradually from the legs to the waist, then carved the robes, armor, armor studs, and knotted cords. I’ve taken close-ups of torsos; magnified, you can see the traces of clay coils stacking and tightening upward.

As for the heads: a rough core was made first, then ears, topknots, braids, and caps or headcloths attached, followed by the fine carving of the facial features. This was the heart of the entire production — and the people responsible were probably not ordinary craftsmen, but a group of highly skilled sculptors and their assistants.

Sixth Tone: What evidence led you to that conclusion?

Zhao: Look carefully at the faces, and you’d reach the same conclusion. Those vivid, highly individualized faces are works of art: brows range from thick to sword-shaped; eyes are wide open, slightly narrowed, or upturned; the fullness of the cheeks, the height of the cheekbones, the roundness or squareness of the chins — all of them are different. These details embody each figure’s appearance, character, and psychology.

By carefully comparing different images, I can even recognize the signature techniques and styles of individual sculptors. Now, whenever I see a certain technique, I feel I’ve run into an old friend, and I want to say to that nameless sculptor: “Hi, it’s you again.”

In my view, these face-makers who left no names behind can rightly be called China’s Michelangelos.

Sixth Tone: But there’s a problem here. Even a sculptor as industrious as Michelangelo only produced a few dozen sculptures in his lifetime, while the Terracotta Army contains an estimated 8,000 figures. It’s hard to imagine so many high-level sculptors were available at that time.

Zhao: Good point. These sculptors made only faces — far less work than carving an entire figure — but 8,000 is still a staggering number. So I expect there was a “master-and-apprentice” model being used during production.

I’ve found some supporting clues: comparing groups of figures similar in style and technique, I often find that within a group there is one figure of finer modeling and more accurate proportions, while the others are relatively rough and unpolished. The former likely came from a master’s hand, the latter from apprentices.

Even so, the scale of the project still astounds me. In just over three years, they produced some 8,000 life-size figures with varied faces — a feat that pushed the limits of stamina and craft, and a testament to the Qin Empire’s extraordinary organizational capacity.

Sixth Tone: Back to your methodology. Your findings are largely based on observing the warriors up close through high-definition photographs. Now that 3D digitization technology is maturing, do you think it could provide further research breakthroughs?

Zhao: Digitization shouldn’t be oversimplified. If you can’t even take a good flat photograph, then creating a 3D model will be even harder. The workload and cost of 3D data acquisition are far higher than in 2D, and the processing difficulty grows exponentially.

Of course, photographing the warriors does “distort.” Turning three dimensions into two — how could it not? A single photograph is never a complete replica of “reality”; it is constrained by angle, lighting, and timing, and it carries the photographer’s choices and judgments. It is essentially a limited rendering of the objective world under specific conditions.

But don’t forget: my photography is a long process. When one photograph becomes 1,000, then 10,000; when images of different times, angles, and individuals converge into a system that can be cross-verified — photography becomes a cognitive tool for observing, comparing, and deducing. It prompts people to see cultural relics anew and provides material for further historical interpretation. That’s why I now call my work the “Visual Art of Archaeology.”

(Header image: Terracotta Warriors. Photo by Zhao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019171/Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.title: Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019171/Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.content:
A new study has found that women and adolescents, not only men, helped build China’s 2,000-year-old Terracotta Army.

The study used fingerprints found on a portion of the 8,000 statues of soldiers and horses in the tomb of China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, to assess their makers’ ages and sexes for the first time, domestic media reported this week. The research was conducted by the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum in Xi’an, capital of the northwestern Shaanxi province, and Shandong University’s School of Archaeology, in the eastern city of Jinan, and will be published in Volume 82 of the Journal of Cultural Heritage at the end of the year.

Past studies of labor forces during the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) relied primarily on legal texts and largely treated men as the default workers, with 15 reportedly the minimum age for service. Prior research has also neglected to examine the genders and ages of the workers behind the Terracotta Army.

Previous analysis of the identities behind ancient fingerprints has also failed to account for factors such as similarities in fingerprint size and ridge distribution between women and teenage boys, differences between ancient and modern fingerprint size, and clay shrinkage after firing, the researchers said.

In contrast, the new study used a Bayesian mixture model to account for these factors and estimate fingerprint-related parameters at both the individual and population levels through probabilities. The model assigned the fingerprints possible ages and sexes, analyzed their mean ridge breadth (MRB) or thickness, and compared these to growth curve-projected values.

The team analyzed 79 well-preserved fingerprints from 36 figures in Pit 1 of the Qinshihuang mausoleum. The results showed that 45% belonged to males, 32.7% to females, and 22.3% to juveniles under 15.

The research provided quantitative biological evidence challenging previous assumptions that large-scale craft production in the Qin dynasty relied only on adult male labor. It also offers a better understanding of the Qin dynasty’s labor systems and institutionalization of apprenticeships.

While textual records and artifact-based inscriptions had previously challenged the theory that the project relied exclusively on male labor, the team’s findings offer a new framework for quantitatively studying ancient craft production and the ages and sexes of the laborers involved.

“This biological evidence highly corroborates numerous historical records, vividly reconstructing the production scene in the Qin dynasty’s state-run workshops where men and women served together, and adult artisans worked alongside juveniles, who may have been helpers or apprentices,” the study’s authors wrote.

However, they also identified several limitations of the study. For one, the percentages attributed to adult and juvenile, and male and female fingerprints may not equal the percentages of actual workers with those traits, they said, as multiple fingerprints may have come from the same person.

They also wrote that more experienced workers may have left fewer fingerprints, which may have increased the proportion of juvenile prints, while the reference database was both based on modern Czech-Caucasian fingerprints, not East-Asian prints, and contained more female samples, potentially skewing the results.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Types of fingerprints on the terracotta figures. From Journal of Cultural Heritage and Xinhua)
