World.title: Reel to Real: The ‘Voy Boys’ and the Movie That Never Was
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019166/Reel to Real: The ‘Voy Boys’ and the Movie That Never Was
World.content:
It’s late 2024, and Bilali Yasen barrels toward goal, the football skipping at his feet as he narrowly passes his opposition. In the pitch darkness, he hears only the sound of his heartbeat and the faint calls of his teammates.

He shoots and hits the back of the net, capping a 5-1 rout.

Having lost their first four games at China’s 2024 National Blind Football Championship, the win marks a major milestone for the 16-year-old striker and the rest of the “Voy Boys,” a newly formed team of visually impaired players from China’s northwestern Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

Born with glaucoma and cataracts, Bilali had never expected to play football again after his sight began fading at age 7. But at the final whistle, he is brimming with confidence and even envisioning a call-up to the national squad.

China has had a national men’s blind football team since 2006, winning eight Asian titles as well as silver at the 2008 Beijing Paralympic Games.

Yet the sport remains largely unknown in the country. For this young Xinjiang team, the struggle to secure sufficient long-term funding, along with professional coaching and management, is just beginning.

Even more improbably, the Voy Boys wouldn’t exist if not for a movie that was never made.

Cameras, action!

Su Yiyan, a dancer turned movie producer in Beijing, had been toying with a story about blind football for a while before starting production in 2021. The idea centered on a disillusioned big-city football coach who takes over a small-town team of visually impaired children, with both sides finding healing in each other.

Initially, she planned to base the movie in the southwestern Yunnan province, which already had a relatively strong tradition in the sport, but was encouraged instead to head north by Shanghai’s Xinjiang aid office, part of a national paired-assistance program in which wealthier cities coordinate economic, educational, and infrastructure projects in underdeveloped areas.

In the spring of 2021, Su and her crew arrived in Xinjiang to find local boys who could appear in the movie. The only real criteria were that they needed to be visually impaired and in good physical condition.

After visiting schools in several towns and cities, they traveled to Shache County, on the southern rim of the Taklimakan Desert in Xinjiang’s Kashgar prefecture, where they invited 13 students aged 13 to 14 from its Special Education School to take part in a basic running test.

“I was stunned. Every one of them had the bravery to run,” recalled Su, highlighting the fact that it takes immense courage to do that when you can’t see clearly.

The following summer, two physical education teachers from Kashgar were drafted in to begin training the children in skills and tactics at the school.

Blind football uses a modified ball with bells inside, allowing players to locate it by sound, and is played on an enclosed 40-by-20-meter pitch. Each team fields four visually impaired outfield players, all in blackout eye masks, and one sighted or partially sighted goalkeeper. Teams can also use a sighted off-field guide to call and direct players toward the goal.

Much of the initial training focuses on building the players’ courage to run and prepare for the inevitable collisions.

Abudumijiti Memet, a 19-year-old defender with congenital cataracts, said he was frightened at first, and would always lean backward when moving at pace. “The coach told me that the more afraid you are, the more likely you are to get hurt when someone runs into you,” he said. “Players who keep moving forward are less likely to be injured.”

Zhang Jian, head coach for the Shanghai Blind Football Team, provided remote support in 2021 and briefly led on-site training in 2023. He was surprised by how quickly the team took shape and impressed by their boldness, coordination, stamina, and general enthusiasm. Zhang took special note of Bilali, whose performances were “beyond everyone’s expectations.”

“It’s rare for someone of his height to perform as well as he does,” he said, referring to Bilali, who stands at a relatively short 1.65 meters. “He wasn’t good at dribbling at first, and his coordination could be poor … but he was certainly the bravest and the most determined in matches.”

For Bilali, it was a joy to be playing the “beautiful game” again. “Once I started running, I felt I’d rediscovered a familiar feeling,” he said, explaining that football was his favorite pastime before his eyesight faded. “The wind was blowing past my ears — it made me happy. Only on the pitch can we run without fear.”

Missing the target

Although things looked good on the field, by 2022 the movie project was stalling. The pandemic had caused scheduling issues, and some promised production financing never materialized. The money the crew did have — mainly from Su’s friends and connections — was vanishing fast.

Attempts to drum up further investment had all failed.

“To film my original idea required tens of millions of yuan, but we had no backers,” said Su, explaining that she had initially hoped to cast a big-name actor in the coach role. “One director suggested I change the focus of the movie to the children, which would only cost about 5 million yuan ($740,000). But we still couldn’t raise the money.”

With the project still in its early stages, she decided to shut it down. That summer, she flew to Xinjiang to break the news to the cast and their coaches.

Without a movie, there was no one to organize coaching or matches. “We’d just discovered blind football, and with it found hope,” said Bilali. “We all feared that the opportunity would disappear and we’d feel lost again.”

After returning to Beijing, Su couldn’t stop thinking about the children. “You can’t give people something and then take it away, especially a group of visually impaired kids so eager to play football,” she recalled thinking.

A year later, Su quit her job and teamed up with filmmaker Li Zhiwei to continue the project as a documentary about Xinjiang’s first blind football team. They used their own money, a bank loan, and about 260,000 yuan borrowed from friends to rent recording equipment and buy supplies including balls, goals, eye masks, and pitchside barriers.

“To save money, we sometimes took three connecting flights in a single day, getting up at 3 a.m. to reach the airport and arriving in Shache at nearly 11 p.m.,” Su once told domestic media. “Our crew spent no more than 100 yuan a night on accommodation. When we ran out of money, we went back out to raise more funds.”

In the summer of 2023, Zhang invited four boys from the Xinjiang team, including Bilali, to his annual training camp at the Shanghai School for the Blind, where they could learn from veteran players.

In addition to football practice, the trip included visits to the Shanghai Zoo, Shanghai Tower, and a café staffed by visually impaired workers. For Bilali, it was a glimpse into another world.

His elder sister, Maierwanimu Yasen, said her brother was different upon his return. After losing his sight, he’d become withdrawn and less talkative, and physically weaker, “but now he told us much more. He’d realized that visually impaired people could do all kinds of things — not just massage, but run cafés and pursue other careers,” referring to the default vocation for blind people in China.

He also now felt that if the team trained hard enough, it could play in more major cities, taking on China’s 10 or so provincial teams.

Taking another shot

In October 2023, Su’s crew arranged an exhibition match between the Xinjiang youth squad and the Shanghai Blind Football Team. The game was played on the pitch at Shache’s special education school, with relatives and local officials watching on.

“That’s when I first saw them play,” said Maierwanimu. “I felt then that they could really do it. I realized this wasn’t just a game they were playing for fun.”

The Xinjiang team won 2-0.

Almost a year later, the Xinjiang Disabled Persons’ Federation announced the official establishment of the region’s first men’s blind football team, comprising 11 members, and the opening of a dedicated arena and training facility in Korla, almost 1,ooo kilometers by road from Shache.

The team — nicknamed the Voy Boys for the players’ shout of “voy” (Spanish for “I go”) to warn others they are moving — immediately began preparing for the 2024 National Blind Football Championship in Fuzhou, capital of the eastern Fujian province.

Bilali’s five-goal display in the team’s final match of the tournament provided the climax to Su’s documentary, “Voy Boys,” which went on limited release nationwide in July 2026. So far, it has grossed just over 340,000 yuan, far less than the 3 million yuan it cost to make.

Final whistle?

When the cameras stopped rolling in 2024, life carried on for the team.

Xinjiang finished in ninth place in Fuzhou. However, to encourage them and other newly formed squads to keep competing, all participating teams received automatic qualification for the combined National Games for Persons with Disabilities and the National Special Olympic Games, co-hosted in December 2025 by the southern Guangdong province along with the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions.

The team went on to finish seventh in that competition and then fourth at the 2026 national championship, held in Korla.

Luo Chengmian, a 28-year-old former blind football player from the eastern Zhejiang province, took over as head coach in 2024. He was assisted by Mahemuti Rozi, vice principal of the Shache’s special education school, who’d followed the team’s progress from the beginning.

“At first, I thought playing football was unnecessary, so I didn’t pay much attention,” said Mahemuti. “But in every match I saw how they gave everything they had. They fought with everything, always pushing to play out the entire match. It really moved me.”

However, the team has struggled to recruit for certain positions, including goalkeepers and off-field guides. Often, candidates are found just a day or two before a match and lack experience.

The players being separated by large distances is another challenge. Because the Shache school launched its high school program only in 2025, Bilali, Abudumijiti, and five other players had earlier transferred to a special education school in the Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, about 1,700 kilometers away, to continue their studies.

After Luo quit in late 2025 over disputes related to his salary and the players’ subsidies, it was up to Mahemuti to keep the team going. He juggled the job alongside his responsibilities overseeing the school’s logistics and cafeteria, and connected with coaches in Yunnan for remote guidance and training plans. This December, he aims to help the players in Changji arrange internships in Shache so they can restart training with the rest of the team.

Without a regular coach, those in Changji had to organize their own training sessions before morning reading and in the hour between classes and evening study.

“If we get the chance, we just want time to train, a better pitch, medicine, and a coach,” Abudumijiti said. “At least we chose this path ourselves. We want to keep walking it until we can’t go any farther.”

By contrast, Luo now coaches the Sichuan Blind Football Team’s women’s squad, based in Chengdu, capital of the southwestern Sichuan province, where players train six hours a day, receive daily allowances, and enjoy full medical insurance and access to traditional Chinese medicine massage services.

Su told Sixth Tone that the Xinjiang players receive a few hundred yuan a month in food subsidies, and hope for further support, including for medical supplies. The Xinjiang Disabled Persons’ Federation did not respond to Sixth Tone’s request for comment.

At least four of the Voy Boys are expected to graduate high school next June, creating a dilemma over what to do next.

For visually impaired people in China, massage therapy remains one of the most accessible careers. Bilali and Abudumijiti both chose massage courses after transferring to Changji, yet the school didn’t even have textbooks for visually impaired students. They had to take photographs of the materials with their phones and use text-to-speech apps to understand the content.

“And I feel this kind of work often means staying indoors. You can’t feel the sunshine,” Abudumijiti said. “That made me reluctant to pursue it, even though many people told me it was the most suitable profession for someone like me.”

Without that option, though, he’s unsure about the future. The son of a police officer and gas station worker, he’s now thinking about working with his older brother, who plans to open an auto repair shop.

“If we have to rely on our families’ money to continue training outside school, honestly, that’d be too much of a burden,” Abudumijiti added. “A dream is a dream, but we also need to plan. What happens when we get too old to play and haven’t earned enough money? We can’t live on dreams.”

Su, now 51, has quit show business and is paying off her debts working as a bungee fitness instructor in Beijing. She argued that, like anyone, disabled people need opportunities: “It’s us, as able-bodied people, who imagine that they can’t do this or that. We assume they don’t need to create social value, and that as long as they are safe, that’s enough. But they don’t want to live that way. They still want to find their own worth.”

After an accident during training earlier this year involving a Xinjiang player, Su proposed the China Blind Football Players’ Sports Injury Protection Fund, aiming to provide medical insurance coverage to registered players. The idea is still awaiting approval from authorities.

In March 2025, Bilali was selected for the national team’s reserve squad, based in Fuzhou. For the first time, he encountered professional gym equipment, a dedicated medical team, and an individualized training plan. “The intensity was high. I’d never experienced such demanding training in Xinjiang,” he said.

Later, he joined a national team training camp ahead of the recent 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, but wasn’t selected. China took gold on Oct. 23 after defeating the hosts 1-0 in the final.

“I’m looking forward to eventually going back to Xinjiang to see my family and teammates, but I’m also afraid that I won’t be able to train anymore,” he said. “I worry that my skills will fall behind.”

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A poster for “Voy Boys.” Courtesy of Su)

World.title: Rack and Ruin: How China’s Trillion-Yuan Womenswear Market Lost Its Color
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019172/Rack and Ruin: How China’s Trillion-Yuan Womenswear Market Lost Its Color
World.content:
Editor’s note: According to Syntu Data, e-commerce platforms made a combined 1.6 trillion yuan ($239 billion) in sales last year during “Double Eleven,” China’s annual online shopping event in November. Clothing accounted for 14%, driven largely by womenswear.

Zhou Keke used to get excited when she ordered clothes online. Not anymore. Now she returns about 70% of what she buys, either because of poor quality or because the dimensions don’t match what was listed.

Browsing the Chinese e-commerce platform Taobao recently, she stumbled across a store clearing out unsold stock from a decade ago. She says it was like stepping into another world. Compared with the “simple and vanilla” skirts, scarves, and tops on sale today, she found designs that were bold, irregular, thoughtful, even avant-garde and ingenious.

“So this is what fashion looked like when the economy was booming?” thought Zhou, who lives in China’s eastern Zhejiang province. She bought seven pieces for less than 1,000 yuan ($150) and posted a review on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, receiving nearly 10,000 likes and 1,000 comments.

The womenswear market in the Chinese mainland exceeded 1.23 trillion yuan in 2025, up from 619.7 billion yuan in 2011, according to iiMedia Research. Still, social media is today awash with complaints from female consumers over the blandness of modern clothing. As one netizen put it, “Beauty used to come in 100 forms; now even ugliness is mass-produced.”

However, industry insiders argue that this isn’t a one-sided problem but rather a feedback loop. They say that, as China’s economy slows, most online shoppers are tightening their belts and are less willing to spend on distinctive or niche designs, so brands have no option but to follow what’s selling.

Meanwhile, in the physical space, more consumers can only choose between fast-fashion outlets and luxury brands, as mid-range and boutique stores continue to disappear from malls nationwide.

How’s it looking?

Li Li, a 19-year-old university student from Qingdao, in the eastern Shandong province, recently found a matching top and miniskirt — vivid red with huge black embroidered flower buds — at a vintage clothes market.

“You could tell at a glance it was meant to stand out. A lot of womenswear now comes in muted Morandi colors, or other pale shades,” she says, adding that clothes in the 2000s were “much brighter.”

Li notes that when a piece sells well on Xiaohongshu and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, there’s immediately a rush of near-identical versions.

Zhou says clothes today feel cut-and-paste, with only the logos changing. “If everyone’s designing like that, honestly, what am I supposed to choose? All I can do is compare the price and the fabric. It’s so boring,” she adds.

Gu Hawen, a fashion designer at Unreal World, a clothing company based in the eastern Jiangsu province, recalls that when she entered the industry in 2019, designs in the domestic womenswear market were flourishing. She began noticing a slide in 2023.

“Whether you look at high-end luxury, affordable luxury, or ordinary brands, it’s the same story now,” she says. “Everything is more alike. Some clothing has been stripped back so far that there isn’t a single decorative detail.”

She explains that an unspoken chain of imitation runs through the Chinese womenswear industry: mass-market and fast-fashion brands follow designer and luxury brands in terms of color, silhouette, and other details, and online shops follow mass-market brands.

“The public is more receptive to designs from big-name brands. If companies want to sell, we have to keep up with international tastes and aesthetics,” says Gu, although she stresses that “we only take inspiration; we don’t copy outright. Online sellers copy brands wholesale. It’s a vicious cycle.”

Chen Chen launched her own online clothing brand this year, selling products that stick closely to the design concepts of major labels. The first item she listed, inspired by the British fashion house Vivienne Westwood, sold more than 100 pieces — no easy feat. Within six months, several items promoted on her page had become modest hits on Xiaohongshu, approaching 1,000 sales.

Chen feels modern Chinese consumers tend to follow the crowd, and tastes are becoming increasingly uniform as e-commerce platforms grow.

“Instead of discovering things for yourself, you end up in an algorithm bubble,” she says. “Maybe the first time you see an item of clothing, you don’t even like the style. But the platform keeps pushing it, and then it’s all you see. Eventually, everyone gets conditioned into the same very narrow idea of what looks good.”

She argues that not all consumers recognize or value original design. “You can be selling in exactly the same category, but someone else slaps ‘same style as Chanel’ on their listing and wipes the floor with you.”

In Chen’s view, online womenswear brands that invest in developing unique designs are being squeezed out. Spending six months refining a collection no longer works, as everyone is chasing the next viral hit, and keeping up is the only way to make money.

“Trends change way too fast now,” she adds. “A brand might plan its collection for months, but by the time it hits the rails, everything looks dated. Then a new bestseller suddenly appears, and they have no choice but to follow. … Copying a bestseller means lower costs, less risk, and higher profit margins.”

Imitation game

Zhou feels China’s womenswear market is not only becoming more conservative and homogeneous but also that brands are cutting corners on materials compared with a decade ago, creating a false economy. “Brands are becoming less responsible, so more shoppers are sending items back more often. But returns cost the sellers money. It’s a vicious cycle.”

Industry insiders argue the root of the issue lies in an underlying shift in consumer psychology, as younger consumers place greater emphasis on value for money.

“It’s become harder for people to earn money these past few years,” says Chen. “They’re expecting more from every penny.”

With consumers more price-sensitive, brands have grown cautious about what they charge, applying pressure further down the supply chain.

“Sewing workers are putting in more effort, but their pay hasn’t gone up, so the quality keeps getting worse,” Chen explains. “The pressure on workers at the bottom of the industry is intense. They have to get orders out by a fixed deadline. Companies keep squeezing them and demanding more pieces per day.”

Gu also sees the domestic market’s homogenization as a symptom of the broader economic chill. “Staying alive matters far more than being original,” she says. “After all, beyond the designer, there’s a sales team, logistics, and 50 or 60 other mouths to feed. No business owner is going to bankrupt themselves simply to underwrite a designer’s personal aesthetic.”

For clothing companies, a design’s main job is to keep the business alive, so giving the market what’s familiar is the safest survival strategy, Gu explains.

“Designers have the least say in whether a garment gets made,” with the final decision usually in the hands of marketing and store managers, she adds. This group’s preference is for more “universal garments” that match a wide range of body shapes and personal tastes. “Designed pieces are selective — they can depend on a person’s height, figure, looks, their whole bearing.”

Even when an inventive design survives internal vetting, an unusual cut or trim can increase the retail price, potentially sending consumers elsewhere. Gu recently incorporated neo-Chinese style elements including knot buttons, mandarin collars, and wide cuffs into her garments, but they sold poorly. The feedback was that shoppers deemed the items too expensive.

Copycats are also astonishingly fast. Gu says imitations of her designs have appeared for sale online within as little as 24 hours, at a fraction of the price. “It gets to the point where it feels original designs are a bit of a joke,” she says with a resigned sigh.

Market gap

According to the domestic retail industry tracker Linkshop, at least 40 well-known Chinese online womenswear stores announced they were closing or halting new product releases in 2024, while e-commerce news outlet Ebrun reports that more than a dozen more shuttered in the first half of this year.

Meanwhile, many mid-range sellers have withdrawn from city malls across China, widening the gap between high-end and cut-price clothing stores.

“Expensive clothes are just getting more expensive. In malls, items can cost 5,000 or 6,000 yuan, or even more than 10,000. At the other end, there are fast-fashion brands like Uniqlo and Zara,” says Chen. “Some of the really good mid-range brands, ones pricing items at 1,000 or 2,000 yuan, seem to have gone from the malls. Even where you find them, their designs and quality are far less appealing than they used to be.”

Like Zhou, many shoppers are now turning to secondhand and vintage clothing stores. Others are even learning to sew and making their own clothes, to ensure they get the design, fabric, and cut they want.

“I miss a time when imagination could go anywhere, when people dared to design and weren’t in such a hurry to see results,” laments Li.

Some designers have tried to resist uniformity, like Gu, who makes small adjustments while sticking to her company’s established style. Last year, she took one of its hit jackets and added seams at the collar or cuffs, and extra trim, to achieve something “slightly different.”

She hopes the market turmoil will ease within the next couple of years. “When people are doing a little better financially, and companies have some breathing room — when one bad season no longer means bankrupting the business — things should get much better.”

(For privacy reasons, Zhou Keke, Li Li, and Gu Hawen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Xiaotong.

A version of this article originally appeared in Oh Youth! (36Kr). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: 500px Essential/VCG)

World.title: House spends P100M a year on utilities. Why ask for P1B?
World.content:
CONGRESS. The House of Representatives building at the Batasang Pambansa Complex in Quezon City on September 17, 2025.

In 2025, the House secured a billion pesos for the chamber's water and electricity expenses, even though it historically spent only a small fraction of that amount annually. Where did the money go?

In the last five years, the House’s utility expenses averaged only P108 million per year, but the chamber keeps on requesting — and approving — an inflated budget, never mind if it has already reached a billion pesos.

The underspending is a total head-scratcher, especially because it becomes uncertain how the eventual savings are being utilized.

The House enjoys fiscal autonomy, which means that unlike other government agencies, it is not required to return unspent funds to the Bureau of Treasury.

In the absence of transparency, critics warn that the funds may be prone to abuse and corruption.

Electricity, power spending

Take a look at the 2025 budget of the House of Representatives, the latest of which has been subject to complete state auditing.

The General Appropriations Act — signed by the President after it was approved separately by the House and the Senate — gave the House a total of P1.35 billion for the chamber’s water and electricity expenses.

The Commission on Audit’s report, however, learned that the chamber spent only over one-tenth of its actual utility allocation.

Did the House anticipate a major spike in utility needs for 2025 that it needed a gargantuan budget for power and water? They didn’t say so, but trends show that the House has had a habit of securing an inflated utility budget, even though it only needs a small fraction of the funds.

Supplies, too

The underspending goes beyond utilities.

The House’s budget for supplies has also tremendously increased in recent years, from P327.98 million in 2021, to a whopping P1.34 billion in 2025.

That’s even though spending for supplies averaged only P83 million annually in that half-decade.

Graphics by David Castuciano/Rappler

Where did the savings go? Finding out was Congressman Toby Tiangco’s agenda when he interpellated the budget sponsor of the Commission on Audit (COA) during plenary debates in the House.

“COA’s job is to audit what was spent, what is being spent. COA doesn’t know where the savings went,” said COA budget sponsor in the House, Representative John Tracy Cagas.

For Tiangco, the practice of budget allocation does not make sense.

“Why is there high funding for supplies and utilities but are left unspent, and then the following year, you still increase the budget?” Tiangco told Rappler.

Extraordinary expenses

Tiangco’s suspicion is that savings from utilities and supplies are being realigned to extraordinary and miscellaneous expenses (EME).

EME cover unique demands not typically covered by standard budgets. The Department of Budget and Management says these refer to expenses incurred for meetings, seminars, public relations, and official entertainment, among other things. EME should not be used for salaries, wages, allowances, and confidential expenses.

Following those guidelines to the dot may be easier said than done. A 2011 concurrent resolution by Congress states that these funds — which fall under maintenance and other operating expenses (MOOE) — require liquidation only by way of certification.

In other words, no official receipts are needed to justify these expenses.

“Unused funds of the House don’t revert to the Treasury. However, the House Speaker can declare those unused funds as savings as provided under the Constitution and relevant General Provisions on use of savings in an annual GAAs,” budget expert Zyza Suzara told Rappler.

“These savings are typically used to provide hefty bonuses for congressional staff of the House of Representatives,” she added.

The disparity between the allocated extraordinary funds for the House and its actual expenditure is astonishing. In 2025, the overspending reached P3.74 billion. The question arises: where did the extra funds come from?

Budget transparency

Transparency on the MOOE allocated to every congressman has been among Tiangco’s recent crusades. COA, after all, has confirmed that the MOOE for districts are not the same.

Tiangco has been a thorn in the House majority during the budget process this year. He wrote to Speaker Bojie Dy in August, informing him of his decision to break ranks and become an independent, to allow him “greater latitude to raise questions…in the use of public funds.”

This is not the first time Tiangco parted ways with the majority. Close and longtime observers of the House budget process may not find it uncharacteristic of Tiangco to be a champion of budget accountability, but given his background — particularly his perceived kinship to his relative, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. — his vocal opposition to the budget proposal may come across as jarring.

Tiangco, alongside over a dozen lawmakers, voted against the 2027 spending bill approved by the House, citing the chamber’s supposed rejection of his proposed transparency reforms.

His demands are a tough ask anyway. For one, he wanted the budget of the House of Representatives to undergo actual scrutiny.

This meant a public committee hearing for the House’s 2027 appropriations, pegged at P17.6 billion. Tiangco later said the House revised the executive’s proposal and increased its own appropriations by P5 billion for the upcoming fiscal year.

The House in recent memory has not conducted committee deliberations on its own budget. The free pass is similar to what’s been given to the Office of the President, the Supreme Court, and the Office of the Vice President before Sara Duterte parted ways with the Marcos administration.

A proper committee hearing, or even plenary-level debates, could have provided clarity on various questions surrounding the House’s expenditures, including its underspent utilities and supplies funding.

Rappler has emailed Speaker Dy’s office for comment. We will update this story once we receive a reply.

Congressmen’s insertions

Since the House’s approval of the 2027 budget, the chamber has faced greater scrutiny after budget watchdogs crunched the numbers and found that the chamber included nearly P190 billion in public works funding despite the absence of published project attachments.

In simple words, the House appears to have modified the President’s budget proposal so much that it resulted in hundreds of millions to billions of pesos in insertions in congressmen’s respective districts.

Even Tiangco’s constituency isn’t spared. The tracker of People’s Budget Coalition and Better Gov says that P338 million in insertions were made to the district engineering office covering Malabon and Navotas, raising its total funding to P1.12 billion.

Tiangco has disclosed a P2.28-billion public works funding for Navotas, up from the P1.61 billion that he said was included in the executive’s original proposal. But Tiangco insists the increase is backed by project details, and is in line with what the Regional Development Council and civil society organizations originally approved for his city.

But the seeming top offender for the 2027 budget is no less than the President’s son himself, Majority Leader Sandro Marcos. The DPWH engineering office in the Ilocos Norte district he represents has been allocated P4.74 billion in public works projects, up from the P369 million that was originally proposed by the executive.

In short, the House has increased his district’s budget by P4.38 billion. The younger Marcos has not provided an explanation for the budget adjustment.

The staggering figures underscore the alarming need for transparency. The watchdogs based their analysis on figures from engineering offices, but they sometimes cover numerous constituencies.

This means that the exact allocation per congressional district, and the insertions made by party-list lawmakers, cannot be fully determined, unless the House opens up its books to the public.

But does the House really have the guts — or decency — to truly pierce its longstanding veil of secrecy? – Rappler.com

World.title: Philip Juico, former Philippine Sports Commission chair, dies
World.content:
Juico held various leadership positions in Philippine sports, notably heading the country’s sports program in the late ’90s

MANILA, Philippines – Former Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) chairman Philip Ella “Popoy” Juico died on Saturday, October 31, his family announced. He was 78.

“After courageously battling cancer since 2022, my Papa passed away peacefully in his sleep. While our hearts are filled with sadness, we find comfort in knowing that he is finally free from pain and suffering and is now resting in God’s loving embrace,” his son Joseph Juico, a councilor for the 1st District of Quezon City, said in a social media post on Sunday, November 1.

Vincent Juico also announced on Sunday his father’s passing, thanking the public for the “prayers and understanding.”

The elder Juico served as the country’s sports chief from 1996 to 1998 under Philippine president Fidel V. Ramos, who appointed the longtime public servant as the fourth PSC chair.

He held various leadership roles in local sports, including as president of the Philippine Athletics Track and Field Association (PATAFA) from 2015 to 2022.

Juico also became active in volleyball, helping form the Philippine Super Liga in 2013 and the Shakey’s Super League in 2022.

On the international front, Juico acted as vice president and chair of the School and Youth Commission of the Asian Athletics Association from 2015 to 2019.

But before his foray into sports, Juico served as secretary of the Department of Agrarian Reform from 1987 to 1989 under president Corazon Aquino.

In 1987, he was honored as one of the Ten Outstanding Young Men for government service. He was also recognized by his alma mater, De La Salle University, which inducted him into its Sports Hall of Fame in 2001 for his contributions to Philippine sports.

The wake and memorial services will be held from November 4 to 5 at the Santuario de San Antonio in Forbes Park, Makati City. Inurnment will follow on November 6.

Juico is survived by his wife, former Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office chair Margie Penson-Juico, and children Dinggay, Vincent, Joseph, and Mayen. – Rappler.com

World.title: Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win
World.content:
PLAN. US President Donald Trump speaks with the media as he arrives at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida, US, on October 31, 2026.

White House counsel Will Scharf and his team are looking at 'what [Donald] Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court,' an official says

WASHINGTON DC, USA – President Donald Trump‘s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.

Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at “what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court,” the White House official said.

The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday’s midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and constrain his spending priorities. But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call.

For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.

The White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.

“This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.

Federal agencies have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said.

Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said.

He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programs receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.

Trump has been briefed on the preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.

When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, “very comfortable.”

Governing without Congress

Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws.

A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.

“President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. “I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities.”

Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.

A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.

Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to block Trump’s judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme Court pick.

“I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president’s appointments,” said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.

Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he doesn’t like, and Democrats are unlikely to have enough votes in the House to override him.

Courts could block executive actions that exceed Trump’s legal authority. The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the people said.

Democratic investigations

One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations.

Reuters previously reported that senior House Democrats and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors.

Trump aides have been preparing for that prospect for months, all three people said.

White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency leaders on how to handle congressional inquiries, document requests and subpoenas, one person said. They have advised officials to be careful about what they put in writing.

They also sought a Justice Department opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, the person said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why ‘2 Valid IDs’ is on track to make PH film history
World.content:
The movie about the Philippines' broken health system and bureaucracy may become the country's top grossing indie social realist film

MANILA, Philippines – Independent movie 2 Valid IDs is on track to make Philippine film history, as it recorded P80 million at the box office, the film’s director, Ma-an L. Asuncion-Dagñalan, disclosed on Sunday, November 1.

The film grossed P80 million in its first 18 days after opening in cinemas nationwide on October 14. It is expected to cross the P100-million mark this week.

2 Valid IDs was the top-grossing film in the 22nd edition of Cinemalaya last August, and Marietta Subong, more popularly known as “Pokwang,” won the festival’s Best Actress along with Ruby Ruiz (for Status: Rejected). The film also got Cinemalaya’s Audience Choice Award (full-length film category).

Play Video

And since the movie will likely extend for another week considering the strong support from moviegoers, 2 Valid IDs’ success at the box office is likely to continue.

“Nadagdagan pa tayo ng mga sinehan! (We’ve got additional cinemas). We are on our third week strong and still showing in 100 cinemas nationwide! Maraming maraming salamat, mga ka-#2 ValidIDs!” film outfit Super Entertainment, which has been promoting the film, posted on Sunday.

Ticket prices for 2 Valid IDs are P200 for a student/teacher; P275 for regular patrons in Metro Manila; and P230 for regular patrons in the provinces. Seniors get a 20% discount. Assuming a ticket price of P250, P80 million at the box office means that roughly 320,000 people have seen the film.

What makes 2 Valid IDs success unique is that it’s a social drama; most commercially successful indie films are love stories. 2 Valid IDs tells the story of Sylvia and her ailing farmer-husband, Ramon (played by Joey Marquez), and how red tape, corruption, and a broken health system fails a poor family.

Most cinema patrons don’t spend their hard-earned money for social realism, as movie-going is generally a form of escape.

The indie movie that holds the record at the box office is the 2017 romantic comedy, Kita-Kita, starring Alessandra de Rossi and Empoy, the love story of two migrant workers in Japan.

Play Video

Kita-Kita started with a whimper at the box office, but ended with a bang as word of mouth about the movie spread. Kita-Kita earned a total of P320 million at the box office. Given a production cost of P10 million, the film gave a windfall to producers Piolo Pascual and Spring Films, and catapulted comedian Empoy’s acting career. Kita-Kita even got an Indonesian remake in 2017, Cinta Itu Buta (Love is Blind).

Unlike Kita-Kita, 2 Valid IDs is a drama that makes its viewers angry and frustrated over the Philippines’ broken hospital system and bureaucracy. The movie is more comparable to the second most successful indie film, Heneral Luna, than to Kita-Kita.

Starring John Arcilla and helmed by Jerrold Tarog, the 2015 surprise hit about the hot-tempered military general Antonio Luna during the Philippine-American war, is the country’s highest grossing historical indie film. It earned around P250 million, allowing it to break even given producer Artikulo Uno’s high budget of P240 million. The film resonated with lines that evoke patriotism, including,“Negosyo o kalayaan? Bayan o sarili? Pumili ka.” (Business or freedom? Country or self-interest? You choose.)

Play Video

Most indie films don’t last a week in theaters, especially now with streaming platforms becoming the preferred platform for watching films and other entertainment content.

Critics and analysts have lauded the film for portraying an issue that resonates among Filipinos: the difficulties often encountered when they deal with most front-line government agencies.

“The film is a searing ethnography of cascading exclusion. Each door that closes on Sylvia also closes the next. Without an ID, she cannot claim money that is already hers. Without the money, her husband cannot be moved up for surgery,” said UP professor emeritus and political analyst Randy David in a recent column.

Edielyn Mangol, writing for People, Places, Plates, said: “Films tackling poverty, bureaucracy and access to public services can sometimes be perceived as difficult or niche compared with mainstream commercial releases. 2 Valid IDs is showing that a story rooted in an everyday Filipino problem can still attract paying audiences when it is told in a way that feels personal and relatable.”

Asuncion-Dagñalan, in a film director’s statement on Cinemalaya: “It’s only in the Philippines that we are asked to show 2 valid IDs to get another ID. What happens to those who don’t have any? What happens to the people trapped in a chaotic and inhumane system?

“2 Valid IDs is more than a story of bureaucracy, it is a reflection of the truth where access to basic needs is hindered by poverty, excessive red tape, rigid rules, and a system that demands documentation rather than urgency and compassion. Hence, many Filipinos are pushed into a world of ‘fixers’, forged identities, and moral compromise. They are doing this not because of selfishness, but out of necessity and love….

“Ultimately, the film 2 Valid IDs is a cry for empathy, reform, and a more humane way of treating the most vulnerable. It’s a film that calls us to look at our institutions and ourselves with a greater kindness, some added sensitivity, and more humane concern.”

The movie’s popularity prompted Akbayan Representative Chel Diokno to remind the public that only the National ID is needed for transactions with the government and private companies under Philippine laws, and requiring other IDs can penalized by up to P500,000.

“Sa ilalim ng PhilSys Act (RA 11055) at Executive Order No. 162, opisyal at sapat na patunay ang National ID sa anumang transaksyon sa gobyerno man o sa bangko at pribadong kompanya. Ang sinumang tumanggi rito nang walang valid na dahilan ay pwedeng magmulta ng hanggang P500,000,” he said in a social media post following the film’s surprise at the box office.

After the film crossed P50 million in ticket sales last week, its producer reminded the public to vote wisely in the elections: “P.S. Sana ay pagdating ng botohan ay makapag-desisyon tayo para mabago ang sistemang nagpapahirap sa mga Pilipino.”

(Hopefully, when we vote, we are able to decide to change the system that impoverishes the Filipino.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Lawmakers say US briefing showed Russia targeting Democrats with misinformation
World.content:
ELECTIONS. File photo shows Bartow County Elections Supervisor Joseph Kirk demonstrates a voting machine as new strategies are being adopted to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyberattacks, and physical threats ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Top Democratic lawmakers says Russia was waging the same kind of online misinformation campaign that the intelligence community had tracked in US elections in 2016, 2020, and 2024

WASHINGTON DC, USA – The top Democratic lawmakers on the congressional intelligence committees on Wednesday, October 21, said they received an intelligence briefing that Russia has been waging a misinformation campaign against Democrats running in next month’s midterm elections.

The comments by Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes come as Republican President Donald Trump has in recent weeks eased economic sanctions on Russia and increased pressure on Ukraine to end its fight against Russian forces.

Warner and Himes told reporters they were limited in revealing what they had learned in an election security briefing that they had requested from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton because it was classified.

But, they said, Russia was waging the same kind of online misinformation campaign that the US intelligence community had tracked in US elections in 2016, 2020, and 2024.

“And the state of play, I would argue, is that, you know, Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats,” Warner said.

He noted news reports that Democrat James Talarico, who is running for the US Senate in Texas, and Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election in Georgia, “in particular are being dinged” by fake s created with AI.

The White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Moscow in the past has denied meddling in US elections.

Himes said the pair could not provide details of the misinformation spread by Russia because the material was classified. But he added that Moscow’s conduct has been “the same old, same old.”

“The Russians are kind of throwing everything out there,” said Himes. “Chaos, you know, don’t trust your voting machines.”

He added there was “no reason to believe” that China has not been conducting “extremely targeted” efforts as it has done in the past to influence voters.

Beijing has previously denied interfering in US elections and the Chinese Embassy in Washington on Wednesday described Himes’ comment as “a false allegation and serious smear that has long been proved to be unfounded.”

Recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has shown Democrats leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by high single digits to low double digits nationally, bolstering Democratic hopes of regaining control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate.

The lawmakers said they were concerned that Trump could pursue efforts to contest election results, including by claiming foreign hacking of voting infrastructure.

Himes emphasized that there was no evidence that any country could penetrate US election systems and change results.

“Nothing out there suggests that there is even the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment,” said Himes. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] The DICT circus, Almirol’s suspension, and our tech coverage refocus
World.content:
We are living in a world where technology is no longer optional. It has invaded our homes and each of our personal spaces.

On October 21, the Office of the Ombudsman ordered a six-month preventive suspension without pay against Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Undersecretary David Almirol Jr.

It cited findings of conflict of interest: the eGov project, which Almirol led, awarded contracts worth P1.55 billion to a company that eventually subcontracted work to Multisys Technologies Corporation, a company he founded.

The suspension order came almost a year after Rappler exposed the issue in an investigative report published in December 2025.

The report was triggered by a DICT internal audit report that Rappler got hold of. To get to the bottom of the issue, we spent months scouring through corporate information and financial disclosures submitted by Multisys to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as well as DICT procurement records. We interviewed numerous sources, including Almirol himself.

Hello! I am Gemma Mendoza, head for strategic programs and one of the geeks minding our technology coverage here at Rappler.

Apart from this story, we have also been closely monitoring the circus at the DICT, including:

This is part of an effort in Rappler to cover technology and platforms from the perspective of public welfare, rights, safety, and accountability.

To maximize our energies, we do less reviews of the latest gadgets and gizmos and do more stories that help the public understand how innovations and developments in technology — and how the policies and actions of governments, including our own government, in relation to this sector — could affect their lives.

For instance, an investigative report we recently published uncovered how a sprawling online community of 430,000 members abuses women by gamifying the non-consensual disclosure of their intimate moments. The report also exposed gaps in laws that allow such platforms to flourish.

We will continue scrutinizing developments in Silicon Valley and the giant companies behind these technologies. But we will be looking at these from the perspective of citizens from the global majority whose voices and perspectives are often taken as an afterthought in a world dominated by the tech titans.

We feel this is critical because digital technologies have become so pervasive that it is virtually impossible for the ordinary individual to evade them. From the moment we wake up in the morning to when we go to sleep — and even as we sleep — we take these technologies with us.

In workshops we conduct across the country, I often joke that our phones and the digital platforms we use know more about us than the people closest to us.

This is the reason our newsroom’s technology and platforms cluster decided to revive our #EverydayTech chat room in the Muni tab of Rappler’s app.

We realized that while technologies and platforms are so much a part of our lives, very few people really understand how they work.

For instance, Digital 2027, the latest report by creative marketing agency We Are Social, shows that 3.24 billion individuals or nearly 40% of the global population already use generative AI tools each month.

However, few people realize that, beyond the seeming magic, generative AI is basically a tool that processes huge amounts of data scraped — often without permission — from various websites all over the internet.

Few also realize that when they talk to that friendly chatbot, they are in fact potentially giving away precious sensitive personal information which could be abused and used against them.

These are among the things we discuss daily, at 10 am and 4 pm in the #EverydayTech chat room.

You might ask, what does this have to do with the story on Almirol and the DICT?

Simple: the DICT is primarily responsible for promoting the Philippine government’s national information and communications technology (ICT) development agenda. It is supposed to ensure that Filipinos benefit from emerging technologies while also ensuring that our people are not being harmed by such technologies.

Our coverage intends to not just scrutinize how the technology platforms are behaving and operating, but also how various responsible agencies of government tasked to protect our interests are responding to such developments.

We invite you to collaborate with us in this journey.

Jump in whenever you can and join the conversation in the #EverydayTech channel. Do invite others to join as well.

And if you have leads on stories involving platforms and government agencies that are supposed to be regulating them, send us tips through investigative@rappler.com.

If you have the wherewithal, do support our investigations by joining Rappler+ or by giving whatever you can to our crowdfunding effort.

We are living in a world where technology is no longer optional. It has invaded our homes and each of our personal spaces. Let us explore, understand, and investigate how it affects us together. – Rappler.com

World.title: Explainer: How could Israel break the election deadlock?
World.content:
A woman passes by a banner depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump day after the country held a national election, in Jerusalem, on October 28 , 2026.

Israel's election leaves no clear path to forming a government, with Benjamin Netanyahu facing an opposition majority. Here are four possible scenarios that could determine the country's political future.

JERUSALEM – Israel’s election this week was indecisive and there is no clear winner poised to form a government. Benjamin Netanyahu remains in office as caretaker prime minister, but faces a parliament stacked with an opposition majority vying to oust him.

Here are some scenarios that could follow:

Another election

After the formal final election results are published next week, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party representatives and then taps the candidate whom he deems to have the best chance to form a government.

If the candidate fails, another can try and if that candidate fails, the Knesset can nominate another. There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is held.

Herzog said on Wednesday that everything must be done to avoid another election and urged the parties to come with an open mind to the consultations with him.

Unity government

Netanyahu’s Likud party, emerging as the largest in the Knesset, forms a coalition that would likely include centrist and right-wing opposition parties such as Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, the second-largest party, Avigdor Lieberman’s Israel Our Home and Naftali Bennett’s Together faction.

That grouping would secure 66 seats, a majority in the 120-seat parliament.

However, this option appears remote at this point because it would mean Netanyahu would likely have to abandon his natural political allies, the far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Further, the opposition parties would have to break their main election pledge to their voters: unseating Netanyahu.

Still, if neither camp is able to form a government at the end of weeks of protracted negotiations, a unity government may emerge as a last option.

Renewed fighting with Iran, or other players, could also push the sides together.

Eisenkot minority government

If Herzog taps Eisenkot first, he could try to form a government with Yashar’s natural allies — Together, The Democrats and Israel Our Home — propped up by Israel’s two Arab parties, even if they are not members of this government: Ra’am and the Joint List.

Eisenkot’s camp would number 48 seats, according to the latest vote tally, with the Arab parties numbering 19 seats that together reach a 67-seat majority.

But even if Eisenkot reverses his campaign pledge not to have Arab parties in government and accepts their support, it would be a hard sell to many Israelis whose attitudes toward Israel’s Arab minority have hardened further since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack.

Netanyahu has focused his campaign on delegitimizing support from Arab parties, who surged to record heights in Tuesday’s election, and for now, only The Democrats, a centre-left party, has come out publicly calling for their inclusion.

Both Arab parties have signalled that they are prepared to cooperate with Eisenkot’s camp.

Ra’am joined Bennett’s government ​in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months.

Netanyahu finds a majority for a right-wing government

Netanyahu’s coalition has fallen from its original 64 seats to 53, according to the latest election results. But Israel’s longest-serving leader is viewed as one of its most skilled politicians and he could split the opposition by peeling away members of its parties and bringing them over to his side.

He has managed to do this before, including as opposition head in the run-up to the 2022 election, which he won. But the coalition he was battling at the time had a far narrower lead and he did not need too many defectors to destabilize his political rivals. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rakhine Civil Society Urges UN No-Fly Zone as Civilian Deaths Soar
World.content:
Rakhine civil society organizations have urged the United Nations and international actors to declare a no-fly zone over the western state as civilian deaths from regime airstrikes surge to unprecedented levels.

The regime has bombed dozens of civilian targets in the month since a Sept. 28 aerial attack on a busy market killed at least 50 people and drew widespread international condemnation.

The Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO), an umbrella group of 70 local and international Rakhine groups, is urgently calling on the UN Security Council (UNSC), the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), international governments, and global humanitarian organizations to back their statements with immediate action to prevent further loss of civilian life.

Along with a no-fly-zone, the ASCO is demanding international sanctions to cut off the supply of aviation fuel, weapons and other military equipment that sustain the regime’s aerial campaign.

The appeal follows an escalation in deadly strikes on civilian areas since the market massacre.

“Our local humanitarian workers were on hand to witness the slaughter of children and pregnant women in the Kyauktaw bombing,” an ACSO official told the Irrawaddy, explaining the urgency behind the appeal.

Requesting anonymity for safety reasons, he stated the regime had conducted over 600 airstrikes across Rakhine over the past six months, targeting markets, displacement camps, and monasteries in Thandwe, Ponnagyun, Mrauk-U and Sittwe, and in neighboring Chin State’s Paletwa Township.

Data from the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute, a research body founded by military defectors, shows the regime launched 136 aerial attacks across Rakhine in September alone, leaving 144 civilian casualties — 62 dead and 82 injured. Rakhine logged the highest civilian casualty count in the country, followed by Sagaing with 101 and Magwe (61).

Additionally, the ACSO urged the international community to establish cross-border channels to deliver food, medicine, and basic necessities directly to displaced populations facing severe hardship in war-torn Rakhine.

It also called on the UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar to document human rights violations and ensure that perpetrators are held accountable through national and international justice mechanisms.

The regime ramped up airstrikes in Rakhine after the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) seized 14 of its 17 townships along with Paletwa during its 2023-2024 offensive. Intense battles continue around the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone, as AA forces push to capture the regime’s last remaining Rakhine strongholds.

On Tuesday, the regime’s key allies — China, Russia, and Belarus — blocked international condemnation over its human rights record at the UN General Assembly.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic push for legitimacy since installing himself as president in April after a widely derided election, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, and India. Critics have condemned the diplomatic thaw as normalizing a regime that is deploying military force to subdue its own population.

“If the international community continues to turn a blind eye to the suffering public, we can only conclude that it lacks any empathy,” the ACSO official said.

World.title: Regime Threatens Migrant Workers in Thailand Over Document Boycott
World.content:
Myanmar regime Labor Minister Maung Myint on Thursday warned that migrant workers who boycott the Certificate of Identity (CI) process in Thailand would be banned from returning home if they failed to apply for the document.

With its CI-issuing centers in Thailand seeing very few applicants, the junta’s Labor Ministry has intensified its threats. Before the regime began enforcing remittance requirements as part of the CI application process, the facilities were regularly overcrowded with thousands of Myanmar migrants eagerly seeking the documents.

Migrants are boycotting the CI process as the cash-strapped junta attempts to wring more money out of them. Workers applying for the document must now prove that they remit at least 25 percent of their wages to Myanmar through official channels, as well as a 2 percent income tax payment. Official channels offer far less favorable exchange rates than unofficial channels.

Fearing their hard-earned wages will fund the regime’s military campaigns against civilians, workers have launched an online campaign demanding the Thai government grant legal stay and work permits without requiring a CI, which serves as an alternative document to the Myanmar passport.

The Thailand Migration Reform group urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the framework based on the Pink Card, an identity card issued by Thailand for undocumented foreigners residing in the country.

Maung Myint said the CI process was “a project implemented in cooperation with the Thai authorities,” adding that migrant workers without a CI or a passport and an Overseas Worker Identification Card (OWIC) “would be undocumented.” He added that they would not be allowed to travel back to Myanmar during their time off.

The regime started operating five CI centers across Thailand on October 14, but they have seen few applicants. Those who have attended have paid the extra cost for the application, while most are holding off to monitor the situation.

The boycott campaign has derailed Maung Myint’s goal of matching last year’s total of US$5.6 billion in remittance inflows in 2026. Thailand hosts Myanmar’s largest migrant population, estimated at approximately 4 million.

Since he was appointed labor minister earlier this month, Maung Myint has been pushing for enforcement of the remittance and tax rules in order to squeeze foreign currency from overseas workers, who have emerged as a major source of foreign currency for the regime amid shortages and international isolation.

On Tuesday, he said that by trying to cut off foreign currency inflows to the regime, the campaign was only “driving the people of Myanmar and migrant workers into ruin, instead of damaging the government.” He said the funds were to be used for fuel and gas imports, a claim he has often made.

He accused the campaign organizers of being “gaslighters,” claiming they themselves hold CIs or passports while urging workers not to apply for them.

“He is just acting like a psycho,” Khin Soe, a board member of the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT), which is organizing the campaign, told The Irrawaddy in response to the minister’s claim. “He may not even understand what he said. He just seems to follow orders from above.”

He added that there would be no reason to oppose the regime, or campaign against the CI process, if its policy benefited workers. “I don’t take [his accusation] seriously,” he said.

An ultranationalist with a military background, Maung Myint is known for spreading hate speech against the Muslim community and slandering the National League for Democracy.

During his election campaign in 2020, when he represented the Union Solidarity and Development Party, a lawsuit was filed against him over his use of an inflammatory song that urged voters to choose the party “to protect race and religion and to drive out a group that destroys the race.”

Winning seats in elections in 2010, 2015 and 2025-26, he has served as a minister and deputy minister in various ministries—including labor and foreign affairs—under successive regimes since 2004.

In his new role as labor minister, Maung Myint has become the face of the regime’s efforts to extract funds from Myanmar workers and their families amid the country’s political and economic crises.

World.title: Big Brother Defends Myanmar Regime at UN, Chinese Aid Shortfall, and More
World.content:
China defends Myanmar regime at UN

The UN General Assembly’s Third Committee devoted its 29th plenary session Tuesday to Myanmar’s human rights crisis, hearing reports from Special Envoy Julie Bishop, Independent Investigative Mechanism head Nicholas Koumjian, and Special Rapporteur Kelley Currie. All three highlighted the war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the military regime.

Of the 23 countries whose delegates spoke, only Belarus, Russia and China defended the regime. Finding nothing good to say about it either, Beijing instead urged the international community to say fewer bad things. “The international community should focus on helping bridge differences and resolving problems rather than intensifying tensions and aggravating turbulence,” China’s representative said.

Myanmar, after all, is “an important member of the ASEAN family and an equal member of the international community,” he added, voicing support for the regime’s pursuit of a development path “suited to its national conditions and supported by its people.”

Beijing bristled when Currie noted that during Min Aung Hlaing’s first 100 days after declaring himself president, he deployed new coercive surveillance technologies “gifted” by China and Russia to suppress dissent.

China’s representative rejected the allegation, calling it “false information,” and urged Currie to carry out her mandate “objectively and impartially” and avoid spreading “unverified” claims that could mislead the public.

Currie hit back directly: “Countries that are most loudly complaining about interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs are ones that are most actively interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs. Those that are talking most loudly about peace are the ones selling the weapons to Min Aung Hlaing that he uses against his own people.”

She challenged Beijing’s denial, saying she would welcome any evidence refuting that China was selling arms or providing political and economic support to the regime. Currie reminded delegates that under UN procedures, China, Russia and Belarus had been given five days to respond before her October report was published—and none of them had.

She cited the 2023 report “The Billion Dollar Death Trade” by her predecessor Tom Andrews as the proof of her claim. The report found Myanmar’s military imported over US$1 billion in arms and dual use goods since the 2021 coup, with China and Russia identified as top suppliers. Chinese state-linked firms provided raw materials and equipment for Myanmar’s ordnance factories including aircraft parts and explosives precursors used in attacks on civilians.

A milestone for China’s cross-Myanmar pipeline

The Myanmar–China crude oil pipeline has transported more than 100 million metric tons of crude oil since it began operations in 2017, PipeChina announced earlier this week. Stretching 771 km from embattled Kyaukphyu in Rakhine State through northern Shan State to Yunnan Province, the twin oil and gas pipelines are strategic lifelines that reduce Beijing’s dependence on the congested and vulnerable Malacca Strait.

One of China’s four major energy import corridors, the pipelines traverse 22 townships across Rakhine, Magwe, Mandalay and Shan, and today ethnic armed organizations such as the Arakan Army (AA), Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) control substantial sections there.

Myanmar is projected to receive around $1.5 billion annually from the pipelines, though the exact profit structure is unclear. It certainly receives a fixed, annual right-of-way payment of $13.81 million for both pipelines plus $1 per ton of crude transiting through the country—PipeChina reckons at an average rate of 35,000 tons a day, most of it disgorged at Kyaukphyu from the Middle East. PipeChina and CNPC own 51 percent, while state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE) holds 49 percent.

The gas pipeline, meanwhile, started operation in 2013 and carries output from the offshore Shwe fields, with a a design capacity of 12 billion cubic meters per year. China National Petroleum Corporation holds a controlling 50.9 percent stake and MOGE just 7.365 percent. Sales of natural gas from Shwe to China are estimated to generate around $1 billion annually.

To finance its stakes, MOGE borrowed around $1.5 billion from the China Development Bank at an interest rate of 4.5 percent, according to Sandhi Governance Institute. Nobody knows how much of that has been paid back or ever will be.

Chinese aid bottleneck throttles Myanmar regime’s budget

Myanmar’s military regime faced severe fiscal strain in the 2025–2026 fiscal year when China withheld approval for multiple projects under the Lancang–Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Special Fund. Naypyitaw’s budget deficit shot up amid overspending by ministries and loss‑making state enterprises.

Deputy Planning and Finance Minister Kyaw Htin admitted that the deficit was exacerbated by failure to secure expected grants, project approvals, and technical resources from Beijing. The Ministry of Cooperatives and Rural Development did submit proposals for LMC financing in 2025, but the response was deafening silence. Likewise, the Industry Ministry budgeted for computer hardware and technical equipment for Chinese experts who were to come to Myanmar for a technology transfer, but they never turned up and the equipment was not delivered.

The reasons are shrouded in mystery. In a recent article in regime newspapers, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia claimed China had backed 140 development projects in Myanmar through the LMC Special Fund. In March, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said the country benefited from 132—worth $38.6 million—since 2017.

Either way it would be the biggest handout to any Mekong country.

Some older Chinese projects are already falling to pieces. Kyaw Htin admitted that power transmission lines from two China‑backed hydropower plants—the 240 MW Dapein Hydropower Station in Bhamo, Kachin State and the 600 MW Shweli 1 Dam in Namhkam Township, northern Shan State—were damaged and could not be repaired due to “security conditions,” depriving the regime of projected electricity revenues.

Russian grant money that had been promised was also not forthcoming, Kyaw Htin said. The rest of the world has suspended official development aid since the 2021 coup.

More trouble in Shan over Kokang ‘Sinicization’

The past two weeks have seen growing tensions between Shan communities and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) that is consolidating its control in territories it has seized over the past three years.

The Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—comprising the armed Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the civilian Shan Nationalities League for Democracy, and other Shan opposition groups—issued a statement accusing the MNDAA of undermining ethnic rights, erasing Shan cultural heritage, and imposing Chinese language and governance systems there.

The MNDAA rejected the allegations as “baseless” and “politically motivated” and accused the SSJAC in turn of stirring the ethnic pot.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations also released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and stability on the Chinese border. And in April, Ta’ang civil society groups condemned the MNDAA after it seized Kutkai, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

Founded in 1989 from the remnants of the Communist Party of Burma, the MNDAA is rooted in Kokang, an enclave that is 90 percent ethnic Chinese. Once limited to Laukkai and Kongyan townships, the group has expanded its territory west of the Salween River since Operation 1027, and locals report a great deal of painting over of signboards and other attempts to suppress their languages and identities by their brash new masters.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Hosts Russian Mining Billionaire After Approving Gold Ventures
World.content:
Russian mining billionaire Vladislav Sviblov — head of Russia’s Areal Group — met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Wednesday to discuss cooperation in mineral exploration and mining between the two Western-sanctioned actors.

According to regime media, both sides spoke of “mutual trust and friendly relations” between Myanmar and Russia and discussed cooperation in education, science, and technology.

Formerly known as Highland Gold Mining Limited, Areal Group rebranded after expanding beyond precious metals into base, rare, and strategic minerals. Areal and its owner have been under U.S. and EU sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Similarly isolated by international sanctions after the 2021 coup, Min Aung Hlaing and his regime have been courting economic and diplomatic support from Russia.

On the day that Sviblov arrived in Naypyitaw, Myanmar’s Investment Commission approved 16 new investment proposals — including large‑scale gold mining ventures. The green lights came just weeks after Min Aung Hlaing invited investment in Myanmar’s mineral sector at the Russia–Myanmar Economic Forum in August, touting “value‑added mineral products” as a new export base.

Russia’s sanctions‑hit companies have leaned toward Asian markets since 2022, while Myanmar’s regime, starved of foreign currency, is eager to attract Russian capital.

Regime insiders suggest rare earths may have been on the agenda of Wednesday’s meeting, given the presence of natural resources minister Khin Maung Yi, while Sviblov himself spoke on on rare earths at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum in June.

Myanmar boasts rich deposits of the critical minerals, exporting roughly half of the world’s heavy rare earth elements over the border to China.

Meanwhile, the U.S.’s recent reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that a global scramble for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. Regime supporters now boast that the junta has a “rare earth card” to play, pointing to parallel interest from India.
