South American-focused developer Aguia Resources looks to have rounded the corner after its latest quarterly report showed customer receipts more than tripled to $639,000 as its twin gold and phosphate projects begin to deliver cash flow. The revenue surge from $200,000 in the previous quarter signals a significant operational turnaround, with the company’s high-grade Santa Barbara gold mine in Colombia hitting breakeven for the first time and early sales flowing from its massive phosphate stockpile in Brazil. Development work at Aguia Resources’ Santa Barbara mine in Colombia, which is now covering its own costs and helping drive a tripling of the company’s quarterly revenue. The Colombian operation has been the star performer, with record September production covering all local operating and corporate costs. The mine produced 36.75 ounces of gold from 105 dry tonnes of ore, generating gross revenue of $218,000 for the month. Notably, the ore processed in the quarter through a third-party plant owned by the Colombian Mint averaged a solid 10.88 grams per tonne (g/t) of gold. The most recent batch hit an even more impressive 12.75g/t. With the operation now standing on its own two feet, Aguia is looking to double monthly output from 100 tonnes to more than 200 tonnes in the coming months.



While the Colombian gold mine rings the till, the company is also advancing its flagship Três Estradas phosphate project in Brazil, where it has built a 30,000-tonne stockpile of ore - with an estimated value of $5,000,000 - ready for processing. A further 1600 tonnes of processed ore is also available for sale at its Cacapava plant, which operates under a separate licence to the mine. At the current production rate of 4000 tonnes per month, Aguia expects this inventory to support sales for the next six months. The company has already demonstrated a strong local appetite for its fertiliser product, locking in a whopping $2.3 million in sales for 11,000 tonnes within just six weeks of commissioning its plant. More recently, it landed payments for 825 tonnes of its Pampafos organic phosphate product at an average price of A$192 per tonne. The timing of the newly operational phosphate venture looks spot on, with Brazil’s government keen to bolster domestic fertiliser production to reduce its heavy reliance on imports. A federal $2.7 billion program known as “Profert” was recently approved to incentivise local producers, providing a powerful tailwind for projects such as Três Estradas. With the incumbent government returned to power in the recent election, that policy support looks set to continue. While Aguia continues to mine, process and sell phosphate under its existing operating licence, a legal challenge to its environmental licensing process remains unresolved. However, the company expects the Federal Regional Court to revisit the case within 30 to 60 days after a dissenting judge prioritised the matter for review, while the local municipality of Lavras do Sul has also sought to overturn the earlier ruling. The project has attracted significant political support, with more than 20 mayors, councillors and parliamentarians attending a recent public rally in Porto Alegre to back Três Estradas and the regional investment it promises.



The company is also shoring up its future ore supply, having kicked off an environmental assessment for its nearby Passo Feio tenement, which could provide a replacement feedstock for Três Estradas down the track. Aguia ended the quarter with $499,000 in cash after spending $1.2 million on exploration and $1 million on property, plant and equipment as it ramped up its projects. Management says it is currently in mature discussions for a $5 million financing package to bolster its balance sheet. After weathering some serious operational and legal headwinds, the company is now showing the market the power of its two-pronged South American strategy. Aguia’s Colombian gold project is no longer just a prospect; it’s a cash-generating engine providing the financial muscle to help navigate the legal process in Brazil. With its Brazilian phosphate project backed by favourable government policy and a massive stockpile ready to go, the sharp jump in quarterly revenue might just be the first chapter in a significant turnaround story. World.title: ‘Enough is enough’: Wanderers boss attacks NSW Police over heavy-handed fan treatment
World.content:
Dear Wanderers Members and Fans,

Over the opening weeks of this season, I have been immensely proud of the unwavering support shown by our Members, the Red and Black Bloc (RBB) and our wider fan base in challenging circumstances. You have continued to stand by the Wanderers, and I want to personally thank you for your support.

That loyalty deserves to be met with the same respect in return.

Since the beginning of the season, we have witnessed repeated issues surrounding the treatment of our supporters. The events of this weekend have brought those frustrations to a tipping point.

The treatment of our Members and fans has been totally unacceptable. Enough is enough.

The RBB are an integral part of our club which we are extremely proud of. That will never change, and we will continue to stand behind the positive contribution they make to the Wanderers and football in this country.

Our supporters should never be made to feel like second-class citizens simply because they choose to support a football club.

We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for equal treatment and common sense.

For too long, our supporters have faced excessive policing, policing that you as members and fans pay for. Recent examples of this include, hundreds of fans being withheld from entering the Sydney Derby for up to 30 minutes, the moving goalposts around concession items, and over the weekend, up to 20 Public Order and Riot Squad officers were positioned at times behind our supporter bays in Campbelltown.

This only adds to the feeling of intimidation experienced by the families that largely make up our supporter base.

This level of treatment is neither reasonable nor proportionate, and there is no justification for a Riot Squad presence at our football matches.

Let me be clear that we do not condone anti-social behaviour from any individual. Those who do the wrong thing must be held accountable. But the actions of individuals should never define an entire fan base. The overwhelming majority of our supporters are everyday people who simply want to enjoy football and passionately support their team. We will never allow anyone to take that away from them.

We recognise and respect the responsibility of NSW Police, stadium authorities and the A-Leagues to ensure everyone’s safety. But that responsibility must be exercised fairly, consistently and with respect for those attending our matches.

For over a decade, we have worked in good faith with the relevant authorities, investing significant time in constructive dialogue and building relationships to address longstanding challenges.

But our patience and willingness to work collaboratively should never be mistaken for acceptance. Our Members and fans have waited long enough, and deserve to be treated with common sense and the utmost respect.

Most recently, our active supporters chose silence to make their voices heard. For 20 minutes, the absence of their voices spoke volumes.

The drums, the banners, the singing, the colour and the passion are not inconveniences to be managed. They are the heartbeat of our club and part of what makes our game extraordinary.

As Chairman, I have a responsibility to protect the future of the Western Sydney Wanderers. That means standing up for the people who give this club life.

I will not accept our Members and fans being treated as though their passion makes them any less deserving of respect. Neither will this club.

We will continue to raise our concerns directly with NSW Police, the A-Leagues and relevant stakeholders, seek clear answers and push for fair, consistent and respectful treatment.

To every Member, active supporter and fan who proudly wears the Red and Black, thank you.

You have never stopped standing up for this club. And as your Chairman, I want you to know that we will never stop standing up for you.

Paul Lederer

Chairman

Western Sydney Wanderers FC

World.title: Airport rail study doctored to ‘bake-in’ Sunshine as preferred route, commission told
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Airport rail study doctored to ‘bake-in’ Sunshine as preferred route, commission told Chip Le Grand Updated November 2, 2026 — 1:50pm ,first published November 2, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. State Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has urged the Big Build royal commission to fully investigate allegations that former premier Jacinta Allan coerced public servants to back her government’s plans for the Melbourne Airport Rail Project. But Wilson said that if the Coalition government is elected, the project would continue as designed. Jacinta Allan, pictured next to Daniel Andrews, announces Sunshine as the preferred route for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link before the 2018 election. Paul Jeffers This masthead on Monday reported allegations before the royal commission that financial estimates were doctored, and a senior public servant was threatened with the sack to ensure the proposed MARL ran through Sunshine instead of a more direct route to the city. The allegations challenge the integrity of the business case for Premier Ben Carroll’s priority project, call into question a $12 billion joint funding commitment by the state and federal governments, and plunge the Big Build into fresh scandal a month before the state election.



Related Article Victorian election Wilson insists SRL position is ‘very clear’ despite days of confusion Wilson said the royal commission needed to examine the claims. “What we need to get to the bottom of is how, eight years ago, a minister – Jacinta Allan at the time – was intimidating, bullying and threatening public servants to get a political outcome,” she said on Monday. “That is what the royal commission needs to look into.” Pressed on whether a Coalition government would review the project in light of the allegations or consider an alternative route, Wilson said it would be built as planned. “The route is the route. The contracts have been signed, the project is underway and the Coalition is committed to delivering airport rail.”



Allan denies the allegations. She is expected to be called as a witness before the commission. A confidential submission to the royal commission by a planning expert who advised on the airport rail link reveals that a secret working group was established in late 2017 or early 2018 at the direction of then-public transport minister Allan to allegedly bake in the case for the Sunshine route. It says the small group, which included public servants within the Transport Department and outside consultants, was told to not discuss its work with any of their colleagues, including direct reports, or diarise their meetings. All instructions were given verbally. The group’s brief, according to the submission, was to study four shortlisted routes for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link (MARL) and build evidence supporting the state government’s politically favoured outcome – that the new train line, if ever built, would have to go through Sunshine.



“The task was to produce a document, or set of documents, prior to the 2018 election so that after that election there would be no further consideration of any alternative routes for the MARL other than through Sunshine,” the submission reads. Carroll did not address the allegations before the royal commission when questioned by this masthead. On Monday, he cancelled a pre-scheduled press conference. Premier Ben Carroll axed a pre-scheduled press conference on Monday. Louis Trerise “The premier’s first act was to establish the toughest royal commission into the construction industry to leave no stone unturned,” a spokesman said on Sunday. “The terms of reference are broad and expansive. Nothing is off limits. We won’t pre-empt its findings.” Opposition transport infrastructure spokesman Evan Mulholland said Victorians were owed a more substantial response. “Ben Carroll was sitting around the table as a deputy premier and as a senior minister in the government. He needs to explain what he knew and when he knew it.”



The submission from the planing expert is one of four to the royal commission raising concerns about the integrity of the current MARL project. All were provided to this masthead by their respective authors. The most serious allegation raised by the planning expert is that, to make an iron-clad case for Sunshine, the estimated cost of a more direct route through Maribyrnong was intentionally inflated by exaggerating the amount of tunnelling required. And the winner is – Sunshine. The state government announced its preferred route in 2018. Paul Jeffers The Maribyrnong route would have run beneath Highpoint shopping centre and opened up disused defence land for residential development. An earlier 2012 study, commissioned by the then Liberal state government, top-scored Maribyrnong, known at the time as the “direct tunnel” option, out of 22 possible routes, with Sunshine ranked a close second.



The allegation that costings were deliberately inflated to rule Maribyrnong out of contention is contained in a separate, contemporaneous file note made by a solicitor when the planning expert first sought legal advice about blowing the whistle. The note, dated August 23, 2018, and seen by The Age, reads: “Untenable. Serious matters ignored, not acted upon. “4 options – one particular route better but more expensive (doctored to make it unviable).” The solicitor who wrote the file note confirmed its authenticity. The planning expert, who spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, decided against making a disclosure to the Victorian Ombudsman or IBAC due to fears of personal and professional recriminations. They subsequently quit the department, leaving the information buried for eight years.



“This is fraud on a billion-dollar scale,” they said. The planning expert, working with trusted former colleagues experienced in rail engineering and major project costing, has calculated that an unnecessary 3.5 kilometres of tunnelling was included along the proposed Maribyrnong route to add between $3.8 billion and $4.6 billion to the estimated cost. A price tag of $20 billion to $25 billion for Maribyrnong – double the estimated $8 billion to $13 billion cost of the Sunshine route – was included in a strategic appraisal of the airport rail link published by Transport for Victoria in July 2018 and built into the 2021 business case for the project. A truer, average cost estimate of the Maribyrnong route, according to detailed calculations provided to this masthead by the group of experts, is $16.5 billion in 2018 dollars.



Maribyrnong was the federal government’s preferred route when then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull came to Melbourne in April 2018 to announce $5 billion in funding towards the project. Related Article Public service Thrown in a loop: How Daniel Andrews’ biggest project was cooked up behind closed doors Then-premier Daniel Andrews, who did not appear at the funding announcement alongside Turnbull, was blindsided by the move. At the time, he was more focused on his government’s plans to unveil the Suburban Rail Loop, a project being developed in secret, as a vote-grabbing election promise. The Victorian government formally endorsed the Sunshine route for the airport rail link in August 2018 and the federal government followed suit three months later. The comparative cost of the Maribyrnong route was a critical factor in tipping the scales towards Sunshine in the published assessment. According to the Transport for Victoria analysis, Maribyrnong was the top-scoring route for the benefits it would bring to travellers using the line, Victorian businesses and the economic development of Melbourne’s inner north-west. Due to its prohibitive cost, it was ranked last for deliverability.



When the planning expert saw the assessment, he challenged an executive working in the department. “I just said to him, “How could you produce documents like this, and think this is OK?” the planning expert told this masthead. “He said to me, ‘The minister said to me that either these documents say Sunshine or I’ll sack you. So they say Sunshine.’” Allan, who is retiring from politics after losing the Labor leadership to Carroll in July, was the minister for public transport and major projects at the time the assessment was done. “The allegations made are incorrect,” a spokesman for the former premier said. “Ms Allan will co-operate with the important work of the royal commission. She will answer whatever questions the royal commission has for her about these allegations, but it is not appropriate to pre-empt the royal commission’s work.”



Related Article Analysis

Big Build royal commission Royal commission hints at original sin of Big Build A colleague of Allan, who was unauthorised to publicly discuss the matter, said the former premier was furious at the suggestion she would coerce public servants to support a particular outcome. Allan made no secret during her time as a minister responsible for what became known as the Big Build that she wanted the MARL to run through Sunshine. The benefits of Sunshine, which Allan advocated within government and to her federal counterparts, was that it required no tunnelling, would accelerate Sunshine’s development as a second central business district, and would link the airport line with rail services to regional centres. A former cabinet colleague of Allan’s, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the former premier was insistent the airport rail line had to run through Sunshine so that people travelling to the airport by train from Ballarat or her home town of Bendigo only needed to change trains once.



In December 2018, when defending the government’s decision not to make public a preliminary business case for the project, Allan hinted at a Sunshine bias. “We’ve released previously ... the strategic assessment of the four alignments, which is really what the preliminary business case was about, looking at those four alignments and giving [state and federal] governments the confidence that Sunshine stacked up the best,” she said. Allan’s confidence in the strategic assessment was not shared by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office (VAGO). The Big Build royal commission led by Chris Kourakis will begin public hearings next week. Joe Armao A 2022 VAGO report into the quality of government business cases used to support major projects was highly critical of the way that route options for the MARL were assessed, describing the work done as “not sufficiently rigorous” and lacking in transparency. The auditor-general noted that the options assessments “significantly influenced” a state government decision to commit $5 billion to the project and were not “validated or revisited in any depth” before they were included in the published business case.



The airport rail allegations go to the heart of a question that commissioner Chris Kourakis has flagged will be central to his inquiry into the Big Build – whether the state government’s $100 billion infrastructure program was primarily designed to advance the public interest or Labor’s electoral prospects. In his opening address to the inquiry, Kourakis noted that “governments must select and design infrastructure projects around the socioeconomic needs of the Victorian public, and not party political interest”. William McDougall (pictured in 2019) worked on most of the major transport construction projects in Victoria since the late 1990s. Jason South The royal commission is scheduled to hold its first public hearings next week. William McDougall, an independent transport planner who has worked in Britain, the Middle East and on signature Big Build projects including the West Gate Tunnel, North East Link, Suburban Rail Loop and the MARL, has told the commission this is not his experience.



“Throughout my career, I have seen an accelerating shift away from integrated, evidence-based planning towards politically selected and prioritised projects,” he writes in a submission provided to this masthead. “The most egregious issue of all is that large projects are chosen for political reasons, announced and funded without the context of an integrated land use and transport plan.” Premier Ben Carroll, pictured with Anthony Albanese near Sunshine, has declared the MARL his “highest priority”. Jason South McDougall, who is aware of the allegations about the development of the MARL now before the royal commission, believes the project is a case study of where Victoria’s planning for and delivery of major transport projects has gone wrong. “A strategic assessment of options … was used to justify the Sunshine/Albion route, but it was a highly skewed assessment with direct, political interference aimed at ensuring that the Sunshine route was the best,” he writes in his submission. “Faster, shorter and cheaper routes were rejected.”



Two further submissions to the royal commission, both made confidentially by former public servants, question the planning process and decisions taken that resulted in Sunshine being chosen as the route for a new airport line. Carroll, since becoming Labor leader, has declared the airport rail link his “highest priority” major project. The government has selected a preferred bidder to redevelop Sunshine station, and Carroll last month was alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to announce forward plans to lay down airport rail tracks to a proposed new station in Keilor East, in the middle of his electorate of Niddrie. The Victorian Coalition has also backed the MARL. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promised to deliver the project, including a new station at Keilor East, if she becomes Victoria’s next premier. Both the Maribyrnong and Sunshine routes run through Keilor East. Wilson has promised to expand the royal commission’s terms of reference so that it examines whether “any project was conceived, selected, prioritised, expanded, re-scoped, funded or continued, wholly or partly, to confer an industrial, financial, organisational or political benefit” to a trade union or political party.

World.title: One Nation vows spending transparency but refuses to release policy costings
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election One Nation vows spending transparency but refuses to release policy costings Angus Delaney November 2, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One Nation has vowed to create an online, real-time expenditure tracker as a way of revolutionising “the way that that budgets are done in this state” if elected, while refusing to release costings for its policy proposals before Victorian voters head to the polls. Speaking on Monday, the party’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, criticised the financial records of the major parties and questioned the accuracy of the Parliamentary Budget Office, which is responsible for independently costing policy proposals. One Nation recently came under scrutiny from the PBO for what the office found to be a massive underestimate of the cost of a group of policies. One Nation Victorian leader Warren Pickering and federal leader Pauline Hanson in Melbourne on Monday. Jason South Asked how voters could trust the minor party to deliver financially stable and transparent policies when it had refused to release costings and use the PBO, Pickering said the independent agency had been inaccurate over the past decade.



“We know there’s some great people at the PBO, but the reality is, when has one of their cost projections been accurate in the last decade?” he said. “Why would we waste energy, effort and resources utilising a system that we know they don’t have access to everything they need? “No, we won’t be engaging in that until we have an opportunity to blow the books open ourselves and revolutionise the way that that budgets are done in this state.” The PBO was established in 2018 to provide all MPs with independent expertise, including policy costings around elections. It acts as the state’s fiscal umpire and is staffed by economists and researchers who use financial modelling systems and can access public service information, making its predictions comparable to government costings. One Nation has had access to PBO services since its MP Rikkie-Lee Tyrell was elected to the upper house in 2022.



Asked about Pickering’s comments, Parliamentary Budget Officer Xavier Rimmer encouraged all parties to make use of the office’s unique insights. One Nation’s Pickering, Colleen Harkin and Hanson. Jason South “While there are alternatives to the PBO’s election costing service, only the PBO’s service combines expertise and independence, with comparability across parties,” Rimmer said. One Nation’s refusal to release costings for its policies raises major questions ahead of an election in which debt is a major concern for voters and a threat to the state’s prosperity. Last month, One Nation was forced to clarify its costings for proposed family policies after PBO costings commissioned by the Liberal Party found they could blow out by more than $500 million.



One Nation deputy leader Colleen Harkin initially told reporters the party’s plan to cover out-of-pocket pregnancy expenses for women in public hospitals, give $2000 payments to pregnant mothers in the private system and provide two $150 sport vouchers for school-aged children every year would cost $136 million over a four-year term. Related Article Victorian election The government just quietly ‘dumped’ 192 reports at once. Here’s what they reveal But at the request of the Liberal Party, the PBO independently costed the plan at $688.7 million – $553 million more than One Nation’s estimate. The independent costings showed the sports voucher policy alone would be likely to cost taxpayers $471.3 million. The figures prompted Harkin to revise her position, telling The Australian the estimate was per year, not over four years. This would still create a $144.7 million shortfall on the PBO costings. Pickering said on Monday that the party would not be making any costings public because it first wanted to conduct an audit of the government’s finances.



“We believe that the books are sufficiently cooked to warrant a full investigation,” he said. “Now, having done that, we will then resource, allocate according to need.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: State teammate stakes a claim for Labuschagne’s Test spot as selectors eye future
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket State teammate stakes a claim for Labuschagne’s Test spot as selectors eye future Nick Wright November 2, 2026 — 1:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Far removed from the scrutiny that surrounded Australia’s horror capitulation against South Africa, an unheralded southpaw was building his case for a call-up at a time when the nation’s under-siege batting line-up has been berated across the cricketing landscape. Jack Clayton played a lone hand in wrestling Queensland back into their Sheffield Shield clash with Victoria at the Gabba, bringing up his seventh first-class century early on Monday morning to thwart a bowling attack boasting fringe international prospect Fergus O’Neill, seven-Test spinner Todd Murphy and one-day international representative Will Sutherland. Jack Clayton is scoring runs at the right time. AAPIMAGE The 27-year-old left-hander played a composed knock in Brisbane, bringing up his ton from 194 deliveries while striking eight boundaries. He was dismissed for 104, as his attempted cut shot flew to Campbell Kellaway at gully off the bowling of Matt Hennig. His dismissal left the Bulls at 6-211, before they ultimately succumbed for 280 in response to Victoria’s first innings of 307.



Clayton’s knock may just be the most timely of his career, as he seeks to thrust his name forward as an option to usurp his state teammate Marnus Labuschagne in the baggy green. Labuschagne’s place appears untenable at No.3 after averaging 21.83 in the 2-1 series defeat in South Africa at the end of a period in which he has gone more than three years without a Test century. Rookie Cooper Connolly failed to ignite coming in for the dropped Beau Webster, but the whole batting unit have faced criticism after being rolled for 99 and 111 in the second and third Tests. Marnus Labuschagne barren tour of South Africa has heightened the pressure on his place in the Test team. Getty Images Unless selectors are willing to move either Steve Smith or third-Test centurion Josh Inglis to No.3, they will be on the hunt for a top-order specialist ahead of the four-match series against New Zealand should Labuschagne’s form woes – averaging 28.87 with one century since the start of 2023 – result in his axing. Clayton, who struck half centuries in each of Queensland’s first two Shield games of the summer, now trails only New South Wales opener Ollie Davies for runs this season. The Queenslander and former Brisbane Lions AFL academy prospect’s career average sits at 39 to be one of the few batsmen in the country with an average near 40.



A reshuffle of either Travis Head or Matthew Renshaw back to the middle order could open the door for Victorian Sam Harper, who’s stint as an opener since the latter stages of the 2025/26 summer (scoring two centuries and a 93 after the Big Bash) has reaped rewards. Related Article Analysis

Steve Smith Steve Smith’s wizardry can be developed. These cricket experts reveal how The wicketkeeper, who was called into the Test squad in South Africa following a century in India for Australia A, scored a first-innings 63 before being clean bowled by Cameron Gannon shouldering arms on day one. He has since been called into Australia’s T20 squad to face England later this month, while his partner at the top of Victoria’s order – 14-Test opener Marcus Harris – supported him with a measured 56. Kellaway made 64 batting at No.3, however appears to be a long-term proposition, as does teenage ODI representative Ollie Peake (0). Neither Sam Konstas nor Kurtis Patterson impressed in New South Wales’ comprehensive loss to Tasmania as the Blues were dismissed for 202 and 144, however each have centuries already this campaign and have Test runs on the board. South Australia’s Nathan McSweeney, who struck a one-day hundred for Australia A on the subcontinent, boasts a 50-over ton and two Shield half-centuries thus far this season.



Beardman’s time nears as selectors look to future Jon Pierik A West Australian fast bowler mentored by Dennis Lillee has been all but anointed as a future Test player after being drafted into Australia’s one-day international squad to face England. Mahli Beardman has already played T20s for Australia earlier this year. Getty Images Pace ace Mahli Beardman, 21, was named in a 14-man ODI squad on Monday that will play three matches against England this month, beginning in Perth next Friday.



Beardman has battled lower-back stress fractures through his young career but impressed on the recent Australia A tour of India, claiming 4-23 and notching speeds in excess of 140km/h in his third game back from injury. Australia have rested frontline quicks Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood for the series, ensuring Beardman will have ample opportunity to show what he is capable of. Australia ODI and T20 squads vs England ODI squad: Mitchell Marsh (capt), Xavier Bartlett, Mahli Beardman, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Jack Edwards, Cameron Green, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Spencer Johnson, Ollie Peake, Matthew Renshaw, Liam Scott, Adam Zampa T20 Squad: Mitchell Marsh (capt), Xavier Bartlett, Mahli Beardman, Nikhil Chaudhary, Tim David, Joel Davies, Jack Edwards, Nathan Ellis, Jake Fraser-McGurk, Sam Harper, Spencer Johnson, Mitchell Owen, Lachlan Shaw, Adam Zampa Selection chairman George Bailey said Beardman, who has had pace great Lillee as his mentor since his mid-teenage years, was firmly in his panel’s plans. “Mahli Beardman’s recent performances for Australia A were impressive and we are incredibly excited for his return to the national team across the ODI and T20 formats,” Bailey said.



“We think he can continue to develop into an all-format player across the coming years.” Related Article Australian cricket Coach calls for calm, keeps door ajar for Labuschagne, as Healy turns torch on selectors Beardman has also been named in the T20 squad, which will play five games against England, beginning November 21. Mitch Marsh will skipper both teams. Emerging batting star Ollie Peake is the only Victorian in the ODI squad. Xavier Bartlett and Spencer Johnson will join Beardman as the specialist fast bowlers for the ODI series, while all-rounders Jack Edwards and Liam Scott can also provide pace. Victorian Sam Harper and NSW wicketkeeper-batsman Lachlan Shaw are potential debutants in the 14-man T20 squad. Travis Head and Cameron Green are among those rested.



“We are in the middle of a highly demanding phase of our schedule,” Bailey said. “Our multi-format players are transitioning directly from the tour of South Africa into an ODI and T20 series, leaving a narrow window to ensure the squad is physically prepared and fresh for the upcoming New Zealand Test series. “Then, from when the Test players assemble in Perth through to the conclusion of the 150th anniversary Test against England, the team will have been on the road for more than 100 days.“ Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Crocodile spotted near Rocky rowing venue, but Premier unconcerned
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Crocodile spotted near Rocky rowing venue, but Premier unconcerned William Davis November 2, 2026 — 1:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Queensland’s premier says he has no concerns about the viability of rowing in Rockhampton at the 2032 Games after a crocodile was sighted near the Fitzroy River. A photo shared by the North Rockhampton Golf Club on Sunday showed a croc just off the 11th hole, on Splitters Creek which runs off the Fitzroy. A manager at the venue told this masthead the photograph was taken by a member, and claimed animal was significantly smaller than it appeared in the image. The crocodile photograph shared by the North Rockhampton Golf Club near the Fitzroy River hasn’t worried premier David Crisafulli. North Rockhampton Golf Club “It has been a resident … for the past 12 months,” president Brian Phelan said.



“It has never been a problem, members and visitors are very aware of its presence with signage throughout the course.” He described it as a “baby crocodile” and estimated its length at about 1.2 metres, while a report from local ABC estimated the animal was 3 metres. The presence of crocodiles in the proposed Olympic venue has raised eyebrows. Sylvia Liber Asked if the government had concerns about the sighting on Monday morning, Premier David Crisafulli said: “No.” He said he believed the Fitzroy River was a world-class venue that held excellent rowing events.



“It’s a magnificent community, and they’ll do it very well,” Crisafulli added. Related Article Wildlife Was a crocodile really spotted in Noosa? Some locals think so, but this expert is dubious Transport and Main Roads Minister Brent Mickelberg said later in the morning he was also confident the venue would be safe for rowers at the Olympics. “I challenge anyone who thinks rowing can’t be delivered in Rocky to head up to Rocky and have a look,” he told reporters at Central Station in Brisbane. “The rowing club on the banks of the Fitzroy there is exceptional, and I’m sure it’ll be a great success in 2032.”



The government’s decision to push for rowing in the Fitzroy River has attracted pushback from some, and been a major talking point in Olympic preparations. Related Article Updated

Brisbane 2032 Olympics Rocky rowing course passes assessment ‘with flying colours’ The Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club is directly opposite the North Rockhampton Golf Club. Dr Ross Dwyer, a senior lecturer in animal ecology at the University of Sunshine Coast, said crocodile sightings in the area were not unusual. He added the animals would likely be less active during the winter months when the Olympics would be held, though reiterated crocodiles near humans were always a threat.



“They’re cold-blooded … if it is winter time, crocodiles are less mobile,” Dwyer said. “They’re certainly still moving around, and you would certainly want to be careful. “I’m sure I’m sure efforts will be done to make sure it’s safe at that time.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

This week’s picks include Stephen Graham as a menacing serial killer in the worthy thriller Nocturne, plus Hamish Blake tries to lend a hand in Unskilled Adult, while Making Marie Antoinette goes behind the scenes of Sofia Coppola’s iconic film and Ethan Hawke returns in the comedy noir The Lowdown. Nocturne ★★★ (Apple TV) Filmed shortly after Adolescence rattled the world, Nocturne is a victory lap for Stephen Graham, who elevates Apple TV’s latest indistinct thriller into a worthy watch with his menacing portrayal of a manipulative, meticulous serial killer. Renowned for raw portrayals of men at the brink of collapse long before co-creating and starring in Adolescence (This Is England, Boiling Point), the British actor tempers decades of raw energy into Jurek Walter – a psychopath who presents as diabolically relaxed and controlled. Locked away in a psychiatric facility after unleashing terror on a small Pennsylvanian town, Walter relishes his powers of manipulation. In Nocturne’s opening scene, he successfully taunts – using just words – a neighbouring inmate into an act of self-harm. Stephen Graham stars in new Apple TV thriller Nocturne. Apple TV For that reason, he’s not supposed to talk to anyone, though he breaks out a giggle and creepy childish voice to lure in new nurse Karl (Rory Culkin, the younger brother of Macaulay and Kieran). Karl is immediately identified as an easy target, the sunken sadness in his eyes giving away a weakness: an empathy not yet eroded by the job. Where a lesser actor might have pushed harder on the creepy voice without reason, Graham uses it only how Walter would: as a trap. Walter’s hackneyed stereotype of a patient needing help proves catnip for a do-gooder like Karl.



Editor's pick Spoilers

Streaming This episode was the best romcom of the year. I wish TV had more like it Graham’s magnetism wouldn’t work without Nocturne’s steady reveal of Walter’s masterplan, the audience discovering puzzle pieces as investigators do. Creators Rowan Joffé (Tin Star) and John Hlavin (Shooter) clearly have a great sense for pacing, never relying on the Scandi-noir gloom of the show’s source material – Swedish novel series Joona Linna – to provide suspense alone. What is immediately clear, both to viewers and grizzled ex-cop Jonah (Liev Schreiber), is that nothing is by chance. When a missing boy suspected to be one of Walter’s victims walks out emaciated from a Pensylvannia forest three years after Walter was imprisoned, Jonah and the audience both know that it’s the first move of a bloody chess game. Rory Culkin as Karl, a do-gooder who Graham’s killer sets in his sights. Apple TV He and his goddaughter FBI agent Saga (Zazie Beetz, Joker) volunteer to help find the boy’s sister, kidnapped at the same time. Both scarred by Walter’s crimes, the two regularly break protocol to follow their instinct, including Saga going undercover as a patient at Walter’s asylum. Like many Apple TV shows, Nocturne is solid but unassuming. It doesn’t puff up its importance with prestige flair, nor is it insultingly twist-led or designed for second-screen viewing. Across the seven of 10 episodes available for review, Nocturne’s cop cliches and clunkier moments were easy to forgive, with Graham and the cast – including Chrissy Metz (This Is Us) as the returning boy’s mother – firing on all fronts. Just a man and his truck: Hamish Blake goes all tradie in his new show, Unskilled Adult. Stan



Unskilled Adult (Stan*) ★★★ Hamish Blake’s new show, essentially a series of DIY tasks, is baffling even to Blake at first. In the pilot, he’s understandably overwhelmed over how to use power tools and build planter boxes to a tight deadline while cracking jokes. Unskilled Adult’s premise is that Blake, after decades as a comedian and TV personality, is now a 44-year-old with no practical life skills outside of talking – something non-famous people can also relate to, given Google’s robbed our need to retain basic information. Related Article ★★

Review Another cookie-cutter comedian game show? Yep, and we’re sick of them Across each of the show’s eight 50-minute episodes, Blake and a rotating cast of comedians and entertainers take on an odd-job sent in by a stranger that they possess none of the know-how or technical skills to pull off. Sophie Monk and Dom Littrich (Inspired Unemployed) help Blake take on panel beating; Anne Edmonds and husband Lloyd Langford work on welding a surfboard stand for a surf-lifesaving club; Ryan Shelton and Susie Youssef cater for an 80-person wedding. After the first episode, Unskilled Adult is far funnier than a show featuring several paint-drying scenes should be. If anything, that the show grows into itself mirroring Blake’s compounding skill-set and confidence each episode is genuinely quite sweet to witness. While its low-fi looks and casual hang-out tone feel much more better-suited to YouTube than a standard TV show, I suspect it’ll find most of its audience via social snippets anyway. Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman on set during the filming of Marie Antoinette. Sofia Coppola



Making Marie Antoinette (Mubi) ★★★★★ Marking 20 years since Sofia Coppola’s subversively stylised masterpiece, Making Marie Antoinette is a posthumous documentary from her mother Eleanor Coppola – best known for Hearts of Darkness, a behind-the-scenes look at Apocalypse Now’s notorious production. With far less drama on Sofia’s set, this is a much more gentle watch. It’s more like a Coppola family vacation video, albeit with 1700s costuming. Eleanor’s admiration for her daughter’s creative talents shines through every shot, though the film, finished by Sofia after Eleanor’s death in 2024, is really a two-way tribute. It’s immensely touching and understated, with Diane Lane narrating from Eleanor’s diaries. Anthony Phelan stars in Storm Bird. Storm Bird (Stan*) ★★★ Set and shot in Far North Queensland, Storm Bird is an intriguing debut from Australian filmmaker James Ivor, co-directed with Eryk Lenartowicz. Ivor plays Jack, a laconic construction worker who, facing jail-time, focuses on drinking. Those plans are interrupted when he saves his older neighbour, classical composer Richard (Anthony Phelan, Top of the Lake), from a heart attack. Having previously written off Richard as pompous, Jack is drawn into his life – as is Carla (Serena Ven Sandalwood), a writer visiting from New York. A sweet character study, suffused with tropical heat and small, well-studied details. It Gets Worse, a new British sitcom from comedian Leo Reich (right). Binge



It Gets Worse (Binge) ★★★★ For once, the comparisons to Girls are apt – and not just because British comedian Leo Reich’s sardonic sitcom about 20-somethings in London features Lena Dunham as a guest star. With six episodes under 30 minutes, It Gets Worse is as brash, bold and unflinching as its protagonist Ethan (Reich), a self-obsessed gay man who, as per the narration by Zadie Smith, has had “one of the easiest lives in human history”. The messiness – outrageous sex scenes, anarchist warehouses, boring boyfriends – is fun but, as with Girls, there’s a generational gut-punch to the chaos. Betty Gilpin and Ethan Hawke in season two of The Lowdown. FX The Lowdown (Disney+) ★★★★ Ethan Hawke’s charisma paved over the uneven edges of The Lowdown’s first season, a comedy-noir set in Oklahoma from Sterlin Harjo (Reservation Dogs) focused on Lee Raybon (Hawke), a shaggy amateur journalist and deadbeat dad who follows a head-spinning and history-spanning conspiracy through history. Season two streamlines things with one question: how can a man disappear from jail records? To find out, Lee teams up with Ginger (Betty Gilpin, GLOW): a glamorous public defender who, much like the audience, is equally attracted and frustrated by Lee’s reckless passion for the truth. *Stan is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead.

World.title: Westpac expects 11 per cent house price fall, posts $6.8 billion profit
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeBig four Westpac expects 11 per cent house price fall, posts $6.8 billion profit Millie Muroi Updated November 2, 2026 — 1:13pm ,first published November 2, 2026 — 8:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Westpac expects interest rates to remain “elevated” into 2027 and house prices to fall by nearly 11 per cent by March as it reported a $6.8 billion profit. On Monday, the country’s oldest bank said the Australian economy was holding up “relatively well” on the back of strong business investment, but that price growth remained above the Reserve Bank’s target. Westpac has posted a $6.8 billion profit. Eamon Gallagher “This is presenting challenges for many households and businesses, although impacts are uneven across the economy,” it said in an announcement to the ASX ahead of the next RBA meeting on Tuesday, when the bank is widely tipped to raise rates for the fifth time this year. Westpac also said it expected house prices to fall by 10.9 per cent from March 2026 to March 2027. In September, house prices nationally were 5.2 per cent below the peak reached in March.



Westpac’s $6.8 billion profit in the year to September was down 1 per cent from the previous year. The bank’s net interest margin – a key measure of profitability – fell by 3 percentage points to 1.86 per cent for the second half of 2026 as lending competition remained strong and more customer accounts qualified for savings bonus rates. Westpac said it expected house prices to fall by 10.9 per cent. Sitthixay Ditthavong This was partly offset by stronger business and institutional lending, which grew 12 per cent and 18 per cent, respectively. “Business investment has strengthened, supported by infrastructure, data centres and the energy transition,” Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller said in an analyst and media call following the latest results.



Despite cost of living pressures, the bank said the share of mortgage balances in hardship “remained low” at 0.6 per cent. Related Article Property prices Homes losing $9000 a month as RBA mulls another rate hike “In the space of six months, we’ve seen four rate rises, likely a fifth, we’ve had Hormuz, oil, Middle East conflicts, cost of living challenges ... so it does make sense that there would be a shift in hardships,” Miller said. “Hardship has picked up a little bit … but it feels incredibly proportionate and appropriate in the context of what has gone on.” While there are several reasons people can enter into hardship, including divorce, injury, death or losing a job, Miller said the only one that had increased in the past 12 months was overcommitment. “What’s driving that [overcommitment] is just how fast things have moved,” he said. “Three rate cuts, and then 12 months later, four rate rises.”



Westpac provided more than 42,000 tailored financial hardship assistance and disaster relief packages over the year, but said more than 60 per cent of assisted customers required less than three months of hardship support. The bank said credit quality metrics “continue to reflect customer resilience” despite cost of living pressures and higher interest rates. “We are cautious of the impacts of the ongoing Middle East conflict and higher rate environment, with the balance sheet provisions well-placed for potential deterioration,” Miller said. “The unemployment rate will continue to be the major determinant of mortgage asset quality.” Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller. Peter Rae In September, the unemployment rate hit 4.7 per cent, the highest level since October 2021 but below historical standards.



The bank said while consumer spending had slowed marginally, it remained at a “reasonable rate of growth” by historical standards and that businesses continue to show resilience. Mortgage applications were 15 per cent lower in the fourth quarter than a year ago, but total applications remained above their five-year average. Related Article Big four NAB slashes 2500 jobs amid fears other banks will swing the axe The share of accounts held by customers ahead on their mortgage repayments – including offset account balances – remained steady at 86 per cent. Nearly four in ten customers are more than two years ahead on their repayments, about one in ten are on-time and only 1 per cent are behind on their repayments. However, Westpac’s credit impairment provisions – money set aside for potential losses when borrowers fail to repay loans – increased to $5.2 billion with the bank citing “economic and geopolitical uncertainty” affecting energy-intensive sectors and discretionary spending.



UBS head of Australian bank research John Storey said Westpac’s results showed weaker revenue in the second half was offset by the bank’s cost discipline and lower than expected credit impairment charges. “The result confirms competitive pressure remains material, with deposit competition combined with lending shaving 5 basis points off [the bank’s] core net interest margin,” he said. The bank will pay a final dividend of 77 cents a share, taking the full-year dividend to $1.54, up 1 per cent from the previous year. Shares in Westpac were trading mostly flat around midday after an initial jump following the latest results. World.title: Significant concerns held for missing Aucklander Luke Ganz after backpack found in water
World.content:
Police say they have significant concerns for the wellbeing of missing Aucklander Luke Ganz.

Ganz was last seen on Queen Street at about 4.46pm on 29 October travelling south between the intersections with Wyndham and Victoria streets.

The 34-year-old was wearing a blue temporary overall suit.

Detective Senior Sergeant Martin Friend says police are now appealing for information about his whereabouts.

Luke Ganz. Supplied / Police

"Luke has several distinctive tattoos across his forearms and neck, one of which being a wooden cross on the centre of his neck.

"Just after midday on 31 October, Police located a backcountry-style backpack in water at the entrance to the Auckland Viaduct.

"A search of the backpack has located documentation relating to Luke, which increases our concerns for his wellbeing."

World.title: Crown already has the man who killed Kyle Whorrall, says defence lawyer
World.content:
The Crown already has the man who killed Kyle Whorrall, says a defence lawyer, who argues that his client had no part in the American student's murder.

Whorrall, 33, was left with a "a catastrophic and ultimately fatal wound" following an attack in April 2025 at the stop in Auckland's Meadowbank. He died in hospital shortly after.

One teenager has already pleaded guilty to Whorall's murder and to aggravated robbery.

Another four teens are currently standing trial in the High Court at Auckland having pleaded not guilty.

The Crown said Whorrall was on his way back from a routine evening shopping trip when he was attacked with a machete.

Paul Borich KC, who is acting for one of the defendants, said there was no evidence his client knew there had been a plan to rob and attack Whorrall that night.

There had also been no evidence presented to the jury identifying which of the four defendants was the second person seen at the bus stop alongside the murderer.

"There are good, legitimate arguments for all of the four persons who are on trial who could fit into that number two slot and it depends on the parts of [witness evidence] you like and the parts you don't like."

It is alleged the five young men were driving in Borich's client's mothers car. Borich asked the jury to consider why his client would get out to participate in the attack if he was the one driving.

"If the Crown case is that there was a plan to rob Kyle Whorrall in the bus stop to do a street robbery, effectively pull the car over, park up so that you can do the getaway... is it really suggested that the getaway driver's going to get out to do the robbery?

"Not only do the Crown have a plan now that [the defendant] is supposed to know about, but it's a particularly dumb one."

Borich also said his client's stepfather, who was called as a key Crown witness, was a self-confessed compulsive liar.

"For obvious reasons [the witness] is a person with nil, zero credibility at all," Borich said.

He told the jury the man responsible for his murder has already pleaded guilty.

"You have your murderer, I suggest it could not be clearer. He is the user of the machete," Borich said.

Panama Le'Au'Anae - the lawyer for another of the defendants - told the jury the reason he had not said very much during the trial is because there had not been much he needed to address.

"There hasn't been the evidence that has met the level that would satisfy you that my client was involved in an aggravated robbery nor was he involved in a murder," he said. "The problem with the Crown case is that it is full of holes, it's full of gaps."

Le'Au'Anae urged the jury to put aside any feelings of sympathy or prejudice they may have.

"It would be very easy to be sympathetic to Mr Whorrall and his family, you wouldn't be human otherwise. You might look down and see these four young men in the dock and think, 'young guys, shouldn't have been doing that'."

He urged the jury to put any emotions they may have to one side and to look at the evidence in a cool, calm manner.

World.title: Nine arrested during 'unacceptable' Rugby League World Cup celebrations
World.content:
Over-exuberant rugby league celebrations have seen nine arrested for disorder-related offences.

Rugby League World Cup pool play reached a climax over the weekend, with a much-anticipated showdown between Tonga and Samoa, with both teams assured of progress to next week's semifinals.

Tonga prevailed 20-18 in a thriller at Sydney, earning top spot in their pool and the right to face NZ Kiwis for a spot in the final. Samoa will take on champions Australia in the other semi, edging England on points differential.

South Auckland police were kept busy controlling the emotions of tens of thousands of fans on this side of the Tasman, deploying 160 staff to the task on Sunday.

"It was concerning for police to witness individuals putting themselves and others in harm's way with high-risk behaviours, including running into roads, poor driving choices and public intoxication," said Counties Manukau district commander Superintendent Shanan Gray.

"In some areas, excessive noise from loudspeakers and car horns continued into the early hours of the morning.

"This is unacceptable, and it has a significant impact on the wellbeing of local residents and businesses."

On Saturday, police intervened, when hundreds of cars formed convoys that blocked intersections and generated loud noise in Tauranga, as communities expressed their patriotism.

Gray appealed to fans to think about how their actions impacted the community.

World.title: Youth moving overseas will cost NZ $76b in GDP, say Greens
World.content:
The Greens say a surge in young people moving overseas since 2023 will cost the country $76 billion in GDP, $40 billion in lost earnings and $6 billion in foregone net tax over the next four decades.

The party commissioned Victor Consulting - run by Clint Smith, who has previously worked for the Labour and Green parties - to look at the country's financial losses as a result of more young people moving overseas.

The Greens said the findings showed the need for government investment in job creation to keep young people in New Zealand.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407766300112

Victor Consulting used official sources to estimate lost public investment, net tax revenue, earnings from work, and GDP.

The study found 77,500 New Zealanders aged 18-30 left the country "long term" between 2023 and 2025, which is 60 percent more than the 2016-2019 average of about 16,000 a year.

It said $29 billion of public spending on health and education had gone into this group before they left, and $12 billion of that would be lost for good with those who do not return. (The paper said Treasury observed 43 percent of young people who leave, never return).

The research said the government would lose $4 billion in tax over their working lives: $18 billion in net tax, partly offset by $14 billion of Superannuation and health costs avoided.

It said New Zealand would forego $104 billion in earnings from work and $196 billion of GDP over the next four decades.

"Compared to pre-Covid levels of emigration, this represents a loss of $6 billion in lost public investment and net tax, $40 billion in earning, and $76 billion in GDP."

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said young people were following the jobs.

"It's normal for a number of young people to want to go on their OE. But what we've seen in the last three years is not normal," she said.

"We do not need to wave goodbye to young people who don't actually want to leave this country. We can have a sensible Government that invests in improving lives, lowering the cost of living, stimulating employment and economic resilience."

World.title: Fires, rubbish and roaming dogs plague Gulf Harbour Country Club's fairways
World.content:
A spate of fires, piles of rubbish and a pack of roaming dogs are all plaguing Auckland's once-prestigious Gulf Harbour Country Club.

The club was abruptly closed in 2023, and the main building burned down in 2024, in circumstances Fire and Emergency described as suspicious.

Since then, Auckland Council has been in a stalemate with the owners of the club over its future, and now a community trust is considering buying it.

As well as two fires in recent months, rubbish has piled up and residents have reported a pack of roaming dogs that belonged to a squatter living there.

Dalen McLean, volunteer coordinator for the Gulf Harbour Community Trust. RNZ / Luka Forman

It was "sad for the community to see it be degraded", volunteer coordinator for the Gulf Harbour Community Trust Dalen McLean said.

The trust had set up regular volunteer days to mow the course and keep weeds in order, he said.

"The team has cleared the banks all along here. You can see the piles of dead gorse just waiting to be collected up and moved away. So that was a fantastic team effort."

The Gulf Harbour Country Club was once a prestigious course, played on by Lydia Ko and host to the World Cup of Golf and two New Zealand Opens.

But despite that history, the owners of the property, Long River Investments, did not seem interested in maintaining it.

Auckland councillor John Watson at the Gulf Harbour Country Club. RNZ / Luka Forman

Local Auckland councillor John Watson believed it had been left to go to ruin to get around a 999-year covenant on the land that it had to be kept as green space.

"To make this look like an abandoned chunk of land that you can't do anything with. Both have failed; the community maintains the land," he said.

The director of Long River Investments, Wayne Bailey, appears to have moved to Australia and RNZ was unable to contact him.

Auckland Council community manager Rachel Kelleher said the council was owed $44,209 by the company and was seeking a further $244,631 in court for demolition costs.

Watson said that with the owners not willing to cooperate, the council was in a stalemate over the course's future.

In the meantime, he worried about fires at the course getting closer to property.

"There's a real concern that these people aren't going to stop and the fact that they're getting away with it means effectively, given the psychology of arson, that they're encouraged to keep going."

Rubbish gathers in the remains of a building at the Gulf Harbour Country Club. RNZ / Luka Forman

Local Matt Travell said people in the community had also felt threatened by a pack of around six roaming dogs at the golf course.

"I can't say whether they're dangerous or not. But definitely they're not under control at all times. There was an incident where the pack of dogs surrounded a guy in a mobility scooter and he was afraid to leave in case they chased him."

However Koa Koangi, who has been living in a caravan at the property, said his dogs were not harmful and he kept the biggest ones tied up.

Travell said the dogs and rubbish at the course were just symptoms of the bigger problem, and he too pointed the finger at the course's owners.

World.title: Fiji PM Rabuka delays vote on Constitution Bill after mounting pressure
World.content:
Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has given in to public pressure and decided to extend the timeline for a major constitutional reform process only a day after he confirmed that he would table a bill to change the country's constitution.

In a complete U-turn from his position on tabling the controversial Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 this week, Rabuka announced on the floor of parliament on Monday that the Special Parliamentary Committee on the bill would "table its review report at a later sitting date".

The prime minister did not provide a date for when that would be, stating only that the final report would be presented back to parliament in "due time".

"During the extension or extended period, we intend to listen to more submissions from the public, and also give time to our very hard-working parliamentary staff, who have been supporting us in the collection, collation, and compilation of the final report to be presented back to parliament in due time," Rabuka said.

He had previously told RNZ Pacific that he had not announced an election date - which has a hard deadline of 6 Febraury 2027 - due to the constitutional reform process that was running in parallel.

Rabuka also replaced his coalition partner and leader of the National Federation Party (NFP), Biman Prasad, as a member of the committee after Prasad had announced on Saturday that the party would vote against the bill.

"Constitutional legitimacy cannot be sacrificed for political expediency," Prasad said over the weekend.

"There should be no shortcuts or fast-tracking of any constitutional process.

"We will no longer participate in the special parliamentary committee nor will I be a signatory to the report of the committee to parliament next week," he said.

Rabuka needed a two-thirds majority - at least 36 votes - to pass the bill through a 53-seat parliament following the passing of two MPs from the original 55-member parliament.

With the NFP and the Social Democratic Liberal Party (Sodelpa) both having objections about the process and the contents of the bill, it meant Rabuka was not likely to get the numbers required for the bill to pass the third reading.
